lead: Two frightened men stand at the centre of today's readings. Abraham is afraid of a foreign king and misjudges him; yet God still uses Abraham's prayer to heal that king's house. Peter is afraid of the wind and begins to sink; yet the hand of Jesus is there at once. The short Epistle (2 Thessalonians 3:16–18) gives the word that both needed: “Now may the Lord of peace himself give you peace at all times in all ways.” This week carries us across the middle of the Great Fast, and it begins with what to do when fear takes over.

set: Abraham has come to Gerar, in the south of the land, and has said of Sarah, “She is my sister.” King Abimelech takes her into his house. In Saturday's reading God warned the king in a dream, told him that Abraham was a prophet, and said that Abraham would pray for him (20:7). Today's passage opens on the following morning. Genesis tells a similar story in 12:10–20 and again of Isaac in 26:6–11. In each, the bearer of the promise puts the promise at risk, and God protects it.
str: v. 8: the king tells his servants, and they are afraid.
vv. 9–13: the king questions Abraham; Abraham explains himself.
vv. 14–16: the king restores Sarah and gives gifts.
vv. 17–18: Abraham prays, and God heals.
kw: In the Old Testament this means reverence that shapes conduct, not terror. Abraham assumed that Gerar had none of it. The story shows the king and his servants fearing God while Abraham fears men.

Literally “a covering of the eyes”. The Hebrew phrase in verse 16 is obscure. It seems to mean a public settlement that closes the eyes of others to any suspicion against Sarah, and the NRSV gives this sense.
Verses 7 and 17 of this chapter are the first places in the Bible where this common Hebrew verb for prayer appears, and here it is prayer for someone else.
vv: What have you done to us?
The rebuke comes from the outsider, and the man of promise has no reply ready. Scripture lets a foreign king speak the truth to Abraham.
I did it because I thought, There is no fear of God at all in this place
Fear made him judge a whole people without knowing them. The events of the chapter prove him wrong.
Besides, she is indeed my sister, the daughter of my father but not the daughter of my mother

Abraham offers a half-truth that protected only himself, while it left Sarah exposed. The text reports his defence without approving it. The rebuke of verse 9 stands, and the king's gifts in verse 16 are for clearing Sarah's name.
Then Abraham prayed to God; and God healed Abimelech
The one who was in the wrong is the one asked to pray, and God hears him. His calling does not depend on his having behaved well this time. This is grace, and it should humble him.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the prayer of intercession is a mark of a heart in harmony with God's mercy (CCC 2635). The Church reads such stories not to excuse sin but to see God's fidelity at work through weak servants. In the Great Fast this is a word of hope: a failure in one's own conduct is no reason to stop praying for others.

set: The scene follows straight on from the feeding of the five thousand (14:13–21). Jesus had tried to go away alone after he heard of John the Baptist's death (14:13), and only now does he find the time to pray. He sends the disciples across the lake at evening, and for most of the night they struggle against the wind. Mark 6:45–52 and John 6:16–21 also tell of the walking on the water. Only Matthew tells of Peter's own walk.
str: vv. 22–23: Jesus sends the disciples off and goes up to pray.
vv. 24–27: the boat in difficulty; Jesus comes and speaks.
vv. 28–31: Peter walks, sinks and is caught.
vv. 32–33: the wind stops, and those in the boat worship him.
kw: An ordinary way of saying “it's me”, but in Greek these are also the words of the divine name (Exodus 3:14 in the Greek Old Testament). Matthew's readers would hear both senses, since only God walks upon the sea (Job 9:8).
A word Matthew likes. Jesus uses it of disciples, of people who have some faith. It is a rebuke, but it does not put them outside.
To be drawn two ways. In the New Testament it appears only here and in 28:17, where the disciples worship the risen Jesus and some doubt. Doubt and worship can be found in the same boat.
vv: But immediately Jesus spoke to them and said, “Take heart, it is I; do not be afraid.”
The first thing he does is to speak. The wind has not yet stopped, and his voice comes before the calm.
Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the water.
Peter does not ask to walk on water as a display. He asks to be told to come. It is a good way of asking.
But when he noticed the strong wind, he became frightened, and beginning to sink, he cried out, “Lord, save me!”
The wind was as strong as it had been before he got out of the boat. What changed is where he looked. His three words are a complete prayer, and it is answered.
Truly you are the Son of God.
Those who were terrified in verse 26 now worship. They reach this confession through fear and rescue, not by avoiding them.
ch: Tertullian saw in the little ship a figure of the Church, tossed by the waves of persecution and temptation while the Lord seems to be away, and calmed by his coming (On Baptism 12, in substance). St Augustine says that Peter stands for all of us: by the Lord's strength he walks, by his own weakness he sinks, and then he must call out (Sermon 76, in substance). So the Church takes the scene as a picture of her own life. She is not spared the crossing, but she is not left alone in it.

qa: Did Abraham do wrong, and does the Bible approve of it?

Yes, he did wrong, and no, the Bible does not approve. He exposed his wife to danger to protect himself, and the king's words in verse 9, “You have done things to me that ought not to be done”, stand without a reply. Scripture does not make its heroes perfect. God's faithfulness to Abraham is the point of the story, not Abraham's conduct.
study: Whom have I judged in advance, as Abraham judged Gerar, without knowing them? Is there someone I have wronged for whom I could pray each day of this week?
Where do I look when the wind is strong? Can I make “Lord, save me” my prayer for the rest of the Fast?

lead: God keeps his word in today's first reading, and an old woman laughs for joy. The Epistle (Galatians 3:26–29) tells the baptized that they too belong to this family: “if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to the promise.” The Gospel then asks the hard question. What happens when a town sees God's mighty works close up and carries on as before? God's gift is sure; our answer to it is the part still open.

set: The promise of a son has run through Abraham's story since chapter 12. Three chapters earlier the Lord said at Mamre, “Is anything too wonderful for the Lord?” (18:14), and Sarah laughed behind the tent door (18:12). After many years of waiting, and after Abraham's failure at Gerar, the child comes. The text tells the fulfilment plainly and quietly: no angel appears and no vision is seen.
str: vv. 1–2: the Lord does as he said.
vv. 3–5: naming and circumcision; Abraham's age.
vv. 6–7: Sarah's two sayings.
v. 8: the child is weaned, and there is a feast.
kw: The Hebrew verb in verse 1 can mean to visit, or to attend to. It is used when God comes in to act on behalf of someone (as in Exodus 3:16). The NRSV has “dealt with”.
The name means “he laughs” or “may he laugh”. Abraham laughed at the promise (17:17), and so did Sarah (18:12). Their disbelief and their joy are held in one word.
An appointed time, the same word the Lord used in 18:14 (“the set time”). God's delay was never forgetfulness.
vv: The Lord dealt with Sarah as he had said, and the Lord did for Sarah as he had promised.
The sentence says the same thing twice, and verse 2 says it a third time. The writer wants one fact to stand out: God did what he said.
And Abraham circumcised his son Isaac when he was eight days old, as God had commanded him.
Abraham obeys the covenant command of 17:12. The gift is received within the covenant, and the child belongs from the first to the God who gave him.
Now Sarah said, “God has brought laughter for me; everyone who hears will laugh with me.”

The Hebrew may also be taken as “laugh at me”, and some translations, among them the Malayalam POC, lean in that direction. Either way, Sarah is amazed at what has happened to her, and she is at ease with being amazed.
ch: The Catechism says that against all human hope God promised descendants to Abraham, as the fruit of faith and of the power of the Holy Spirit, and that this progeny is Christ himself (CCC 706). It lists Sarah, who conceives in spite of her great age, among the holy women who prepared for Mary (CCC 489). St Paul calls Christians “children of the promise, like Isaac” (Galatians 4:28), since, like Isaac, they are born of God's gift and not of human strength.

r.h: Woe to the cities that did not repent
set: The chapter has been about how people respond to Jesus. John the Baptist has sent his question from prison (11:2–6), and “this generation” has found fault with both John and Jesus (11:16–19). Now Jesus names three towns on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee, close to one another and close to his work. Capernaum is the town where he made his home (4:13). Immediately after this he will thank the Father for revealing these things to infants (11:25).
str: v. 20: the reason: they did not repent.
vv. 21–22: Chorazin and Bethsaida are compared with Tyre and Sidon.
vv. 23–24: Capernaum is compared with Sodom.
kw: The usual word for miracles in the first three Gospels. It points to God's strength at work. Miracles are meant to lead somewhere, namely to a change of life.
A cry of grief as well as a warning, familiar from the prophets (Isaiah 5:8–22). It is not a curse. Jesus speaks in the tone of one who mourns over what is coming.
To change one's mind and direction. This is the word with which Jesus began to preach (4:17).
vv: Then he began to reproach the cities in which most of his deeds of power had been done
The Gospels record no miracle at Chorazin. So this verse is a reminder that they tell only part of what he did.
they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes.
Tyre and Sidon were old Gentile trading cities, the targets of prophetic oracles (Isaiah 23). Jesus surprises his hearers by saying that they would have responded better.
And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? No, you will be brought down to Hades.
The words echo the taunt against the king of Babylon in Isaiah 14:13–15. The town that had most reason for pride is warned in the words once used for a boastful empire.
ch: The Catechism says that, following in the steps of the prophets and John the Baptist, Jesus announced the judgment of the Last Day in his preaching (CCC 678). The Church reads these woes as a warning spoken in love, and not as a statement about these towns' people as such; Jesus' own first followers came from this same lakeside. The saying applies to everyone who has received much (Luke 12:48), above all to those of us who hear the Gospel and receive the Holy Qurbono week after week.

qa: Is it fair to compare a town with Sodom?

Jesus' point is that judgment takes account of what each has been given. Sodom never had what Capernaum had. Saying “more tolerable” implies degrees, and it does not say what becomes of any single person; that belongs to God, who wants all to be saved (1 Timothy 2:4). The Church teaches that God predestines no one to go to hell (CCC 1037). The saying is meant to wake us up and not to help us count who is lost.
study: What promise of God have I given up on, because it has been so long in coming? What might Sarah's laughter say to me?
Where have I seen God at work close up, and what has changed in me because of it?

lead: At the middle of the Great Fast our Church lifts up the Cross. The Panchangam calls the day Pakuthi Nombu and names it “the setting up of Golgotha”, and it gives a long set of readings. The Evening Gospel (Matthew 17:22–27) has Jesus foretell his death and his raising. In 1 Samuel 7:5–9 the people gather at Mizpah, fast, and say, “We have sinned against the Lord”, as Samuel prays for them. Psalm 34 invites us: “O taste and see that the Lord is good”. Zechariah 12:6–14 speaks of those who “look on the one whom they have pierced” and mourn. In Acts 15:22–33 the apostles and elders lay “no further burden than these essentials” on the Gentile believers. We study here the three that speak most directly to the day.

In Numbers, a serpent of bronze is set on a pole in the wilderness, and those who look at it live. In First Corinthians, Paul reads the wilderness story as written for us, serpents included, and tells tired believers that “God is faithful”. In John, Jesus himself explains what the serpent was for. The key words are looking, testing and lifting up. Halfway through the road, the Church shows us where we are going and what we are to look at.

set: Israel is near the end of the wilderness years. Miriam and Aaron have died (20:1, 28). The chapter opens with a short, hard episode: Israel is attacked by the king of Arad, in the dry south of Canaan, vows to destroy his towns, and does so. The name Hormah recalls that vow. Such war stories belong to an ancient setting, and the Church does not hold them up for imitation (see the question below).

Then the journey turns back to go around the land of Edom (20:21), and the people lose heart. This is the last of the great complaint stories of the wilderness. Their language is worse than before: they speak against God as well as Moses, and they call the manna that has kept them alive “this miserable food”.
str: vv. 1–3: victory at Hormah.
vv. 4–5: the people's impatience and complaint.
v. 6: the serpents.
v. 7: confession, and Moses prays.
vv. 8–9: the remedy.
¶ The people ask God to take the serpents away. The text does not say that he does. He gives them something to look at while the danger is still there.
kw: From a root meaning “to burn”, perhaps because of the burning of the bite. The same word gives the “seraphs” of Isaiah 6:2. In verse 8 the Hebrew has only this word, “Make a śārāp”, and verse 9 says that Moses made it of bronze.
A sound-play in Hebrew between the words for serpent and for bronze. The later name of the object, Nehushtan (2 Kings 18:4), comes from the same sounds.

Not an ordinary stick. The word means a banner or standard raised high so that a scattered people can see it from a distance. Isaiah 11:10 uses it of the root of Jesse, who stands as “a signal to the peoples”.
vv: The people came to Moses and said, “We have sinned by speaking against the Lord and against you; pray to the Lord to take away the serpents from us.”
An honest confession, in place of complaint. The man they had spoken against is the one they now ask for help, and the text records no word of reproach from him: “So Moses prayed for the people.”
Make a poisonous serpent, and set it on a pole; and everyone who is bitten shall look at it and live.
The cure has the shape of the wound. Nothing is asked of the bitten person except to look. No sacrifice is mentioned, and no great effort. They do have to raise their eyes.
So Moses made a serpent of bronze, and put it upon a pole

The wording is simple, and the object itself has no power. The Book of Wisdom makes this plain: “the one who turned toward it was saved, not by the thing that was beheld, but by you, the Savior of all” (Wisdom 16:7).
ch: Wisdom 16:6 already calls the serpent “a symbol of deliverance”. Jesus takes it up in today's Gospel. St Justin Martyr asks why the God who forbade images commanded this one, and answers that it was a sign by which the serpent's power would be broken and salvation proclaimed to those who flee to the Crucified (Dialogue with Trypho 94, in substance). The Catechism names the bronze serpent among the images God ordained or permitted, which pointed in symbol toward salvation by the incarnate Word (CCC 2130).

r.h: These things were written to instruct us
set: Paul is answering a question from Corinth about eating food sacrificed to idols (chapters 8–10). Some Christians there felt secure. They had been baptized, they shared the Lord's table, and they knew that idols are nothing. So why worry? Paul answers from the Exodus story. Israel also had its baptism and its spiritual food, and most of them still did not reach the land.
The argument works only if the story is taken seriously as Scripture for Christians, and it is one of the New Testament's clearest examples of reading the Old Testament in the light of Christ.
str: vv. 1–4: all of them: cloud, sea, food, drink, rock.
v. 5: yet God was not pleased with most of them.
vv. 6–10: four warnings: idolatry, immorality, testing Christ, complaining.
vv. 11–12: written to instruct us; let the one who stands take care.
v. 13: God is faithful.
kw: The word in verse 6 (with the adverb typikōs in verse 11). It first means the mark left by a blow or a seal, and so a pattern. It is the source of our word “type” in the study of the Scriptures: events that are real in themselves, and that also point ahead.
The one Greek word means both testing and temptation. The NRSV uses “testing” in verse 13, where the POC has “temptation”. The same word appears in the Lord's Prayer (Matthew 6:13).
A way out. Paul does not promise that there will be no trial. He promises that there will be a road through it.
vv: and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ.

The water from the rock is told in Exodus 17 and Numbers 20. Later Jewish tradition speaks of a well that travelled with Israel, and many scholars think that Paul knows some form of it. His own point is that Christ was already present to Israel in God's care for them.
We must not put Christ to the test, as some of them did, and were destroyed by serpents.

This is the verse that ties the reading to Numbers 21. Ancient manuscripts differ here, some reading “Christ” and others “the Lord”; the NRSV follows the first, and the POC the second. In verse 8 Paul counts twenty-three thousand who fell, where Numbers 25:9 has twenty-four thousand. Perhaps he is quoting from memory; the point does not depend on the number.
So if you think you are standing, watch out that you do not fall.
This is meant for those who feel secure. Sacraments are real gifts and not a protective charm; they ask for a life that matches them.
God is faithful, and he will not let you be tested beyond your strength, but with the testing he will also provide the way out so that you may be able to endure it.
After the warnings comes the comfort. The strength of the believer rests on the faithfulness of God. People in the middle of a long fast, or a long illness, can lean on this verse.
ch: The Catechism says that the Church's catechesis unveils what lay hidden in the Old Testament, and it reads the crossing of the sea as a figure of Baptism, the water from the rock as a figure of the spiritual gifts of Christ, and the manna as a figure of the Eucharist (CCC 1094). It also says that Christians read the Old Testament in the light of Christ crucified and risen, and that the Old Testament keeps its own value (CCC 129). Paul's warning does not mean that Israel was rejected and the Church replaced it. He calls them “our ancestors” (10:1), and he speaks to the Church in order to warn the Church.

r.h: So must the Son of Man be lifted up
set: Nicodemus, a leader of his people, has come to Jesus by night (3:1–2) and has asked how one can be born from above. The conversation slowly turns into a long saying of Jesus, and we are not told where it ends. Some scholars take verses 16–21 as John's own reflection, and the punctuation of translations differs. Either way, this is the Gospel's teaching.
The reading contains John 3:16, perhaps the best known verse of the New Testament. In its own place, it explains how the lifted serpent is to be understood: God's love is the reason for the Cross.
str: v. 13: only the one who came down can go up.
vv. 14–15: the serpent and the Son of Man.
vv. 16–17: God's love, and his purpose: to save.
vv. 18–21: judgment: light and darkness.
kw: A word with two meanings at once: to raise up physically, and to exalt in honour. John uses it three times of Jesus (3:14; 8:28; 12:32–34), and he explains that it points to “the kind of death he was to die” (12:33). In John the Cross is already the beginning of his glory.
Only-begotten, or one of a kind. It is used of the Son in John 1:14 and 1:18. The Son is not one gift among others. The Father gives what is most his own.
Both a sentence and a separating, as light separates. Here the judgment is not first a later act of punishment. It takes place when a person meets the light and turns toward it or away.
vv: And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him may have eternal life.
What Israel did with its eyes, believers do by faith. The little Greek word for “must” (dei) speaks of God's plan. Where the serpent gave back life for a time, the Son gives eternal life.
For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son
The Cross does not change God's mind toward us. It begins in his love. The “world” in John is often the world that resists God, and that is the world he loves.
Indeed, God did not send the Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him.
The purpose of the sending is plainly stated. A Fast lived in dread of God's anger has not yet heard this verse.
And this is the judgment, that the light has come into the world, and people loved darkness rather than light because their deeds were evil.
People who love the dark are not those who have never seen a light, but those who would rather not be seen. Every one of us knows something of this.
But those who do what is true come to the light

“To do the truth” is a Hebrew way of speaking: truth is something one does as well as something one knows. Nicodemus, who came by night, will appear again at the end, bringing myrrh and aloes for Jesus' burial (19:39).
ch: The Catechism uses John 3:16 to teach that the Word became flesh so that we might know God's love (CCC 458). It says that the lifting up on the Cross signifies and announces his lifting up by his Ascension into heaven (CCC 662). On judgment, it says that the Son did not come to judge but to save, and that by rejecting grace in this life one already judges oneself (CCC 679). This is why the Church's Cross, set up in the middle of a fast, is a sign of the Father's love, and not a sign of threat. We do not look at it in order to feel crushed, but in order to live.

qa: Wasn't the bronze serpent an idol? What about the commandment against images?

God himself commanded it, and it was never meant to be worshipped. When the people later did make offerings to it, King Hezekiah “broke in pieces the bronze serpent that Moses had made” (2 Kings 18:4). So the Bible shows both the proper use of a sacred sign and its abuse. The Catechism draws on the serpent in explaining why the Church's images are not idols (CCC 2129–2132): the honour given to an image passes to the one it represents, and adoration belongs to God alone. Wisdom 16:7 says the same thing of the serpent itself. When we venerate the Cross today, we are looking through it to the one who hung on it.
Why does God send serpents? And what about the destruction of the towns at Hormah?

The Old Testament often speaks of everything that happens as coming directly from God, and it reads suffering as a call to return to him. We should not conclude from this reading that a particular illness or disaster is God's punishment for a particular sin; Jesus himself refuses that conclusion (John 9:3; Luke 13:1–5). As for Hormah, the Church reads such ancient accounts of war in the light of the whole of Scripture and of Christ, who tells us to love our enemies. They are not a command for any later people to do the same to anyone.
“Those who do not believe are condemned already.” What about people who have never heard of Jesus?

John is speaking of those who meet the light and refuse it. The Church teaches that those who, through no fault of their own, do not know the Gospel of Christ or his Church, but who seek God with a sincere heart and try by his grace to do his will as they know it, may also attain eternal salvation (Lumen Gentium 16; CCC 847). This never lessens the urgency of the Church's mission, since Christ is the one Saviour.
rite: In our Antiochene tradition the middle of the Great Fast is marked by the Holy Cross. The name the Panchangam gives to the day, the setting up of Golgotha, says it plainly: the hill of the Cross is brought into the middle of the church, and the people who have walked this far are shown where the road leads. In many parishes the Cross is set up in the middle of the church, honoured with a procession and hymns, and kept there for veneration through the rest of the Fast. Customs vary, so follow the practice of your parish. When you pass that Cross on your way to the Holy Qurbono in the coming weeks, remember the people in the wilderness and do the one thing they were told to do: look, and live.
study: The people called the food that kept them alive “this miserable food”. What gift of God have I grown tired of in this Fast?
God did not take the serpents away at once, but gave something to look at. What does this say to me in a trouble that has not gone away?
“God is faithful”: what testing am I in now, and where might the way out be?
When I stand before the Cross in the middle of the church, what do I see: a threat, or “God so loved the world”? How can I help my family or my catechism class to see it?

lead: The Genesis story left off on Tuesday at Isaac's weaning feast, and today the feast turns to grief. A mother's fear for her son drives another mother and son out of the household, and God does not forget the ones sent away. The Epistle (1 Corinthians 8:1–6) reminds a divided community that “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.” And in the Gospel Jesus asks for the hardest love of all, love for the enemy, because this is how the Father is.

r.h: Hagar and the boy are sent away
set: Hagar is Sarah's Egyptian slave. In chapter 16, Sarah gave her to Abraham so that a child might be born, and then treated her harshly; Hagar ran away, and God met her in the wilderness and sent her back. Her son is now a young boy. Today's reading follows straight on from the feast for Isaac (21:8).

The story does not hide the pain of it. In the law and custom of the time, an heir's standing could be at issue, and that is what Sarah fears. Throughout chapter 21 the narrator never uses the name Ishmael, only “the son of Hagar”, “the boy” and “the child”.
str: vv. 9–10: what Sarah sees, and what she demands.
v. 11: Abraham's distress.
vv. 12–13: God's word: through Isaac, and also a nation from this son.
v. 14: Abraham sends them away with bread and water.
kw: From the same root as the name Isaac, “he laughs”. The Hebrew says only that he was “laughing” or “playing”, and the sense is disputed. The words “with her son Isaac” come from the ancient Greek and Latin versions, which the NRSV follows. Paul knows a tradition that takes it less kindly (Galatians 4:29). The text itself does not accuse the boy of anything.
A harsh word, used of driving out and of sending away a wife. It is the word of Sarah's demand.
Literally “seed”. God uses it for both boys: Isaac's line is the line of the promise (v. 12), and yet the slave woman's son is also “your offspring” (v. 13).
vv: The matter was very distressing to Abraham on account of his son.
The narrator calls him “his son”, not “her son”. Scripture records this love, and does not treat the boy as of no account.
As for the son of the slave woman, I will make a nation of him also, because he is your offspring.
The choosing of Isaac does not mean that God has rejected Ishmael. To be outside the line of the promise is not to be outside God's care.
So Abraham rose early in the morning, and took bread and a skin of water, and gave it to Hagar, putting it on her shoulder, along with the child, and sent her away.
“Rose early in the morning” will come again in the next chapter when Abraham takes Isaac to Moriah (22:3). In both cases Abraham obeys at a great cost, and God watches over the child.
ch: St Paul uses the two mothers as an allegory of two covenants in Galatians 4:21–31, and quotes Sarah's words there. This is a reading about slavery and sonship in Christ. It says nothing against any people, and it does not cancel the plain story, where God cares for Hagar and her son. The Second Vatican Council speaks with esteem of Muslims, who link their faith to Abraham (Nostra Aetate 3; see CCC 841). A Christian hears today's reading with the respect the Council asks for, and with compassion for those who, like Hagar, are put out of a household.

set: This is the last of six sayings in the Sermon on the Mount that follow the pattern “You have heard … but I say to you” (5:21–48). Jesus has just said that he came not to abolish the Law but to fulfil it (5:17). These sayings go to the root of the commandments and ask more, not less.
str: v. 43: what they have heard.
vv. 44–45: the command, and the Father's way.
vv. 46–47: why ordinary love is not enough.
v. 48: the goal.
kw: The command is in the form of a continuing action. This love is not a warm feeling that one has or does not have. It is a decision about what one wills and does for the other person, and it begins here in prayer (v. 44).

Whole, complete, undivided. It recalls “You shall be holy” (Leviticus 19:2) and is the word used in the Greek of Deuteronomy 18:13. It does not mean flawless in performance. In Luke's parallel the word is “merciful” (Luke 6:36). In this context, perfection is a love with no one left out.
vv: You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’

“Love your neighbor” is Leviticus 19:18, but “hate your enemy” is not a command of the Law. The Law also tells people to help an enemy's animal (Exodus 23:4–5) and to feed a hungry enemy (Proverbs 25:21). The Community Rule from Qumran, the writing of one group of that time, speaks of hating the sons of darkness, and some scholars see attitudes of that kind behind this saying. Jesus speaks against a way of limiting the commandment, not against the Law of Israel.
But I say to you, Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you
He says “enemies”, in the plural, and they are real ones. Prayer is the first step because it can be done even before the feeling changes.
for he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the righteous and on the unrighteous.
The reason given is not that enemies deserve it, or that love will win them over. It is what the Father does every morning.
Be perfect, therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect.
This is not a counsel for a few. The Catechism quotes it in teaching that all Christians are called to holiness (CCC 2013).
ch: The Catechism says that the Lord asks us to love as he does, even our enemies (CCC 1825), and that Christian prayer extends to the forgiveness of enemies, which transfigures the disciple by configuring him to his Master (CCC 2844). Among the earliest Christian writings, the Didache says: pray for your enemies, and fast for those who persecute you (1.3, in substance). That old saying joins today's Gospel to the Great Fast. We pray also for all who suffer for their faith or their people in many lands, and for those who have wronged them.

qa: Does God approve of what Sarah did?

God tells Abraham to do as Sarah says, because Isaac is the child of the promise (21:12). This does not make her demand good in itself, and the Bible does not call it so. Scripture often shows God bringing his purpose through the mixed motives of human beings, while keeping faith with those who are hurt by them. God's word about Hagar's son is a promise, and in the next reading the angel of God calls to her in the wilderness.
study: Who has been put out of the household in my family, parish or village? What would it mean for me to see them as God sees Hagar?
Name one person who has wronged you. Can you fast for that person on one day this week, and pray for that person by name?

lead: Today we follow Hagar and the boy into the wilderness, where God hears a voice no one else hears and opens the eyes of a mother who has given up. The Gospel gives the shepherd's own word: “I know my own and my own know me”, and it looks beyond the fold. The Epistle (1 Corinthians 16:13–24) closes Paul's letter with “Let all that you do be done in love”, and with an Aramaic prayer that the Greek text keeps untranslated, marana tha, “Our Lord, come!” Our Church also remembers today the enthronement of our Major Archbishop-Catholicos.

set: Hagar has been wandering in the wilderness of Beer-sheba with bread and a skin of water (21:14). This is the second time she has been in the desert with God's promise. In 16:7–14 she fled there while pregnant, was found by an angel at a spring, and gave God a name: the God who sees. Now the water is gone. The writer tells the scene slowly and in small details.
str: vv. 15–16: the water runs out; she cannot watch the boy die.
vv. 17–18: God hears and speaks.
v. 19: her eyes are opened to a well.
vv. 20–21: God is with the boy; he grows up in Paran.
kw: “God hears”, as the angel explained in 16:11. The name is not used in this passage, but its meaning is the turning point: “God heard the voice of the boy” (v. 17).

The well was there all along, and “God opened her eyes”. Salvation in this story comes as seeing what God has already provided. The same word will come back in the name Beer-sheba in the next reading.
vv: for she said, “Do not let me look on the death of the child.” And as she sat opposite him, she lifted up her voice and wept.

The Hebrew has the mother weeping, and the NRSV follows it. The Greek Old Testament has the child crying, and the POC agrees with that reading. The next verse says that God heard the boy's voice, though in the Hebrew we have not yet been told that he spoke. Both are in pain, and God is listening to both.
And God heard the voice of the boy; and the angel of God called to Hagar from heaven
God does not wait to be asked in the correct words, and he answers a cry from outside the household of the promise.
Then God opened her eyes and she saw a well of water.
Despair narrows sight. God's first gift to Hagar is the ability to see what was close to her all the time.
ch: The Catechism names the cry of the people oppressed in Egypt, and the cry of the foreigner, the widow and the orphan, among the cries that rise to heaven (CCC 1867). Hagar, a foreign slave woman with a dying child, is one of the Bible's strongest witnesses that such a cry is heard. Her son is not forgotten by the family story either: Isaac and Ishmael together bury their father Abraham (25:9). St Paul's allegory in Galatians 4 has its own purpose, and it does not take away this plain word of God's mercy to a slave woman and her child.

set: Jesus has just given sight to a man born blind, and the religious leaders have put the man out (John 9). He now speaks of those who care for sheep. The Old Testament stands behind the discourse: God accuses Israel's bad shepherds in Ezekiel 34 and promises to shepherd his people himself, and to set one shepherd over them (Ezekiel 34:11–16, 23). John's sayings are directed at those particular leaders in that dispute. They are not words about the Jewish people.
The Panchangam's reference for today's Gospel is not clear, and it may mean John 10:1–16 or John 10:14–16. We follow the shorter reading here, and your parish lectionary should be your guide.
str: vv. 14–15a: mutual knowing, like that of the Father and the Son.
v. 15b: he lays down his life.
v. 16: other sheep; one flock, one shepherd.
kw: Kalos is good, in the sense of fine and noble, and it has a sense of beauty as well. He is the true shepherd, the kind that all other shepherds should be measured by.
Knowledge in the biblical sense, a personal relationship and not only information. The astonishing thing here is the comparison: as the Father knows the Son.
A walled yard for sheep. It is a different word from poimnē, “flock”. Jesus speaks of this fold and of sheep outside it, and the end is one flock under one shepherd.
vv: I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me
He does not say first what the sheep must do. Being known by him comes first.
And I lay down my life for the sheep.
The hired hand runs away (10:12). The shepherd gives himself, and verse 18 says that he does so of his own accord (see CCC 609).
I have other sheep that do not belong to this fold. I must bring them also, and they will listen to my voice. So there will be one flock, one shepherd.

Most interpreters take these others to be the Gentiles, who would be gathered with Israel; compare John 11:52. Christians also hear in the verse the wound of our own divisions, and our duty to pray that they may be healed.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Good Shepherd ought to be the model and form of the bishop's pastoral office (CCC 896). It calls the Church a sheepfold whose one gateway is Christ, and says that the sheep, though ruled by human shepherds, are led and nourished by Christ himself (CCC 754). It teaches also that Christ always gives his Church the gift of unity, but that she must always pray and work to maintain, reinforce and perfect it (CCC 820).

qa: Who are the “other sheep”?

In John's Gospel the most natural reading is the Gentiles, who were to be brought in with the believers from Israel: Jesus was to die “not for the nation only, but to gather into one the dispersed children of God” (11:52). The verse should not be used against other Christians. It tells all of us how far the shepherd's care reaches and what he wants: one flock.
rite: Today is the anniversary of the enthronement of Moran Mor Baselios Cardinal Cleemis Catholicos as Major Archbishop-Catholicos of our Church (2007). It is fitting that the Gospel of the Good Shepherd should be read today. Pray for him, for the bishops of our eparchies, and for the priests who share in this ministry, that they may know their people and be known by them. Our Church's own story, of entering full communion with the Bishop of Rome under Mar Ivanios in 1930, gives the words “one flock, one shepherd” a special weight for us, and our prayer for unity goes on.
study: Where have I, like Hagar, sat down at a distance because I could not bear to look? Could there be a well nearby that I have not seen?
Jesus says that he knows his own. In this Fast, what can I do to know him better and to listen to his voice? How can I pray today for our Major Archbishop-Catholicos and our bishop?

lead: This week's story of Abraham ends in peace. The king he once feared comes to him and says, “God is with you in all that you do”, and at a well the two men swear an oath. The Epistle (1 Timothy 4:1–5) guards the Fast against a false idea: “everything created by God is good”, so we fast out of love and not out of contempt for creation. In the Gospel, a crowd wants to keep Jesus to itself, and he says that he has been sent to other towns as well. In all three, God's purpose is wider than the place where we are standing.

set: The same Abimelech who appears in chapter 20, with whom Abraham began so badly, comes with the commander of his army. Water was life in the dry south, and a dug well was property worth fighting for. Abraham is a resident alien: he has no land of his own, and only the goodwill of others to protect him. This passage settles the question of a well and gives us the name of a place that will become important to the patriarchs (26:23–33; 28:10; 46:1).

The text speaks of “the land of the Philistines”. Many scholars note that the Philistines are known from history only at a later time, and think that the writer uses the name familiar to his own readers.
str: vv. 22–24: the king asks for an oath, and Abraham gives it.
vv. 25–26: the complaint about the well.
vv. 27–31: the covenant; the seven ewe lambs; the name of the place.
vv. 32–34: the king goes home; Abraham plants a tree, worships, and remains a stranger.
kw: Bĕ’ēr means well. Sheba‘ can mean seven, and it sounds like the verb for swearing an oath. The story plays on both: seven ewe lambs, and an oath.
Abimelech's word in verse 23: loyal, reliable kindness. It is one of the great words of the covenant, and it is striking to hear it here from the king.
This name for God occurs only here in the Old Testament in this form. Abraham owns nothing lasting in the land, and calls on the God who lasts.
vv: God is with you in all that you do
In 20:11 Abraham doubted that this place had any fear of God. Now its king says that God is with Abraham. Each has seen more of God in the other than he expected.
These seven ewe lambs you shall accept from my hand, in order that you may be a witness for me that I dug this well.
Abraham settles the dispute without force. A public gesture is his way to make peace and secure a right.
Abraham planted a tamarisk tree in Beer-sheba, and called there on the name of the Lord, the Everlasting God.
A tamarisk is a tree of dry places. To plant a tree in a land that is not yet his is a quiet act of hope.
And Abraham resided as an alien many days in the land of the Philistines.
The covenant over the well does not change his status. He is still a guest, and the promise of the land is still ahead.
ch: The Letter to the Hebrews says that Abraham “stayed for a time in the land he had been promised, as in a foreign land, living in tents” (Hebrews 11:9), because he was looking to the city whose builder is God (11:10). The Catechism draws on this praise of Abraham's faith (CCC 145). So the Church sees the believer as a pilgrim, who can plant trees and make peace with his neighbours here, while knowing that this is not his final home. That is a good description of Christian life, and of fasting too.

r.h: I was sent for this purpose
set: Luke has shown a first day of Jesus' work at Capernaum: the teaching in the synagogue, the man with the unclean spirit, Simon's mother-in-law, and the sick who were brought at sunset (4:31–41). Just before that, his own town of Nazareth tried to drive him out (4:16–30). Now the people of Capernaum try the opposite and want to hold on to him. Luke sets the two towns side by side, and neither gets to decide where Jesus goes.
str: v. 42: the deserted place; the crowd finds him and tries to keep him.
v. 43: his answer: other cities; “I was sent”.
v. 44: he goes on preaching.
kw: “It is necessary.” In Luke this little word marks what belongs to God's plan (2:49; 9:22; 24:26). It is why the mission goes on.
Verse 43 is the first time this phrase occurs in Luke's Gospel, and it is Jesus who says it. It means God's reign, and not first of all a place.
vv: At daybreak he departed and went into a deserted place.
After a long evening with the sick he seeks solitude. Luke often shows Jesus withdrawing, and elsewhere says that he went to pray (5:16). Mark's account says so here too (Mark 1:35).
and when they reached him, they wanted to prevent him from leaving them.
This is a natural and even loving wish. It is also a temptation. Even good people can want to keep Jesus for themselves.
But he said to them, “I must proclaim the good news of the kingdom of God to the other cities also; for I was sent for this purpose.”
He knows who sent him and why. St Paul VI quotes this saying in his teaching on evangelization (Evangelii Nuntiandi 6).
So he continued proclaiming the message in the synagogues of Judea.
Here “Judea” seems to mean the whole land of the Jews, including Galilee, as in Luke 1:5. Some ancient manuscripts read “Galilee”, perhaps to make the geography easier.
ch: St Paul VI wrote that evangelizing is the grace and vocation proper to the Church, her deepest identity (Evangelii Nuntiandi 14). The Catechism teaches that everyone is called to enter the kingdom, and that the kingdom was first announced to the children of Israel and is meant to welcome people of all nations (CCC 543). A parish that keeps the Lord to itself has misunderstood him in the way the crowd did at Capernaum.

qa: If everything created is good, why do we fast?

Because we fast out of love and for freedom, and not because food or the body is bad. Today's Epistle warns against teachers who “forbid marriage and demand abstinence from foods” as if creation were evil (1 Timothy 4:3). The Church rejected that error from the beginning. In the Great Fast we give up good things for a time, to make room for prayer and to share with those who have less. Then we receive them again “with thanksgiving”.
study: Abraham made peace at a well with a man he had once misjudged. With whom could I settle an old dispute this Fast, at some cost to myself?
Do I want to keep Jesus to my own family, parish or community? Who are the “other cities” that need to hear of him from me?

lead: K'piphtho Sunday, the fifth of the Great Fast, takes its name from the woman who was bent over for eighteen years. The Sunday's many readings stand around her. The Evening Gospel (Luke 10:25–37) tells of a Samaritan who stops for a wounded man, and ends, “Go and do likewise.” Genesis 9:1–7 blesses Noah and insists on the worth of human life, “for in his own image God made humankind”. In Sirach 51:1–10 a person rescued from distress cries out, “Lord, you are my Father”. Jeremiah 51:1–9 sees the fall of proud Babylon. First Peter 3:8–17 tells us not to repay evil for evil. We study here the three that speak most directly to the Gospel.

In Isaiah, a servant of God receives a word “to sustain the weary”, and God asks, “Is my hand shortened, that it cannot redeem?” In Romans, Paul tells believers to offer their very bodies to God as a living sacrifice. In Luke, Jesus speaks a word to a weary woman, lays his hands on her, and she stands and praises God. The key words are weary, body and set free. God's mercy reaches the body as well as the soul, and it sets us upright so that we can worship.

set: Most scholars place chapters 40–55 of Isaiah among the people exiled in Babylon in the sixth century before Christ. The exiles felt that God had thrown them off. Jerusalem is pictured here as a mother and wife, and her children as people sold into slavery. The first three verses answer their complaint. God asks them to produce the proof that he has divorced her, or sold them to pay a debt. No such document exists. Their own sin brought the exile, not any lack of love or power in God.
Then, at verse 4, a new voice speaks: a servant of God who has been taught to listen. Verses 4–9 are usually counted as the third of the Servant Songs, and today's reading gives us their beginning.
str: v. 1: where is the bill of divorce?
vv. 2–3: God's call was not answered; God's power is not less.
v. 4: the servant's tongue and the servant's ear.
v. 5: the servant does not turn back.
kw: The document a husband gave when sending away his wife (Deuteronomy 24:1–4). God's question implies that this marriage was never ended by such a document. Separation is real, but the bond has not been dissolved.
Disciples, learners. The word appears twice in verse 4. The NRSV has “the tongue of a teacher” for what is literally “the tongue of those who are taught”: only one who has first learned can teach.
A rare verb, found only here, and its exact sense is uncertain. The context makes the general meaning clear: to help the worn-out with a word, as the NRSV has it.
vv: Where is your mother’s bill of divorce with which I put her away?
A question that can have no answer, and it is meant to be so. In the exile's darkest hour, God still speaks as one who has not let go of his people.
Is my hand shortened, that it cannot redeem?
A short hand is a Hebrew image for lack of power. Isaiah 59:1 will say the same. The bent woman of the Gospel will show what this hand can do.
The Lord God has given me the tongue of a teacher, that I may know how to sustain the weary with a word.
The gift of speech is given for the sake of the tired. The verse goes on to say that this ear is wakened “morning by morning”. The servant says nothing that he has not first heard.
The Lord God has opened my ear, and I was not rebellious, I did not turn backward.
Listening leads to obedience, and the next verse (50:6) shows the cost: he gives his back to those who strike him.
ch: The Catechism says that the Messiah's characteristics are revealed above all in the Servant Songs, and that these songs proclaim the meaning of Jesus' Passion (CCC 713). The Church therefore reads this passage of Jesus, the listening Son. In the Gospel of John he says: “I do as the Father has commanded me” (14:31). He teaches in the synagogue today and restores a tired woman with a word, as one who has been wakened morning by morning to the Father's will.

set: For eleven chapters Paul has spoken of God's mercy in Christ, for Jews and Gentiles alike, and has ended in wonder (11:33–36). Now, with the word “therefore”, he turns to how to live. So Christian conduct is the answer to mercy already received. It is not the way of earning that mercy, and by God's grace our good works truly please him.
Many scholars think that the Roman community was made up of Christians from a Jewish background and from a Gentile background, and that the advice on humility and mutual honour has this in view.
str: vv. 1–2: the whole person offered; the mind renewed.
vv. 3–8: one body, many gifts.
vv. 9–13: love in practice.
vv. 14–15: those who persecute, those who rejoice, those who weep.
kw: Paul does not say “souls”. The whole person, the part of us that eats, works and touches others, is what is offered. The body is no enemy of worship.

Latreia is the word for the service of the Temple. Logikē can mean “reasonable”, “of the mind” or “spiritual”. It describes the worship that fits who we are as those who have been given reason and the Spirit.
The word used of Jesus at the Transfiguration in Matthew 17:2 and Mark 9:2. It is in the passive form, as something God does in us, and in the present, as something that continues.
vv: I appeal to you therefore, brothers and sisters, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship.
The language is taken from the altar. A sacrifice that is alive keeps on being offered, day by day. This does not replace the Holy Qurbono; it flows from it, and returns to it.
but be transformed by the renewing of your minds
Fasting works on the body and the mind together. Paul expects a real change in how we see.
so we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually we are members one of another.
Having just spoken of each one's body, Paul now speaks of the one body. Each of us belongs to the others, not just to the same organization.
Let love be genuine
The Greek word is literally “not hypocritical”. This is the same word family that Jesus uses in today's Gospel: “You hypocrites!” Love is not an act one puts on.
Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse them.
Paul echoes the teaching of Jesus (Matthew 5:44). The Catholic Epistle of the day says the same thing (1 Peter 3:9). Verse 15 then asks us to share the joy and the grief of others.
ch: The Catechism says: “The moral life is spiritual worship”, and quotes this verse, adding that we offer our bodies within the Body of Christ that we form and in communion with the offering of his Eucharist (CCC 2031). It also teaches that by prayer we can discern what is the will of God (CCC 2826). St John Chrysostom asks how the body can become a sacrifice, and answers: let the eye look on no evil, let the tongue say nothing shameful, let the hand do nothing unlawful, and more than that, let them do good (Homilies on Romans 20, in substance).

set: Luke places this story on Jesus' long journey to Jerusalem, which starts at 9:51. It is the last time in this Gospel that we see him teaching in a synagogue. Just before it he has told of a barren fig tree given one more year (13:6–9), and just after it he compares the kingdom to a mustard seed and to yeast (13:18–21). Only Luke tells this story.

A leader of the synagogue was a respected local man who took care of its order and worship. His concern for the Sabbath is sincere. The Sabbath was God's gift, a sign of creation and of the release from Egypt (Exodus 20:8–11; Deuteronomy 5:12–15), and Jews of Jesus' day discussed in good faith which works were allowed on it. The woman's condition was not an emergency, so his objection is not absurd. Jesus answers within that discussion.
str: vv. 10–11: the setting and the woman.
vv. 12–13: he sees, calls, speaks, touches; she stands and praises.
v. 14: the leader's objection, addressed to the crowd.
vv. 15–16: Jesus' reply: from animal to daughter of Abraham.
v. 17: shame and joy.
kw: A perfect form in Greek: it is already done, and it stands. He tells her this before he touches her. The same verb, lyō, to loose, comes back: the ox is “untied” (v. 15), and the daughter of Abraham must be “set free” (v. 16). The word links the two.

“It is necessary.” The leader says that there are six days when work “ought” to be done (v. 14). Jesus answers with the same word: “ought not this woman … be set free” (v. 16). Two senses of what God requires meet here.

This is the only place in the New Testament with this phrase. Like the “son of Abraham” in Luke 19:9, it names her dignity in the covenant, which her illness had not taken from her. Through most of this week the first readings have told of Abraham's family, and here is one of his daughters.
vv: She was bent over and was quite unable to stand up straight.
For eighteen years she could see only the ground, and she could not look others in the face. She does not ask for anything. In this story every first step is his.
When Jesus saw her, he called her over and said, “Woman, you are set free from your ailment.”
He notices her first. In the middle of his teaching he calls her forward to where others can see, and the one who was hidden stands at the centre.
When he laid his hands on her, immediately she stood up straight and began praising God.
A word and a touch: this is how the sick are still cared for in the Church. Her first act when she is upright is to praise God, and this is what her straightened body is for.
There are six days on which work ought to be done; come on those days and be cured, and not on the sabbath day.
He does not speak to Jesus directly. Nor does he speak to the woman. He seems unable to see in her the sign of what the Sabbath means.
And ought not this woman, a daughter of Abraham whom Satan bound for eighteen long years, be set free from this bondage on the sabbath day?

If an animal may be loosed to drink, how much more this daughter of Abraham? Luke's account does not set Jesus against the Sabbath. It claims that the Sabbath, the day of release, is the very day for this.
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus never fails to respect the holiness of the Sabbath, and that he gives this law its authentic and authoritative interpretation (CCC 2173). It calls his compassion toward the sick and his many healings a resplendent sign that God has visited his people (CCC 1503). St Gregory the Great takes the bent woman as a picture of the person whose mind is turned only to the things of earth and cannot look up to what is above, until the Lord's word and hand restore her (Homilies on the Gospels 31, in substance). The Great Fast asks us each to look at what has bent us over.

qa: What does K'piphtho mean?

It is a Syriac word that means “the bent one”, from a root meaning to bend or stoop. Our Church names the Sundays of the Great Fast after their Gospels, many of them after healings: this Sunday is named after this woman, who has no name of her own in the Gospel but is called a daughter of Abraham.
Did Jesus break the Sabbath?

Jesus honoured the Sabbath. He was in the synagogue that day to teach. He disputes one reading of what may be done on it, with an argument that those present could follow, and the argument is from their own custom of watering animals. Later Jewish teachers also taught that the saving of life overrides the Sabbath. Luke does not show a contest between Jesus and the Jewish people. The crowd in the synagogue, also Jewish, rejoices (13:17), and the woman is a daughter of Abraham. The issue is who can be set free today.
Does Satan cause illness? Was she being punished for sin?

Luke says that a spirit had crippled her and that Satan had bound her. This expresses the biblical sense that sickness and death belong to a world that is not yet as God wants it, and that Christ's healings are a sign of the defeat of evil. It does not mean that any sick person is possessed or being punished. Earlier in this same chapter Jesus rejects the idea that those who suffer are worse sinners than others (13:1–5). Doctors and medicine are not excluded by this; Sirach 38 honours them, and the Church has always prayed for the sick and cared for them, as in the anointing of the sick (CCC 1499).
rite: The Sundays of our Great Fast form a kind of road, and many of them show by a healing what Christ does for those who come to him. On K'piphtho Sunday we think of all whose lives have been bent by long illness, by age, by heavy labour, or by wrong done to them, and of those who cannot lift their eyes for shame. As we stand for the Holy Qurbono, we can remember that standing upright before God is itself a gift. In the Antiochene tradition, we stand and turn toward the East at prayer, and the body prays along with the heart. Today let us look around our parish for those who are overlooked, and do what Jesus did: see them, and call them over.
study: What has bent me over? How long have I been looking at the ground? Can I bring it to the Lord this week?
The servant in Isaiah has a word “to sustain the weary”. Who near me is weary, and what word could I say to them?
Paul tells me to offer my body as a living sacrifice. What would this mean in concrete terms for my eyes, my tongue, my hands, this week?
The leader of the synagogue was concerned about the rules, and did not see the woman. Where might good rules or habits in our family or parish keep us from seeing a person in need?

lead: In this week of the Great Fast the Church walks with Abraham up the mountain. God asks for the son of the promise, and Isaac asks the question that hangs over the whole Bible: where is the lamb? The epistle (1 Corinthians 11:1–10) opens with “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ”, and goes on to order in worship at Corinth, with customs of that time about head coverings. In the Gospel Jesus calls himself the bridegroom and says he will be taken away. Both the lamb and the fast point the same way, toward the Cross.

set: Isaac is the son Abraham waited for through long years, and God has said, “it is through Isaac that offspring shall be named for you” (21:12). Now God seems to ask back the promise itself. The narrator tells us at once that this is a test, so the reader knows what Abraham does not. Jewish tradition calls the chapter the Aqedah, the Binding, from a verb in v. 9.

People in the ancient world around Israel knew of child sacrifice. The Law and the prophets condemn it without reserve (Leviticus 18:21; Jeremiah 7:31), and this story ends with God stopping the hand.
str: v. 1: God tests Abraham.
v. 2: the command.
vv. 3–5: the journey, and the words to the young men.
vv. 6–8: father and son walk on together, and Isaac asks his question.
kw: To put to the proof. The word is not about God wanting to trap anyone. It brings out what is in the heart, and God already knows the end he intends.
The Hebrew of v. 2 means an only, irreplaceable child. The ancient Greek translation renders it agapētos, beloved, the same word the Father's voice uses of Jesus at his baptism (Mark 1:11).
Abraham says it to God (v. 1), to his son (v. 7) and to the angel (v. 11). It is the answer of someone fully present, and it is the same answer whoever is calling.
vv: Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love

Each phrase tightens the grip, and the name comes only after “your only son”. Moriah appears again in 2 Chronicles 3:1 as the hill where Solomon built the Temple, so Israel's later worship stands on this ground.
we will worship, and then we will come back to you

The “we” is plural in Hebrew. It may be only what a father could bring himself to say, but Hebrews 11:19 hears faith in it: “He considered the fact that God is able even to raise someone from the dead”.
God himself will provide the lamb for a burnt offering, my son.

Literally, “God will see to the lamb for himself”. Abraham does not know how. He answers his son with trust, and “the two of them walked on together”. Christians hear the answer in John 1:29: “Here is the Lamb of God”.
ch: The Catechism sees this test as the final purifying of Abraham's faith, by which the father of believers is made like the Father who will not spare his own Son (CCC 2572). Origen, in his homilies on Genesis, says that Isaac carrying the wood on his shoulders is a figure of Christ carrying his own Cross (in substance). The Church reads this chapter as promise and shadow of the Passion, and honours it first as the real obedience of a real man.

r.h: When the bridegroom is taken away
set: The scene follows the banquet at Levi's house (5:27–32), where Jesus eats with tax collectors. The critics now raise a question about fasting. Fasting was a serious and good practice. The Law itself commands a day of self-denial on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29–31), and devout people added other fasts, as the Pharisee in Luke 18:12 fasts twice a week. Jesus does not mock this. He asks what time it is.
str: v. 33: the question.
vv. 34–35: the bridegroom is here, and he will be taken away.
vv. 36–38: two images, the patch and the wine.
v. 39: a saying found only in Luke.
kw: In the prophets the Lord himself is the husband of his people (Hosea 2; Isaiah 54:5). When Jesus takes this title he says something very large about himself.
In the New Testament this verb occurs only in this saying (Matthew 9:15; Mark 2:20; Luke 5:35). It is an early, quiet hint of the Passion.
A goatskin sewn as a bag. New wine is still working and swelling. An old skin has gone stiff, and it splits.
vv: You cannot make wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them, can you?
A wedding in that world could last for days, and no guest would fast at it. Jesus does not argue about rules. He tells them who is present.
The days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days.
Here is the Christian reason for fasting. We do not fast to earn God's attention. We fast out of love and longing for a Bridegroom who gave himself up, and whose return we await.
But new wine must be put into fresh wineskins.

What Jesus brings cannot simply be added as a patch on old habits of heart. This is no contempt for the Old Testament, which he came to fulfil (Matthew 5:17). In v. 39 he gently notes how human it is to prefer what we are used to, and to say, “The old is good.”
ch: The Catechism notes that the Lord referred to himself as the bridegroom, and that the Church is his bride (CCC 796). The Didache, a very early Christian writing, already speaks of fasting on Wednesdays and Fridays. The Church counts her seasons of penance and each Friday among the intense moments of her penitential practice, in memory of the Lord's death (CCC 1438).

qa: If Jesus said his friends could not fast, why do we fast?

He said it of the days when he walked among them, and he added that they would fast when he was taken away. We live in those days: he is truly with us, above all in the Holy Qurbono, and yet we still await his coming. So the Church both fasts and feasts.
study: Abraham answers, “Here I am”, to God and to his son alike. Where is it hardest for me to be fully present?
Why am I fasting this year: to prove something, or out of love for the Bridegroom?

lead: The story of Moriah reaches its summit. The knife is lifted, the angel calls, and a ram dies in Isaac's place. The epistle (Colossians 1:24–29) speaks of rejoicing in sufferings and of “completing what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions for the sake of his body, that is, the church”. Christ's sacrifice lacks nothing. His body the Church still has its share of suffering to bear with him. In the Gospel Jesus says openly that he must suffer, and calls his followers to take up their cross. Today our Church also remembers the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste, who did exactly that.

set: The narrator slows down. Each act is told separately: building, arranging, binding, laying, reaching out, taking. No word of protest from Isaac is recorded. A boy able to carry the wood could perhaps have resisted, and later Jewish and Christian writers often imagined him consenting. The text itself is silent. God's voice stops the deed, and the promise that began in chapter 12 is sealed with an oath.
str: vv. 9–10: the altar, the binding, the knife.
vv. 11–12: the angel's call.
v. 13: the ram.
v. 14: the name of the place.
vv. 15–18: the oath and the blessing.
v. 19: the return to Beer-sheba.
kw: The verb of v. 9, which occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible. From it comes the Jewish name of the story, the Aqedah.
The verb is “to see”. The Lord sees to it. This is the same verb as in v. 8, where Abraham says that God “will provide”.
Literally “seed”, a singular noun with a collective sense. Paul presses the singular and reads it of Christ (Galatians 3:16).
vv: for now I know that you fear God, since you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me.

God does not learn something he did not know. The story speaks in a human way of faith shown in deed. The word “withheld” returns in Paul: “He who did not withhold his own Son, but gave him up for all of us” (Romans 8:32). What God spared Abraham, God himself gave.
offered it up as a burnt offering instead of his son.
“Instead of” is the key to the verse. Isaac goes home alive and another dies in his place, and the Fathers saw the Lamb of the Cross in this.
by your offspring shall all the nations of the earth gain blessing for themselves, because you have obeyed my voice.

The blessing is for all nations. St Peter quotes this promise to his fellow Israelites in the Temple (Acts 3:25), and Paul calls it the gospel told beforehand to Abraham (Galatians 3:8). Abraham remains the father of Israel, and through his offspring the nations are drawn in.
ch: The Catechism says that in Abraham's offspring all the nations will be blessed, and that this offspring is Christ (CCC 706). Hebrews 11:17–19 makes Moriah a lesson on faith in the resurrection. St Irenaeus says that Abraham readily gave up his only son to God, so that God might be pleased to give his own only Son for all Abraham's descendants (in substance). The Church reads the chapter toward Calvary, where no hand stops the Father's gift, and the Son gives himself.

set: Near Caesarea Philippi Peter has just said, “You are the Messiah” (8:29). Now Jesus says what kind of Messiah he is. This is the first of three such teachings on the road to Jerusalem (8:31; 9:31; 10:33–34). The elders, chief priests and scribes named here were the leaders in Jerusalem at that time. The Church does not lay the Passion on the Jewish people (CCC 597).
str: v. 31: the first teaching of the Passion.
vv. 32–33: Peter's objection and Jesus' rebuke.
v. 34: the call to all.
vv. 35–37: losing life and saving it.
v. 38: the coming glory.
kw: Not fate, but the plan of God found in the Scriptures. The same small word runs through the Passion teaching of the Gospels (Luke 24:26).
To say of oneself what Peter will later say of Jesus, “I do not know this man”. The verb is the one used of Peter's denial (14:30). It means to stop making myself the centre.
The NRSV says “life” throughout vv. 35–37, and the POC moves from ജീവൻ to ആത്മാവ്. One Greek word covers both: my very self, before God.
vv: Get behind me, Satan! For you are setting your mind not on divine things but on human things.

Peter has rebuked Jesus, and Jesus rebukes Peter with the same verb. “Behind me” is the place of a disciple, the same phrase as the first call, “Follow me” (1:17). Jesus does not cast Peter off. He sends him back to his place, and the Lord who gave him his charge will restore him.
let them deny themselves and take up their cross and follow me.

He says this to “the crowd with his disciples”, so it is for everyone. In that world the cross was no figure of speech. Hearers knew what it was to see a condemned man carry his beam through the streets.
For what will it profit them to gain the whole world and forfeit their life?
Jesus reasons like a merchant weighing a bargain. No gain can buy back the self that has been lost.
ch: The Catechism says that Peter scorned the prediction and that the others did not understand it (CCC 554), that Christ calls his disciples to take up their cross because he suffered for us (CCC 618), and that the way of perfection passes by way of the Cross, with no holiness without renunciation and spiritual battle (CCC 2015). The cross of a disciple shares by grace in the one Cross that saves.

rite: Tradition remembers the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste, in Lesser Armenia, as soldiers who refused to deny Christ about the year 320, in the time of Licinius. St Basil the Great preached on them. According to the account, they were left naked on a frozen lake to die. One gave way, and a guard, moved by what he saw, took his place, so that the number stayed forty. They are a Great Fast sermon without words: those who lose their life for Christ's sake will save it.
study: Abraham did not withhold what was dearest. What am I still holding back from God in this Fast?
Peter wanted a Messiah without a cross. In what way do I ask the same of Jesus?

lead: After the mountain comes a list of names. It looks like a pause, but in these names God is already preparing a bride for Isaac. The epistle (1 Timothy 5:17–22) asks that elders “who rule well be considered worthy of double honor”, and gives counsel on the care of the Church's ministers. In the Gospel Jesus feeds four thousand with seven loaves. God's care is at work in family lists, in the Church's ministers, and in bread for the hungry.

set: “After these things” is the phrase that opened chapter 22, so the news reaches Abraham straight after Moriah. Nahor, his brother, stayed in Mesopotamia (the “city of Nahor”, 24:10), and Milcah was the daughter of their brother Haran (11:29). The list is short, but it prepares the next great chapter of the story. When Abraham looks for a wife for Isaac, his servant will go to this family and meet Rebekah (chapter 24).
str: v. 20: the news reaches Abraham.
vv. 21–22: eight sons of Milcah.
v. 23: Bethuel and Rebekah.
v. 24: four sons of the concubine Reumah.
kw: The little word “also” in v. 20 invites a comparison. Sarah bore her one son after long waiting, and Milcah has eight. Abraham's line is narrow and hangs on God's promise.
A secondary wife of lower standing, allowed by custom at that time. Genesis reports it and does not hold it up as the ideal, which is the one flesh of 2:24 that Jesus restores (Matthew 19:4–6).
vv: Uz the firstborn, Buz his brother, Kemuel the father of Aram,

Eight sons and four make twelve, like the twelve of Ishmael (25:13–16) and the twelve of Jacob. Uz is also the name of Job's land (Job 1:1), though any link is uncertain. Aram is the name of the Arameans. Rebekah's father and brother are called Arameans (25:20), and Israel would confess, “A wandering Aramean was my ancestor” (Deuteronomy 26:5). Syriac, the language of our liturgy, grew from Aramaic.
Bethuel became the father of Rebekah.
She is the one person in this list whom the story will follow, and she is the reason for the list. God's promise moves forward through a name that no one at the time would have noticed.
ch: Matthew and Luke open the story of Jesus with such lists (Matthew 1; Luke 3), because salvation has a family history. St Paul remembers Rebekah among those through whom God's own choice is shown (Romans 9:10–12). The Catechism says that the mission of many holy women prepared for that of Mary (CCC 489). A name in a list is never wasted in God's plan.

set: Jesus has answered the faith of the Canaanite woman (15:21–28), and on a mountain by the Sea of Galilee he has healed many, and the crowds “praised the God of Israel” (15:31). This wording, with Mark's mention of the Decapolis (Mark 7:31), leads many scholars and some of the Fathers to think that this crowd was largely Gentile. Matthew does not say so outright. If so, the bread given earlier to Israel (14:13–21) now reaches the nations as well.
str: v. 32: Jesus' compassion.
vv. 33–34: the disciples' question and the seven loaves.
vv. 35–36: the taking, the thanks, the breaking, the giving.
vv. 37–38: all are filled, and seven baskets remain.
v. 39: on to Magadan, a place we can no longer identify with certainty.
kw: From the word for the inward parts. It is felt in the gut, and the Gospels use it above all of Jesus.
The word from which “Eucharist” comes. Any hearer in the early Church would have recognised the actions of v. 36.
A different word from the basket of the first feeding (kophinos, 14:20). A spyris could be large: Paul was let down the wall of Damascus in one (Acts 9:25).
vv: I have compassion for the crowd, because they have been with me now for three days and have nothing to eat
Here Jesus starts it. Nobody asks him. He has noticed how far they have to walk home.
Where are we to get enough bread in the desert to feed so great a crowd?
Moses asked much the same in the desert (Numbers 11:13), and God gave the manna (Exodus 16). The disciples have already seen one such feeding, and they still ask. That should comfort us.
he took the seven loaves and the fish; and after giving thanks he broke them and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds.
The hands of the disciples stand between the hands of Jesus and the hungry crowd. That is still how the Lord's gifts reach people.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the multiplication of the loaves, when the Lord blesses, breaks and gives through his disciples, prefigures the superabundance of the one bread of his Eucharist (CCC 1335). This is why the Fast, even as it cuts down on food, keeps its eyes on the table of the Holy Qurbono and on those who have nothing to eat.

qa: Are these two feedings really one story told twice?

Some scholars think that the two accounts go back to one event. Matthew and Mark present them as two, and in Mark Jesus himself refers to both (Mark 8:19–20). Either way the Gospels want us to hear the second as God's generosity going further.
study: God's plan went forward through a family list. In which ordinary parts of my family's history can I now see God at work?
The disciples' hands carried the bread. Whose hunger can my hands reach this week?

lead: Sarah dies, and Abraham, the man of the promise, must ask strangers for a place to bury her. He owns nothing in the land that God promised him. The epistle (Colossians 1:3–6) gives thanks for “the hope laid up for you in heaven”, which is the hope Abraham was living on. In the Gospel Jesus is asked for a sign from heaven and gives only the sign of Jonah. Faith is asked to walk on what God has said, with death still in view.

r.h: A stranger asks for a grave
set: A whole chapter of Genesis is given to one burial. Sarah is the only woman in Genesis whose age at death is told. She dies at Hebron, in Canaan, and Abraham, who has been living at Beer-sheba (22:19), “went in” to mourn. Then he has to do business. The “Hittites” here are the bənê ḥēt, the children of Heth (10:15). Whether they have any link with the great Hittite kingdom of Anatolia is uncertain, and many scholars take them as a local people of Canaan.
str: vv. 1–2: Sarah's death and Abraham's tears.
vv. 3–4: Abraham's request.
vv. 5–6: the Hittites' courteous offer of their best tombs.
vv. 7–9: Abraham bows, and asks for the cave of Ephron, at full price.
kw: Two words for someone who lives in a land without belonging to it. God will use them of all Israel: “with me you are but aliens and tenants” (Leviticus 25:23).
’Ăḥuzzāh is land held as a lasting right. Abraham does not want a favour. He wants a title.
Literally “a prince of God”, a Hebrew way of saying great or mighty. Abraham calls himself a stranger, and they call him a prince. God's blessing can be seen by others before its owner feels it.
vv: and Abraham went in to mourn for Sarah and to weep for her.
The man who did not hold back his son on Moriah now weeps for his wife. Faith does not forbid tears. At the tomb of Lazarus, “Jesus began to weep” (John 11:35).
I am a stranger and an alien residing among you
This is the voice of the one to whom God said, “To your offspring I will give this land” (12:7). Decades after that promise, he has to ask for a grave.
For the full price let him give it to me in your presence
He asks openly, and he offers to pay. The burial of the dead is worth doing properly, and the promise deserves a public first step.
ch: Hebrews makes this the model of pilgrim faith: “All of these died in faith without having received the promises… They confessed that they were strangers and foreigners on the earth” (11:13). St Peter calls Christians “aliens and exiles” (1 Peter 2:11). The Catechism says that Abraham lived as a stranger and pilgrim in the promised land by faith (CCC 145), and that the burial of the dead, with respect and in the hope of the resurrection, is a corporal work of mercy (CCC 2300).

r.h: No sign but the sign of Jonah
set: Pharisees and Sadducees were usually on opposite sides, on the resurrection for one thing (Acts 23:6–8). Here some of them come together to test Jesus. He has just fed the four thousand and healed many, and they ask for a sign from heaven. The word “test” is the verb used of the devil in the desert (4:1). A similar demand came earlier (12:38–40). The warning is for every generation that wants God on its own terms, ours included, and it is no judgment on a people.
str: v. 1: the demand.
vv. 2–3: reading the sky and reading the times.
v. 4: the sign of Jonah, and Jesus goes away.
kw: In the Gospels a sign points beyond itself. These men want a proof they can control, and Jesus does not offer that kind of sign.
Not time on the clock, but the moment of God's visit. The word “signs of the times” in v. 3 means what God is doing now, in Jesus.
The prophets use marriage for the covenant, and so unfaithfulness to God is called adultery (Hosea 2). The word is about the heart's fidelity.
vv: You know how to interpret the appearance of the sky, but you cannot interpret the signs of the times.

A note on the text. The words from “When it is evening” to the end of v. 3 are lacking in some important ancient manuscripts, as the NRSV's footnote says, and many scholars think they were added early. The Church reads them as part of the Gospel. The point is plain: people clever about the weather can be dull about God.
no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah.
