Matthew has already explained this: “just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the sea monster, so for three days and three nights the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth” (12:40). In Luke, Jonah is a sign to the people of Nineveh (11:30), who repented at his preaching.
Then he left them and went away.
This small sentence is one of the saddest in the passage. He does not force himself on anyone.
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus spoke of his Resurrection itself as the “sign of Jonah” (CCC 994). The Second Vatican Council took up the phrase of v. 3 and taught that the Church has the duty of scrutinizing the signs of the times and interpreting them in the light of the Gospel (Gaudium et Spes 4). The Syriac Churches keep the three-day Fast of Nineveh before the Great Fast, so this sign is close to our prayer.

study: Abraham wept, then he got up and did what love required. How do I carry grief, and whom do I need to help carry it?
What sign do I keep asking God for, when he has already given me the Cross and the empty tomb?

lead: Abraham and Ephron bargain at the city gate, and Abraham pays in full. The epistle (Ephesians 2:11–22) proclaims the peace that Christ has made: “he is our peace; in his flesh he has made both groups into one” (2:14). In the Gospel the disciples have forgotten the bread and are arguing about it, and Jesus asks them, “Do you still not perceive or understand?” The three readings ask what a thing is really worth, and whether we have eyes to see it.

set: The scene is at the city gate, which was the place of law and public business in the ancient Near East, as Ruth 4:1–11 also shows. Everything is said “in the hearing of” the townspeople, so they are witnesses. Many commentators read the exchange as courteous bargaining, in which “I give it to you” is the polite way to open. That is a reasonable reading, but we cannot be certain of it. Ephron is no villain, and the speech on both sides is polite.
str: vv. 10–11: Ephron offers the field and the cave.
vv. 12–13: Abraham bows, and insists on paying.
vv. 14–15: Ephron names the figure, almost in passing.
v. 16: Abraham weighs out the silver.
kw: all who went in at the gate of his city
A way of naming the full citizens. It tells us that this is a legal assembly, and it returns in v. 18 to seal the deal.

Not yet a coin but a weight, from šāqal, to weigh. So Abraham “weighed out” the silver. It is hard to compare prices over the centuries, but David paid fifty shekels for a threshing floor and oxen (2 Samuel 24:24), and Jeremiah paid seventeen for a field (Jeremiah 32:9). Most commentators think that four hundred was a very high price.
Literally “passing to the merchant”, silver of the weight accepted in trade. There will be no later dispute.
vv: I give you the field, and I give you the cave that is in it
It sounds like a gift. A gift, though, could leave Abraham in debt to Ephron and his title open to question, as many commentators note.
I will give the price of the field; accept it from me, so that I may bury my dead there.
Abraham also refused gifts from the king of Sodom (14:22–23). He wants nothing in the land to be owed to anyone but God.
Abraham weighed out for Ephron the silver that he had named in the hearing of the Hittites
He does not haggle. The price is paid in full and in public, and the first piece of the promised land passes to him honestly.
ch: David will say the same at another threshing floor: “I will not offer burnt offerings to the Lord my God that cost me nothing” (2 Samuel 24:24). The Catechism teaches that promises must be kept and contracts strictly observed (CCC 2410). On the coming Sunday the first lesson speaks of honest weights (Deuteronomy 25:13–16). For the Christian reader the price recalls another: “you were bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:20).

set: This scene comes straight after the demand for a sign (8:11–13), and shortly after the feeding of the four thousand. In the boat the disciples have one loaf, and they talk about bread. Mark then places the healing of the blind man of Bethsaida, the one healing done in two stages (8:22–26), and Peter's confession (8:27–30). The disciples, like that man, are coming to see by degrees.
str: v. 14: one loaf in the boat.
v. 15: the warning about the yeast.
v. 16: the misunderstanding.
vv. 17–18: a string of questions from Jesus.
vv. 19–20: the two feedings recalled.
v. 21: the last question.
kw: A little of it works through the whole lump. Paul uses it for an evil that spreads (1 Corinthians 5:6–8). Mark does not explain it here. Matthew 16:12 applies it to teaching, and Luke 12:1 to hypocrisy.

“Are your hearts hardened?” The heart in the Bible is the place of thought and decision. Mark uses it of Jesus' opponents (3:5) and also of the disciples (6:52), and here Jesus says it to their faces.
Mark keeps the two different words for the baskets of the two feedings, as Matthew does.
vv: they had only one loaf with them in the boat.

Mark takes care to say so, and many commentators think that he means more: the one loaf they have is Jesus himself, sitting in the boat. That cannot be proved, but it fits the question of v. 21. Compare “there is one bread” (1 Corinthians 10:17).
beware of the yeast of the Pharisees and the yeast of Herod.

The Pharisees and Herod's supporters appear together in 3:6, and Herod's fear of John comes in 6:14–29. The Pharisees have just asked for a sign, and they cannot stand for every Pharisee, as John 9:16 shows. What Jesus warns against is the settled mind that has seen and refuses to believe. That can be anyone's, and his next words show that the disciples are at risk of it.
Do you have eyes, and fail to see? Do you have ears, and fail to hear?
The words are those of the prophets (Jeremiah 5:21; compare Isaiah 6:9–10). Then Jesus does a surprising thing. He makes them count. “Twelve.” “Seven.” Their own memory holds the answer.
ch: The Catechism says that the human heart is heavy and hardened, and that God must give a new heart; conversion is first of all a work of God's grace (CCC 1432). That is the point of a Fast: we ask for a softened heart. And the Lord does not give up on slow disciples. He asks another question.

study: Abraham would not take for nothing what he could rightly pay for. Where do I need more honesty in my dealings?
What has God already done for me that I need to count up again, as the disciples had to count the baskets?

lead: The long story of the cave ends quietly: the field passes to Abraham and Sarah is laid to rest. All he ever owned of the promised land is a grave, and he holds it in hope. The epistle (Romans 3:27–31) says that boasting is excluded, that we are justified by faith, and that this does not overthrow the law: “we uphold the law” (3:31). In the Gospel Jesus, about to lay down his life, calls his disciples friends. Abraham, whom Scripture calls God's friend, stands behind the whole week.

r.h: A grave in the land of promise
set: These verses read like a deed of sale: the field, the cave, the trees, the boundaries, the witnesses. The care is on purpose. God promised this land to Abraham's offspring, yet St Stephen says God gave him none of it as a heritage, “not even a foot’s length” (Acts 7:5). This cave is the one piece of it that Abraham ever held. Abraham himself will be buried here (25:9–10), and Isaac, Rebekah, Leah and Jacob after him (49:29–32; 50:13). A great enclosure from the time of Herod still stands at the traditional site in Hebron, a place honoured by Jews, Christians and Muslims.
str: vv. 17–18: the property is described, and it passes to Abraham before witnesses.
v. 19: Sarah is buried.
v. 20: the title is confirmed.
kw: The name may be linked to a root meaning “double”. The ancient Greek and Latin translations speak of a “double cave”.
Literally “stood” or “was made firm”, a legal term here: the sale stands.
The phrase of v. 4 returns in v. 20, closing the chapter as it began. He asked for it and now it is his.
vv: the field with the cave that was in it and all the trees that were in the field, throughout its whole area
Even the trees are listed, which is the way contracts of that time could be written. In such plain detail the promise touches the ground for the first time.
After this, Abraham buried Sarah his wife in the cave of the field of Machpelah
The two who left Mesopotamia and lived in tents now have an address, and it is a tomb. Her burial is an act of love and also of faith, since her grave lies in the land God promised.
The field and the cave that is in it passed from the Hittites into Abraham’s possession as a burying place.
The first possession in the promised land is a place for the dead, kept in hope of the living God. Abraham “looked forward to the city that has foundations” (Hebrews 11:10).
ch: The Letter to the Hebrews says of the patriarchs, “they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one” (11:16). The Catechism says that the Christian meaning of death is revealed in the light of the Paschal mystery (CCC 1681), and that the bodies of the dead must be treated with respect and charity, in faith and hope of the resurrection (CCC 2300). The Christian word “cemetery” comes from a Greek word for a sleeping place. Abraham's cave is the first in a long line of graves dug in hope.

set: We are at the table on the night before the Passion, in the long discourse of John 13–17. Jesus has just spoken of the vine and the branches (15:1–10). Now he says what the fruit is: love, and the love he means has the shape of the next day. The word “friends” rises against a dark background, for he speaks it as one going to die.
str: v. 11: joy.
vv. 12–13: the commandment and its measure.
vv. 14–15: friends, not servants.
v. 16: chosen and sent to bear fruit.
v. 17: the commandment again.
kw: From phileō, to love. Isaiah 41:8 calls Abraham God's friend, and James 2:23 repeats it. What was said of the great patriarch Jesus now says to fishermen.
A slave takes orders without being told the purpose. Friendship shares the plan.
One verb serves in v. 13 (“lay down one’s life”) and in v. 16 (“I appointed you”). The friend who gives his life also gives his friends their mission.
vv: No one has greater love than this, to lay down one’s life for one’s friends.
Jesus is about to do this. Paul adds that he did it for us while we were still enemies and sinners (Romans 5:8–10), so the word “friends” does not limit the gift. It tells what he has made of us.
I do not call you servants any longer, because the servant does not know what the master is doing; but I have called you friends
“I have made known to you everything that I have heard from my Father.” The Son opens to us what he hears from the Father, and that is the root of Christian prayer.
You did not choose me but I chose you. And I appointed you to go and bear fruit, fruit that will last
In Jesus' time a student would choose a rabbi. Here the Master does the choosing. So the fruit is his gift, and it remains.
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus makes charity the new commandment (CCC 1823), and that the New Law lets us pass from the condition of a servant to that of a friend of Christ (CCC 1972). St Thomas Aquinas, citing this verse, teaches that charity is friendship between the human person and God (in substance; Summa Theologiae II-II, q. 23, a. 1).

qa: If we are no longer servants, do we still have to obey?

Yes. Jesus says, “You are my friends if you do what I command you” (15:14). Friendship does not cancel obedience. It changes its spirit: we obey one whom we love and whose plan we have been told, by the grace he gives. The saints still call themselves servants of the Lord, as Mary did.
study: Abraham buried Sarah in hope. How does my faith in the resurrection shape the way I treat my dead and visit their graves?
Jesus calls me friend. What would change in my prayer this week if I took that word seriously?

lead: Samio means the blind man, and on this Sunday, the last before Hosanna Sunday, the Fast asks the plainest of questions: can you see? The evening Gospel gives us blind Bartimaeus at Jericho, who cries out, “Son of David, have mercy on me!” and then follows Jesus on the way (Mark 10:46–52). The Old Testament lessons surround the theme. Deuteronomy asks for “a full and honest weight” (25:15). Solomon asks for “an understanding mind” (1 Kings 3:9). Jeremiah sings of the God “who made the earth by his power” (51:15). The Catholic Epistle tells Christians to rejoice “insofar as you are sharing Christ’s sufferings” (1 Peter 4:13).

We study three readings that belong together. Job, after all his arguing, says that he had only heard of God and now his eye sees him. Paul tells the Romans that those who think they see clearly must not despise a brother or sister who sees differently. In John a man blind from birth comes step by step to worship Jesus, while those sure of their own sight grow more and more blind. The key words are sight, judgment and light.

set: The Book of Job is a great poem on the suffering of the innocent. Its date and author are uncertain. Job's friends hold firmly that suffering must be punishment, and that Job must have sinned. Job insists that he has not, and he demands an answer from God. God finally speaks from the whirlwind (chapters 38–41). He does not explain Job's pain. He shows Job the wonders of creation and asks who he is to judge them.
Here we have Job's last words and God's verdict. The verdict is a surprise: God is angry with the friends who defended him with such neat answers, and he praises the man who argued with him.
str: vv. 1–6: Job's answer. He recalls God's words (vv. 3–4) and says what has changed.
vv. 7–8: God's anger at the friends, and his command.
v. 9: the friends obey, and God accepts Job's prayer.
kw: What one knows from what others say, even true things about God. Job's friends have a great deal of it.

This verb in v. 6, and the whole verse, is hard in Hebrew. It can mean to change one's mind, to be sorry, or to be comforted, and the first verb has no stated object. Translators differ. Most agree that Job gives up his claim to judge God, and does not confess to the sins his friends charged him with, since God goes on to praise him.
That which is firm and true. The friends defended God, and yet they did not speak rightly of him, since they turned him into a rule of cause and effect.
In vv. 7–8 God calls Job this four times. It is the title of Moses and of the Servant in Isaiah.
vv: I have uttered what I did not understand, things too wonderful for me, which I did not know.
Job is humbled and not crushed. God has not given him an answer, but he has given himself, and that turns out to be enough.
I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you

This is the verse of the day. The difference is between second-hand religion and meeting God. Job is no less in pain, and his children have not been restored to him yet. What has changed is that God is no longer only a subject of discussion.
you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has.
God prefers honest protest in prayer to tidy theology about him. The disciples of John 9:2 will ask the friends' question again: “who sinned?”
and the Lord accepted Job’s prayer.
The friends must go to the man they accused and ask him to pray for them. The sufferer becomes the intercessor.
ch: St James names Job as a model of endurance and says that “the Lord is compassionate and merciful” (James 5:11). St Gregory the Great, in his long Moralia on Job, reads Job also as a figure of Christ and of the Church (in substance). The Catechism admits that the experience of evil and suffering can shake our faith and become a temptation (CCC 164), and that no quick answer will do: the question of evil is answered only by the Christian faith as a whole (CCC 309). The fullest answer to Job's cry is the innocent Sufferer on the Cross.

set: Near the end of Romans (14:1–15:13) Paul turns to a quarrel in the Roman community. Some in the Church ate no meat, drank no wine, and kept certain days. Others felt no such duty. Many scholars think that the careful ones were mostly Christians who kept Jewish food customs or feared meat from pagan sacrifices, but Paul does not say. He calls them “the weak”, and he counts himself among “the strong” (15:1). And then he aims his warning chiefly at the strong.

Paul is speaking of matters that were then open questions among believers. He is not saying that the moral law is a matter of opinion: in 1:18–32 and in chapters 12–13 he is very clear about right and wrong.
str: vv. 10–12: we will all stand before God's judgment seat.
v. 13: do not judge; put no stumbling block in the way.
vv. 14–16: food is not unclean in itself, but love comes first.
vv. 17–19: what the kingdom truly is.
vv. 20–21: do not destroy God's work for the sake of food.
vv. 22–23: act from conviction.
kw: Something that trips a person on the way. From skandalon comes our word “scandal”: not what shocks someone, but what makes someone fall.
Literally “common”, the word for what is not ritually set apart. Paul is speaking of food, in line with Mark 7:19.
A builder's word. The test of what I do in the Church is whether it builds up the house or knocks it down.
In v. 23 it means the inner conviction that what I am doing is right before God, as v. 22 shows.
vv: Why do you pass judgment on your brother or sister? Or you, why do you despise your brother or sister?
The first question is for the careful one, who judges. The second is for the bold one, who despises. Each has a sin proper to his own position.
Do not let what you eat cause the ruin of one for whom Christ died.
This is the great argument. Before you claim your right, look at what the other person cost.
For the kingdom of God is not food and drink but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.
Said in the Great Fast, this keeps fasting in its place. A fast that makes me harsh toward others has missed the kingdom it was meant to serve.
for whatever does not proceed from faith is sin.
Paul means that acting against one's own conscience is sin. He does not teach that everything done by those outside the faith is sin; the Church has rejected that view.
ch: The Catechism quotes this chapter on conscience: charity always proceeds by way of respect for one's neighbour and his conscience, and it is right not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything that makes your brother stumble (CCC 1789). It uses v. 17 to speak of the kingdom in the Lord's Prayer (CCC 2819). It also keeps the needed distinction: we can judge that an act is gravely wrong, but we must entrust the judgment of persons to the justice and mercy of God (CCC 1861).

r.h: Though I was blind, now I see
set: John 7–8 is set at the Feast of Tabernacles, where Jesus has said, “I am the light of the world” (8:12). Chapter 9 shows that word in action. It is a carefully built drama. Jesus is absent from the middle of it, and the man who has been healed stands alone before his questioners.

Background. Jewish sources describe water being drawn from Siloam during Tabernacles and great lamps being lit in the Temple court. A stepped pool uncovered in Jerusalem in 2004 is widely identified as the pool of Jesus' time. Later Jewish law counts kneading among the labours forbidden on the sabbath, and the making of mud may have been seen in that way. That was a serious religious question for those who loved the sabbath.
str: vv. 1–7: the disciples' question and the healing.
vv. 8–12: the neighbours.
vv. 13–17: the first hearing before the Pharisees, who are divided.
vv. 18–23: the parents.
vv. 24–34: the second hearing, and the man is driven out.
vv. 35–38: Jesus finds him, and he worships.
vv. 39–41: who is really blind?

¶ The man's sight grows through the chapter: “The man called Jesus” (v. 11), “a prophet” (v. 17), one “from God” (v. 33), and then “Lord, I believe” (v. 38). His questioners go the other way, from a division among themselves to “We know that this man is a sinner” (v. 24) and to the man's expulsion.
kw: John himself translates the name. The Hebrew šilōaḥ (Isaiah 8:6) is related to the verb “to send”. Throughout this Gospel Jesus is the one sent by the Father, as in v. 4: “him who sent me”.
The word used in the Greek Old Testament for the clay of our making (Job 10:9; 33:6). Genesis 2:7 has “dust”, but the Fathers heard the Creator at work here.
This word occurs only in John (9:22; 12:42; 16:2). Many scholars think that it also reflects the painful separation between Church and synagogue in John's own time, later in the first century.
The word in v. 38. Earlier in the Gospel it is the word for worship in spirit and truth (4:23–24). The healing story ends with a man bowing in worship.
vv: Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?
This is the question of Job's friends. Jesus does not take it up, and he turns from blame to what God will do.
Neither this man nor his parents sinned; he was born blind so that God’s works might be revealed in him.

Jesus is not saying why every suffering exists, and the text does not picture God blinding a child for display. He says that this man's blindness is not a punishment, and that God is about to act in it.
he spat on the ground and made mud with the saliva and spread the mud on the man’s eyes
The verb is epichriō, to spread on or anoint. In that time saliva was often thought to have healing power. The Fathers saw more: the hands that shaped Adam are shaping eyes.
Go, wash in the pool of Siloam
He has to walk there blind, with mud on his face, trusting a word. Only then does he see. The Sent One sends him to the pool called Sent.
His parents said this because they were afraid of the Jews

Here “the Jews” means the religious authorities at that moment. The parents, the man, the disciples and Jesus himself are all Jews, and it is plainly not a people who are meant. The fear of the parents is a fear that many have known before those with power.
One thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see.
He does not know the theology and he refuses to pretend. A plain witness to what God has done is hard to argue with. The poor man teaches his teachers in vv. 30–33.
Jesus heard that they had driven him out, and when he found him, he said, “Do you believe in the Son of Man?”
The Lord goes looking for the man who has lost everything for him. He healed him once at the start, and now he comes back to him for the deeper healing.
He said, “Lord, I believe.” And he worshiped him.
Here is the true end of the miracle. The man's eyes had been opened at v. 7; now he sees.
But now that you say, ‘We see,’ your sin remains.
There is hope for one who says “I am blind”. The danger is to be sure that I do not need healing. This word is for all of us who know our religion well.
ch: The Catechism notes that Jesus used signs to heal, among them “mud and washing” (CCC 1504). It says that Baptism is called enlightenment, because those who receive it are enlightened in their understanding (CCC 1216). It also records that the religious authorities were not of one mind, and that some believed in Jesus (CCC 595–596). St Irenaeus says that the mud shows the hand of the Creator who first fashioned us (in substance). St Augustine, in his Tractates on John (44), sees the blind man as the human race, the mud as the Word made flesh, and the washing as Baptism (in substance). St Ephrem, too, in his commentary on the Diatessaron, sees the Creator's hand at work in the clay (in substance).

qa: Does God make people suffer in order to show his glory?

No. God does not delight in suffering, and he is not its author in that sense. The Gospel says only that this man's blindness was not a punishment and that God worked in it. The Church's answer to suffering is the whole of the faith, and above all the Cross, where God enters into it (CCC 309).
The man says, “God does not listen to sinners” (9:31). Is that true?

It is the man's own argument, from what his hearers already accept, and it has real force in the scene. It is not the Lord's teaching on prayer. The tax collector prays, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” and he goes home justified (Luke 18:13–14). God hears the repentant sinner.
Does this chapter blame the Jews?

No. Jesus, his disciples, the blind man and his parents were all Jews, and some of the Pharisees defended Jesus in this very chapter (9:16). The Church firmly teaches that the Jewish people as such are not to be blamed for what happened in the Passion (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597). The warning of v. 41 is addressed to anyone sure of his own sight, and first of all to those of us who are in the Church.
rite: Samio is the Syriac word for the blind man. With this Sunday our journey through the healing Sundays of the Great Fast is almost done: next Saturday is the Saturday of Lazarus and next Sunday is Hosanna. In our tradition Baptism is the washing and the light, and this Gospel is a catechism of Baptism. The cry of Bartimaeus is still in our mouths at every Holy Qurbono as we say Kurielaison. As Holy Week comes near, we may ask the Lord to anoint our eyes again. Before the mysteries of Holy Week, Confession is our walk to Siloam: a walk with mud on our face, on the strength of a word, and we return able to see.
study: Job says, “now my eye sees you”. Is my knowledge of God still mostly what I have heard from others? What would it mean to meet him?
Whom do I judge or despise in the Church because they keep the Fast or the faith differently from me? What does Paul ask of me?
The healed man lost his place in the community for telling the truth. Where am I tempted, like his parents, to say “ask him”?
Jesus says that those who say “We see” remain in their sin. Where am I most sure that I need no healing? What would it be to say, with Bartimaeus, “let me see again”?

lead: The sixth week of the Great Fast opens with three scenes about being sent. In Genesis the aged Abraham binds his servant by an oath and sends him on a long journey, trusting that God's angel will go ahead. In Ephesians 6:18–20 the writer asks for prayer as “an ambassador in chains”. In Mark the leaders in the Temple ask Jesus who gave him his authority, and he answers with a question about John the Baptist. The key words are oath, sent and authority.

set: Genesis 24 is the longest chapter of the book, and this week's Old Testament readings walk through it in portions. Sarah has died, and Abraham has bought a burial field at Machpelah, the only piece of the promised land he owns (Genesis 23). The promise of descendants now rests on Isaac, who has no wife.

Abraham's concern has two sides. Isaac must not marry among the Canaanites, and he must not go back to the old country. So someone else has to make the journey that Abraham himself once made in the opposite direction.
str: v. 1: Abraham is old and blessed.
vv. 2–4: the oath and the errand.
v. 5: the servant's sensible question.
vv. 6–8: Abraham's answer: do not take Isaac back; God's angel will go before you.
v. 9: the oath is sworn.
kw: Abraham is zāqēn in verse 1, and the servant is the zāqēn of his house in verse 2, the senior man who has charge of everything. The two old men together carry the future of a young man who does not appear in this scene.
The Hebrew word means one who is sent. Abraham sends a servant, and he is sure that God is sending someone too. The human errand runs inside a divine one.
A solemn promise made before God. Verse 8 shows that Abraham's oath has limits: the servant cannot be made to force a woman to come. Her consent will matter (24:57–58).
vv: Put your hand under my thigh

An ancient gesture of oath, found again in Genesis 47:29. Many scholars think “thigh” is a reverent way of speaking of the organs of generation, so that the oath touches life and descendants, the very subject of this chapter. The exact sense of the custom is not certain.
See to it that you do not take my son back there.
Abraham says this twice (24:6, 8). To return would be to undo the call of Genesis 12:1, “Go from your country”. A blessing received must not be traded for what seems safer.
he will send his angel before you
These verses are the last words of Abraham that Genesis records. They are words of trust: the God who called him will finish what he began, even after Abraham can no longer see it.
So the servant put his hand under the thigh of Abraham his master and swore to him concerning this matter.
The servant is never named in this chapter. Tradition has often thought of the Eliezer of Genesis 15:2, but the text leaves him without a name. All the attention goes to the one who sent him.
ch: The Letter to the Hebrews praises Abraham, who “set out, not knowing where he was going” (Hebrews 11:8), and the Catechism gathers up his faith at CCC 145–146. Here that faith has grown old and is still looking ahead. Origen, in his homilies on Genesis, reads the search for a bride as a spiritual picture (in substance), and many Fathers saw in the servant those whom God sends to gather a people for Christ. The Church keeps the plain story too: an old man's trust, and a faithful servant's obedience.

set: Jesus has entered Jerusalem and has driven the traders out of the Temple (11:15–19). In Mark's order, “these things” most naturally point to that action. The chief priests, the scribes and the elders are the groups Jesus named when he foretold his Passion (8:31). They have the care of the Temple, so their question is not strange in itself. Someone has acted there without any commission from them.
str: vv. 27–28: the question about authority.
vv. 29–30: Jesus' counter-question about John.
vv. 31–33a: the leaders talk it over and decline to answer.
v. 33b: Jesus declines in turn.
kw: The right to act, given by someone with the power to give it. Mark has used the word since the start: Jesus teaches “as one having authority” (1:22), and the Son of Man has authority to forgive sins (2:10).
A reverent way of saying “from God”. The choice Jesus offers is the choice about himself: is this from God, or is it only human?
vv: By what authority are you doing these things? Who gave you this authority to do them?
There are two questions: what kind of authority, and from whom? Each reader of Mark already knows the answer from the voice at the Jordan (1:11).
Did the baptism of John come from heaven, or was it of human origin?

Asking a question in reply was a normal way of arguing among teachers of the time. It is also the true answer. John pointed to Jesus, and Jesus was baptised by him. Whoever accepts John has the answer to his own question.
they were afraid of the crowd, for all regarded John as truly a prophet.
The men are not weighing what is true, only what each answer will cost. The sentence breaks off in the Greek as if their thoughts were overheard.
We do not know.
Jesus does not force the matter. A person who will not answer honestly about John is not ready to hear about the Son. He will speak again, in a parable, in the verses that follow (12:1–12).
ch: The Catechism says that the people and their leaders viewed Jesus as a rabbi, yet he “taught them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes” (CCC 581). This scene is about particular leaders at a particular moment, and it does not describe a people (CCC 597). In the Great Fast it is a question for each of us: when the truth would cost something, do we too say “we do not know”?

qa: Did Jesus avoid the question?

No. His question contains the answer. John's baptism came from God, John bore witness to Jesus, and at that baptism the Father spoke of his Son. Jesus refuses only to hand a truth to people who have just said they will not judge honestly about the truth they already have.
study: Abraham trusts God for a future he will not see. What future for your children or your parish do you need to leave in God's hands?
When has fear of what people would say kept you from saying what you knew to be true?

lead: In Genesis the servant reaches the end of his long road and begins with a prayer at a well. In Colossians 1:24–29 the apostle rejoices in his sufferings for the Body of Christ, and names the secret he preaches: “Christ in you, the hope of glory”. In Mark, Jesus tells his disciples for the second time that he will be handed over, killed and raised, and they are afraid to ask what he means. All three readings speak of a purpose larger than the person who serves it, and of how little that person may see at the start.

set: The servant travels north with ten camels and gifts to Aram-naharaim, “Aram of the two rivers”, in the north of Mesopotamia. The city of Nahor is the place where Abraham's brother and his family have settled (22:20–23). The journey itself is told in a single verse, because what matters is not the road but what happens at its end.

Wells were a meeting place in the ancient world, and the Bible tells several important meetings at them: Jacob and Rachel (Genesis 29), Moses and the daughters of Reuel (Exodus 2), Jesus and the woman of Samaria (John 4).
str: v. 10: the journey.
v. 11: the camels kneel at evening by the well.
vv. 12–14: the prayer: a request, the situation, and a sign.
kw: God's loyal love within a covenant. The servant uses it in verses 12 and 14 and thanks God for it in verse 27. He is asking God to be true to what he has promised Abraham.
Literally, “make it happen before me”. The verb comes from the root for something that happens or meets a person. The servant asks God to arrange the very thing that others would call chance.
vv: Then the servant took ten of his master’s camels
Ten camels are real wealth, and they will soon become a real test. A thirsty camel drinks a great deal.
O Lord, God of my master Abraham, please grant me success today

This is one of the first prayers for guidance in the Bible. The servant does not yet call the Lord “my God”. He comes under the faith of the one who sent him, and that is enough for his prayer to be heard.
Let the girl to whom I shall say, ‘Please offer your jar that I may drink,’

The sign he asks for is not a wonder in the sky. It tests character: a woman who gives water to a stranger and offers, unasked, to do the heavy work of watering his camels. He is looking for the mark of Abraham's own house, the hospitality of Genesis 18.
ch: The Catechism says that the wonder of prayer is revealed beside the well, where Christ comes to meet every human being (CCC 2560). This servant's prayer is short, concrete and made at work. It shows that one may ask God for help with an ordinary task on an ordinary evening. The Church does not teach us from this to test God with signs of our own devising (compare Deuteronomy 6:16). The servant's request rises out of an obedient errand, and it looks for a virtue, not for a spectacle.

r.h: The second foretelling of the Passion
set: Mark records three foretellings of the Passion on the road to Jerusalem (8:31; 9:31; 10:33–34). After each one the disciples misunderstand, and Jesus teaches them about service. This one comes after the Transfiguration and the healing of the boy at the foot of the mountain. They now pass through Galilee quietly, because Jesus is giving his time to teaching the disciples.
str: v. 30: the journey in secret.
v. 31: the teaching: handed over, killed, risen.
v. 32: they do not understand and are afraid to ask.
kw: The Greek verb paradidōmi covers what Judas does (14:10), what the Sanhedrin does in passing Jesus to Pilate (15:1), and what Pilate does (15:15). Many interpreters hear God's own plan behind the passive form here, since Paul uses the same verb when he says that the Father “gave him up for all of us” (Romans 8:32).
Jesus' favourite way of speaking of himself. Daniel 7:13 sees “one like a human being” receiving a kingdom. Here that glorious figure is put into human hands.
The ending is always part of the teaching. In all three of these foretellings in Mark, Jesus also foretells the Resurrection.
vv: He did not want anyone to know it;
There are no crowds on this stretch of the road. In the Great Fast too, the Lord takes his disciples aside to teach them what they could not take in among the crowds.
The Son of Man is to be betrayed into human hands, and they will kill him,
“Son of Man” and “human hands” make a sharp contrast in Greek, where the same word for human stands in both. The one who is truly human falls into the hands of others who share his humanity.
But they did not understand what he was saying and were afraid to ask him.
They may be afraid of the answer. In the very next verses they are arguing over which of them is the greatest (9:33–34). It is easy to find a safe subject when the Lord has just spoken of the Cross.
ch: The Church teaches that Jesus' death was not the result of chance, but belongs to the mystery of God's plan, as Peter says at Pentecost (CCC 599; Acts 2:23). The Catechism also says that from Peter's confession onward the Master began to show his disciples what he must suffer (CCC 554). Mark's disciples are a comfort to anyone who has not understood the Cross at the first hearing. They were slow, and they were afraid, and yet the Lord kept teaching them.

qa: In today's epistle Colossians says, “I am completing what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions”. Is something lacking in the Cross?

Nothing is lacking in the redemption Christ won. The Cross is complete. The verse speaks of Christ's body, the Church, whose suffering goes on until the end, and the apostle shares in it by serving her. The Catechism applies this verse to all who suffer in union with Christ (CCC 1508), and St John Paul II develops it in Salvifici Doloris 24. Many scholars think a disciple wrote Colossians in Paul's name, while others hold that Paul wrote it. The Church receives it as inspired Scripture in either case.
study: The servant prays in the middle of his work, in a few plain words. What task this week could you begin in the same way?
Is there something about the Cross that you are afraid to ask the Lord about, as the disciples were?

lead: In Genesis the prayer of the servant is answered before he has finished it, and Rebekah gives far more than she is asked. In Ephesians 5:1–4 the Christian is told to be an imitator of God and to live in love, as Christ “gave himself up for us”. In Luke, Jesus opens the scroll at Nazareth and reads his own mission: good news to the poor and release to captives. All three speak of generous giving, and the Church today remembers St Patrick, who once was a slave in Ireland and went back to bring the Gospel to the land of his captivity.

set: The narrator tells us who Rebekah is before the servant knows it: she belongs to Abraham's own family, the granddaughter of his brother Nahor (see 22:20–23). The reader watches and waits while the servant, who does not yet know, sees her come down to the spring and go up again with a full jar. The test he set in his prayer now unfolds in front of him.
str: vv. 15–16: Rebekah arrives.
vv. 17–20: the request, and more than the request.
v. 21: the servant watches in silence.
vv. 22–25: gifts, and the question about her family.
vv. 26–27: he bows down and blesses God.
kw: “Quickly” in verses 18 and 20, joined by “ran” in verse 20 and, in tomorrow's reading, verse 28. The storyteller lets the speed of the verbs show the generosity of a young woman who does not count the cost.
The classic pair of words for God's covenant loyalty. The servant had asked for ḥesed. When it comes, he sees that it has come with ’ĕmet, fidelity, which is the firm reliability of God.
A young woman not yet married. The narrator adds “whom no man had known” so that the point is clear. She can be promised to Isaac.
vv: Before he had finished speaking, there was Rebekah,
The narrator stresses how sudden this is. Isaiah will say of God: “while they are yet speaking I will hear” (Isaiah 65:24). The answer was already on its way while the servant was still praying.
I will draw for your camels also, until they have finished drinking.
This is the very sign the servant asked for, and she goes further: “until they have finished”. Ten camels mean many trips down to the spring and up again, for a stranger, at the end of the day.
The man gazed at her in silence to learn whether or not the Lord had made his journey successful.
He does not rush to a conclusion. Faith has its own way of watching: it has prayed, and now it looks to see what God is doing.
As for me, the Lord has led me on the way
His blessing has been all about “my master”. At its close he adds a word about himself: the servant has walked into a story and found that God was leading him as well.
ch: Origen in his homilies on Genesis notes that Rebekah came to the well every day, and sees in her the soul that comes each day to the wells of Scripture and so meets the servant of God (in substance). Many readers have seen in the scene at the well the pattern of John 4, where Jesus asks for a drink and the woman receives far more. The Catechism begins its teaching on prayer at that very well (CCC 2560). In the Great Fast, Rebekah teaches that charity does not stop at what is required.

r.h: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me”
set: Luke places this visit at the start of Jesus' public work, right after the temptation in the desert. It serves as the opening statement of his whole ministry. In the synagogue service of that time a passage of Scripture would be read and then explained. Jesus stands to read, as a member of the community might, and the scroll of Isaiah is handed to him.

What he reads is mainly Isaiah 61:1–2, with one line added from Isaiah 58:6 (“to let the oppressed go free”). Luke's quotation stops before Isaiah's next line, “and the day of vengeance of our God”, and the reading ends on the Lord's favour.
str: v. 16: Nazareth, the sabbath, his custom.
v. 17: the scroll.
vv. 18–19: the text: the Spirit, the anointing, and the four groups who receive the good news.
¶ The reading stops before the verses about his sermon and its reception (4:20–30).
kw: From the same root as Christos, the Anointed One, the Greek for Messiah. Luke has just told of the Spirit descending at the Jordan (3:22). Here is the meaning of that anointing.

Used twice in these verses, and also Luke's usual word for the forgiveness of sins (1:77; 3:3; 24:47). In the Greek Old Testament it is the word for the Jubilee release in Leviticus 25. Debt, slavery and sin are all held together under one word.
the year of the Lord's favor
Many commentators hear the Jubilee here, the year when slaves went home and land returned to its families (Leviticus 25:10). Jesus announces a time of grace that is not bound to the calendar.
vv: He stood up to read,
Luke notes that going to the synagogue “on the sabbath day” was “his custom”. Jesus' mission begins inside the faithful worship of his people, and not in opposition to it.
The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to bring good news to the poor.
The Spirit, the Lord and the Anointed One are named together. The first of those to receive the good news are the poor, those who have no one to lean on but God.
to proclaim release to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind,
Luke will show each of these things happening: the unclean spirit driven out (4:35), the blind man seeing (18:42), the sinful woman forgiven (7:48).
to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor.
The reading breaks off here, on a note of welcome. In the next verse Jesus will sit down and say that this has been fulfilled today (4:21).
ch: The Catechism says that Christ inaugurates the proclamation of the Good News by making this passage of Isaiah his own (CCC 714). It is why the Church serves the poor as part of her mission and not as something added on. In the Fast, when we are asked to give what we save, this reading says whom it is for.

qa: Why did Luke leave out “the day of vengeance” from Isaiah?

Luke does not explain, and we should not say more than the text does. Judgment is not removed from Jesus' teaching: he speaks of it elsewhere in Luke. Yet by closing on the Lord's favour, the passage places this first announcement under the sign of grace. Many commentators see in this a deliberate emphasis on the present time as a time of mercy.
rite: The Church today commemorates St Patrick, bishop and apostle of Ireland, of the fifth century. He tells in his own Confession that as a youth in Roman Britain he was captured by raiders and made a slave in Ireland, where he kept flocks and learned to pray, and that after escaping he went back as a bishop to preach to the people who had enslaved him. He also wrote a strong letter against a chief whose soldiers had carried off newly baptised Christians. Today's Gospel of release to captives was something he had lived in his own flesh.
study: Rebekah does more than she was asked. Where is the Lord asking you this week to go past what is merely required?
St Patrick returned to those who had wronged him, in order to bring them the Gospel. Whom might you serve or pray for in that spirit?

lead: In Genesis a servant, with food set before him, refuses to eat until he has told his errand, and when he speaks, he speaks of his master. In Colossians 3:12–17 the baptised are told to clothe themselves with love and to let “the word of Christ dwell in you richly”. In Matthew, Jesus tells his disciples that they are salt and light, so that others may give glory to the Father. The readings suit the memory of Mar Cyril of Jerusalem, who spent his strength passing the faith on to those preparing for Baptism. The key words are errand, word and light.

r.h: “I will not eat until I have told my errand”
set: Rebekah runs home, Laban runs out to the well, and the guest is brought in. Laban will be a major figure in the story of Jacob (Genesis 29–31), where he shows himself a shrewd man in matters of property. The narrator's small remark about the nose-ring and the bracelets prepares for that, yet Laban is courteous here, and he speaks a true blessing.

From verse 34 the servant begins to tell again what we have already read. This long repetition is a feature of ancient storytelling. It lets the hearer enjoy how the events are retold and notice how the speaker fits them to his listeners. Today's reading stops at verse 41, in the middle of his speech.
str: vv. 28–32: the welcome: Laban, the camels, water for the feet.
v. 33: the refusal to eat.
vv. 34–36: “I am Abraham’s servant”; the Lord's blessing on Abraham and Isaac.
vv. 37–41: the oath retold.
kw: The servant says, in effect, “I will not eat until I have spoken my words.” The same Hebrew word means both a word and the thing it concerns. His mission is a word to be delivered.
Laban's greeting in verse 31. In verse 35 the servant will say that the Lord has “blessed” his master. Blessing is the thread that ties this chapter to the call of Abraham (12:2–3).
Found in verses 21, 40, 42 and 56. The verb says that a journey arrives where it should. The success belongs to God, and the servant says so at each step.
vv: As soon as he had seen the nose-ring, and the bracelets on his sister’s arms,
The narrator gives this detail quietly and makes no comment. The reader who knows the later story smiles. Yet God's plan moves forward through a man whose motives are mixed.
Come in, O blessed of the Lord.
Laban speaks the truth, perhaps without knowing how much truth it is. The hospitality that Abraham showed in Genesis 18 is shown here in turn to Abraham's servant.
I will not eat until I have told my errand.

In the ancient world the meal came first when a guest arrived. The servant holds it back. There is a kind of fasting in this: what he has been sent to do comes before his hunger. Compare Jesus at the well: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me” (John 4:34).
I am Abraham’s servant.
His first words about himself are the only ones he needs. He gives no name and asks for no honour, and for the rest of the speech he talks about his master and his master's God.
ch: The Church has seen in this nameless servant a model of everyone who carries the Gospel. Paul describes the same attitude: “we do not proclaim ourselves; we proclaim Jesus Christ as Lord and ourselves as your slaves for Jesus’ sake” (2 Corinthians 4:5). The Catechism says that the whole of catechesis is a passing on of the teaching not of oneself but of Christ, who said, “My teaching is not mine” (CCC 427–428; John 7:16). Any catechist can learn that from this scene.

r.h: Salt of the earth, light of the world
set: These verses come straight after the Beatitudes (5:3–12). Jesus has just called blessed the poor in spirit, the meek and the persecuted. Now he tells those same people, a small band on a hillside in Galilee, what they are for the whole world. He does not say “you ought to be” but “you are”.
str: v. 13: salt and its loss.
vv. 14–15: light: the city and the lamp.
v. 16: the point: good works, and glory to the Father.
kw: Salt gave flavour and kept food from spoiling, and in the Old Testament it was added to offerings and tied to the covenant (Leviticus 2:13; Numbers 18:19). The image is simple and need not be limited to one of those meanings.
The Greek verb usually means “to be made foolish”. Commentators often point out the double sense: a disciple who no longer gives flavour has also lost his wisdom.
Isaiah says that God's servant is “a light to the nations” (Isaiah 49:6), and in John, Jesus says “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). The disciples shine with a light that is his.
vv: You are the salt of the earth;
The “you” is plural and is said to the whole company. Salt is useful only when it mixes with something other than itself.
A city built on a hill cannot be hid.
Hearers may have thought of Jerusalem and the mountain of the Lord, to which the nations were to come (Isaiah 2:2–3). Some scholars see that image here. A community cannot hide what it is.
No one after lighting a lamp puts it under the bushel basket,
The bushel was a household measuring vessel. A house in a Galilean village might be a single room, so one lamp on a stand could light the whole family.
so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father in heaven.

This does not contradict the warning in 6:1–4 against doing good in order to be seen. The difference lies in where the glory goes. Works done for our own name hide the Father; works done for him show him.
ch: The Second Vatican Council opens its teaching on the Church with the words that Christ is the light of the nations (Lumen Gentium 1). The Catechism adds a favourite image of the Fathers: the Church is like the moon, all its light reflected from the sun (CCC 748). The Catechism says that the fidelity of the baptised is a primary condition for the proclamation of the Gospel (CCC 2044). What the world will see first is not our doctrine in a book but our works, which by grace point to the Father.

qa: Why does the Bible repeat the story in Genesis 24 at such length?

Ancient storytellers often did this, and hearers enjoyed it. Here the repetition has a purpose as well. Each time the story is told, God's guidance is confessed again. The servant is not only reporting events; he is showing his hearers that the Lord is at work, so that they can say, as they do in verse 50, “The thing comes from the Lord.”
rite: Today the Church remembers Mar Cyril (Koorilos), bishop of Jerusalem and doctor of the Church, who died in 386. He was driven from his see more than once in the disputes of the fourth century. His Catechetical Lectures, given in Jerusalem to those preparing for Baptism, are among the most precious witnesses to the early Church's teaching. In a Great Fast, which from ancient times was a time of preparing for Baptism, he stands beside today's servant as a man who passed on what he received.
study: When you speak of your faith, how much is about yourself and how much about the Lord?
Name one good work in your parish or home that could become a light to others, without drawing attention to the ones doing it.

lead: Two celebrations meet today. The Great Fast reaches its Fortieth Friday, and the Church keeps the feast of Mar Yauseph, spouse of the Virgin Mary, with his own readings. The evening Gospel (Matthew 4:1–11) and the Gospel of the Holy Qurbono (Luke 4:1–13) both tell of Jesus in the desert, and beside them stands Genesis 3, the temptation in the garden. Three other lessons ask what a true offering is: David will not offer what costs him nothing (2 Samuel 24:18–25), Jeremiah warns those who trust in the Temple without justice (Jeremiah 7:1–7), and Isaiah names “the fast that I choose” (Isaiah 58:1–8). Then 1 Peter 1:13–21 recalls the price of our redemption, and Romans 14:1–9 says that whether we eat or abstain, live or die, we belong to the Lord.

St Joseph's readings seem at first to be another subject, but they fit. Where Adam and Eve doubted God's word, Joseph, like Abraham, took God at his word when everything seemed to say otherwise. Hoping against hope, he did as the angel commanded. The key words are tempted, it is written and he did.

set: Genesis 2 has shown a garden full of gift. Every tree may be eaten from, except one (2:16–17). Chapter 2 ended with the man and woman “naked, and … not ashamed” (2:25). Genesis 3 tells how that peace was broken. The Catechism says that this account uses figurative language but affirms a primeval event that took place at the beginning of human history (CCC 390).
The story is told simply, and it is not about a fruit. It is about whether the creature can trust the Creator's word.
str: v. 1: the serpent's question, which distorts God's command.
vv. 2–3: the woman's reply, which adds to it.
vv. 4–5: the open denial and the promise: “you will be like God”.
v. 6: seeing, taking, eating, giving.
v. 7: the eyes are opened, on nakedness and shame.
kw: A wordplay in Hebrew. The man and woman were ‘ărûmmîm, “naked” (2:25), and the serpent is ‘ārûm, “crafty”. One word is just a sound away from the other. The next thing they will learn is that they are naked in a new way.

A created wild animal, as the verse says, so it is not a rival god. Later Scripture sees behind it the devil: “through the devil’s envy death entered the world” (Wisdom 2:24; see Revelation 12:9; CCC 391).
Commentators explain the phrase in various ways. Many take it to mean deciding for oneself what is good and what is evil, in place of receiving it from God. That is what the serpent offers.
vv: Did God say, ‘You shall not eat from any tree in the garden’?
The first temptation begins with a question that turns God's generosity into a prohibition. God had given every tree but one. The serpent makes him sound like a God who gives none.
You will not die;
The question has become a flat denial. Temptation usually moves in these two stages: first “is that really what God said?”, then “it will not harm you.”
good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise,

A threefold attraction: appetite, the eye, and pride of mind. 1 John 2:16 has a similar list (“the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, the pride in riches”). In Luke's Gospel today the tempter comes with three offers.
Then the eyes of both were opened, and they knew that they were naked;
The serpent's promise comes true in a bitter way. Their eyes open, and what they see is their own shame. They make a covering, but it is God who will clothe them (3:21).
ch: The Catechism says: “Man, tempted by the devil, let his trust in his Creator die in his heart and, abusing his freedom, disobeyed God's command. This is what man's first sin consisted of” (CCC 397). The Church reads this passage only in the light of Christ, for the doctrine of original sin is, so to speak, the “reverse side” of the Good News that Jesus is the Savior of all (CCC 389). Paul sets the two men side by side: “by the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19).
In the Syriac tradition, Mar Aprem and others speak of Adam and Eve as clothed in a robe of glory which they lost when they sinned, and which Christ restores to us in Baptism (in substance).

set: Paul writes to the Christians of Rome, a church he has not yet visited, some time in the 50s. Chapters 12–15 turn to daily life. In this chapter the community is divided over food and holy days. Some are “weak in faith” and abstain from certain foods; others eat anything. Many scholars think the “weak” were mostly believers who kept Jewish food and calendar customs, and the “strong” mostly believers of Gentile background, though the text does not say so directly. Paul himself sides with the “strong” on the question (15:1), but his interest lies elsewhere: how they treat one another.
str: v. 1: the command: welcome.
vv. 2–4: on food: neither despise nor judge.
vv. 5–6: on days: each one in honour of the Lord.
vv. 7–9: the ground of it all: we belong to the Lord, in life and in death.
kw: “Receive” into one's company, as one receives a person into a home. Paul returns to the word at the end: “Welcome one another … just as Christ has welcomed you” (15:7).
This does not mean those who believe less in Christ. It refers here to a conscience not yet at ease about certain practices. Paul uses the word without contempt.
The word in verse 9. The whole passage has been leading to this: Christ died and rose to be Lord of the dead and the living. The right to judge a servant belongs to his master (14:4).
vv: Welcome those who are weak in faith, but not for the purpose of quarreling over opinions.
Welcome that is really a chance to argue is not welcome at all. Parishes know this temptation.
while those who abstain, abstain in honor of the Lord and give thanks to God.

Paul does not make fasting unimportant. He gives it its true direction. To abstain “in honor of the Lord” is the very reason for a fast. What he rules out is using one's own practice as a measure of another person's standing before God.
We do not live to ourselves, and we do not die to ourselves.
The Catechism quotes this verse on the communion of saints: no one's life or death concerns that person alone (CCC 953).
so then, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s.
This is one of the great sentences of Christian comfort. At the end of a long fast, it says what the fast has been teaching: we belong to him.
ch: The Catechism opens its teaching on Christ's reign with verse 9: “Christ died and lived again, that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living” (CCC 668). The Church's own laws of fasting are not cancelled by these words. Paul's concern is charity among believers over matters on which they differ. The Church's discipline serves the same aim that he names: all is done “in honor of the Lord”.

set: Luke has just told of Jesus' baptism (3:21–22), and has traced his genealogy back through Adam, who is called “son of God” (3:38). So the next scene follows closely on the words “Adam, son of God”, and here another Son of God faces the tempter. The forty days also recall Israel's forty years in the desert, where the people were tested and often failed (Deuteronomy 8:2), and the fasts of Moses (Exodus 34:28) and Elijah (1 Kings 19:8).
All three of Jesus' answers come from Deuteronomy (8:3; 6:13; 6:16). The devil's one quotation comes from Psalm 91:11–12.
str: vv. 1–2: the Spirit, the wilderness, the fast.
vv. 3–4: bread.
vv. 5–8: kingdoms.
vv. 9–12: the Temple.
v. 13: the devil departs “until an opportune time”.
¶ Matthew puts the Temple second and the kingdoms last. Luke ends in Jerusalem, the city toward which his whole Gospel moves.
kw: The same Greek word means both. What is a test from God's side is a temptation from the devil's side. The Spirit leads Jesus into the desert, and the devil uses the occasion for his own purposes.
Literally “the slanderer”, one who throws a false charge. In Genesis 3 he slanders God; here he tries to do the same with the Father's care for his Son.
A fitting moment, as opposed to mere clock time. Luke will show the tempter returning at the Passion: “Then Satan entered into Judas” (22:3). The struggle in the desert will come again.
vv: Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit in the wilderness,
Being full of the Spirit does not protect him from the desert; it leads him there. A person may be in temptation and yet exactly where God wants him to be.
If you are the Son of God, command this stone to become a loaf of bread.

The voice at the Jordan said “You are my Son” (3:22), and the devil begins by casting doubt on it. The temptation is to use his sonship for himself, whereas later he will give bread to thousands (9:12–17) and give himself as bread.
If you, then, will worship me, it will all be yours.
This offers the kingdom without the Cross. The Father will indeed give him all, by way of the road the devil tries to spare him.
for it is written, ‘He will command his angels concerning you, to protect you,’
The devil can quote Scripture. Knowing the words is not enough; they must be read with a heart that trusts God and does not try to force his hand.
When the devil had finished every test, he departed from him until an opportune time.
“Every” test: these three stand for the whole of temptation. Hebrews says of Christ: “one who in every respect has been tested as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15).
ch: The Catechism says: “Jesus is the new Adam who remained faithful just where the first Adam had given in to temptation” (CCC 539), and that the Church unites herself each year to the mystery of Jesus in the desert (CCC 540). St Irenaeus taught that the Lord fought as a man, and overcame the enemy in the very flesh in which Adam had been overcome (Against Heresies 5.21, in substance). The answer to each temptation is the same in every age: not a clever argument, but obedience to the word of God.

set: Paul has been arguing that God's promise came to Abraham before circumcision and before the Law, and that it came by faith (4:9–15). The conclusion is that Abraham is the father of all who believe, whatever their origin. On the feast of St Joseph, the Church sets the father of faith beside the man who received in faith the child promised to Abraham's line.
str: v. 16: faith, so that the promise may rest on grace.
v. 17: the God who gives life to the dead.
v. 18: hope against hope.
kw: The promise is a gift, and faith is how it is received. Paul is not setting faith against the good works that faith produces (see Romans 2:6; Galatians 5:6), but saying that God's gift comes first.
A play on one word in Greek. “Against” all human reason for hope, and “upon” the hope God gives.
vv: he is the father of all of us,

“Our father Abraham” is a title dear to Israel. Paul widens the circle without removing anyone from it: the promise is “not only to the adherents of the law” but also to those who share Abraham's faith.
who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist.
Abraham's and Sarah's bodies were beyond childbearing. His faith was in a God who creates from nothing and raises the dead. The verse foreshadows Easter, and Lazarus tomorrow.
Hoping against hope, he believed
The Catechism quotes these words on the virtue of hope (CCC 1819). It takes up the hope of Israel, whose origin and model is the hope of Abraham.
ch: The Church honours Abraham as the model of the obedience of faith (CCC 144–146), and Joseph is the one who, at the end of the long line from Abraham, believes in the same manner. St John Paul II says in Redemptoris Custos that in doing what the angel commanded, Joseph showed the “obedience of faith”, and so shared from the first in Mary's faith (sections 4–5, in substance).

r.h: Joseph did as the angel commanded
set: Matthew has just given Jesus' genealogy through the line of David, and has ended it with an unusual phrase: “Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born” (1:16). The present passage explains how this can be. Jesus is truly son of David through Joseph, who gives him legal fatherhood by naming him, and yet he is not conceived by a man.

In Jewish custom of the time, betrothal was a binding legal bond. The couple were already called husband and wife, and it could be ended only by a formal divorce, though they did not yet live together. This is why Joseph is called “husband” and why he must “dismiss” her.
str: v. 18: the situation.
v. 19: Joseph's decision.
vv. 20–21: the angel in the dream.
vv. 22–23: the fulfilment of Isaiah.
vv. 24–25: Joseph's obedience.
¶ Joseph speaks no word in this passage, or anywhere else in the Gospels. All his answers are actions.
kw: In Matthew, the word for a person whose life is shaped by God's Law. Joseph's righteousness shows itself as mercy. Being “righteous” and being unwilling to shame her are held together in one verse.
The Greek form of the Hebrew Yeshua, “the Lord saves”. To name a child was the father's right. In naming him, Joseph takes the child as his own, and the name says what the child will do.

The Greek Old Testament's word in Isaiah 7:14, where the Hebrew has ‘almāh, a young woman of marriageable age. Matthew reads the Greek and sees its full sense in Mary. The Church confesses that Jesus was conceived by the power of the Holy Spirit in the womb of the Virgin Mary (CCC 496–497).
vv: Her husband Joseph, being a righteous man and unwilling to expose her to public disgrace, planned to dismiss her quietly.
Joseph has made a just and gentle decision, but God has something else in mind. God does not rebuke him; he gives him more light. His goodness had reached as far as he could see.
Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife,
The angel calls him by his royal title, and it matters. The Catechism says that this is how Jesus comes to be born of Joseph's spouse into the messianic line of David (CCC 437).
for he will save his people from their sins.
Not from Rome or from their enemies, as some might have hoped. The name of the child states his mission in plain words. It is the answer to Genesis 3.
which means, “God is with us.”
The Gospel opens with this and closes with the Lord's own promise: “I am with you always, to the end of the age” (28:20). Matthew's whole Gospel lies between the two.
When Joseph awoke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him;

This is the first of several times that Joseph rises and obeys (2:14, 21). In Eden, the word of God was doubted and then disobeyed. Here it is received in a dream, in the middle of a crisis, and it is done at once.
ch: The Fathers did not all read Joseph's hesitation the same way. St John Chrysostom praises the gentleness of a man who would not shame her even though he could not explain what had happened. St Jerome, in his commentary on Matthew, thinks Joseph knew Mary's purity and, in the face of a mystery he did not understand, kept silence (both in substance). Either way, he is righteous.

St John Paul II wrote on him in Redemptoris Custos (1989), and Pope Francis in Patris Corde (2020), where he describes Joseph as a father in the shadows, obedient, accepting and courageous. Our own tradition calls him Mar Yauseph, and the feast keeps his quiet obedience before our eyes as Hasha Week approaches.

qa: Matthew says Joseph “had no marital relations with her until she had borne a son”. Does this mean they did afterwards?

No. The Greek word for “until” (heōs) says what did not happen up to a certain time, and says nothing about what came after. Matthew's concern is that Jesus was not conceived by Joseph. The Church confesses Mary's perpetual virginity (CCC 499–501), and notes that the “brothers of Jesus” are close relations in the biblical manner of speaking (CCC 500).
Does Romans 14 mean that fasting does not matter?

No. Paul honours those who abstain “in honor of the Lord” (14:6), and Jesus himself fasted, as today's Gospels show. Paul is speaking of how believers treat one another when they differ. What he condemns is contempt and judging, not fasting. The Fast is a gift the Church gives her children, kept with charity toward those who, through illness or age or other reason, keep it differently.
If Jesus could not sin, were his temptations real?

They were real. The Letter to the Hebrews says he “in every respect has been tested as we are, yet without sin” (4:15). Hunger, the offer of power and the invitation to test God were real pressures on a real human will. That he did not give in does not make the struggle less. It means he knew its full force, since he never gave way before it had done its worst.
rite: The Fortieth Friday is a turning point for our Church. The Panchangam notes that today there is no fasting and there are no forty prostrations (kumbideel). Tomorrow is the Saturday of Lazarus, and on Sunday we bring palm leaves and flowers for Hosanna. Today's readings gather up what the Great Fast has taught, a return to God's word and a fast that feeds the hungry, and hand us on to the days of the Lord's Passion in the company of a man who said nothing and did what he was told.
study: The serpent's first move is to make God sound less generous than he is. In what area of your life are you tempted to see God in that way?
Jesus answers each temptation with a word of Scripture. Which verse from these readings will you take with you into Hasha Week?
Joseph's first decision was gentle and good, but God asked for more. When has God changed a plan you had made in good conscience?
How can your parish keep the fast with one another in the spirit of Romans 14, without contempt or judging?

lead: Between the Fortieth Friday and Hosanna Sunday stands the Saturday of Lazarus. Before the Lord enters his city to die, he goes to the tomb of a friend, weeps, and calls the dead man out. The three readings stand around that scene. Genesis ends its long story of the servant with a young woman's word, “I will”, and she leaves her home to go to a bridegroom she has never seen. Paul says that Christ is “the first fruits” and that “the last enemy to be destroyed is death”. John shows the same victory in one family's grief, at one tomb. The key words are I will, first fruits and come out.

set: This week's readings have followed the servant from Abraham's house to the well and into the home of Rebekah's family. The verses just before today's reading (24:42–49) finish his account and end with a plain request: tell me whether you will deal loyally with my master.

Marriages in that world were arranged between families, and this one is too. So the moment in verses 57–58 stands out all the more, when her own consent is asked for and given. Abraham had foreseen that “the woman” might not be willing (24:8), and the narrator lets her decide.
str: vv. 50–51: the family's answer: “The thing comes from the Lord”.
vv. 52–54a: the servant worships; gifts; a meal, at last.
vv. 54b–56: the request to go, and the plea for delay.
vv. 57–58: the question to Rebekah, and her answer.
vv. 59–61: the blessing and the departure.
kw: Rebekah's whole answer in Hebrew is this one word. It comes from hālak, the verb of God's call to Abraham: “Go from your country” (12:1). She makes the same journey in faith that he made.
An extravagant blessing of descendants, spoken by people who cannot know how it will come true.

“Gain possession of the gates of their foes” repeats, almost word for word, what God promised Abraham after the binding of Isaac: “your offspring shall possess the gate of their enemies” (22:17). Without knowing it, Rebekah's family blesses her with God's own promise.
vv: The thing comes from the Lord; we cannot speak to you anything bad or good.
Laban and Bethuel recognise what has been happening. The servant's careful retelling has done its work. The story that was told as God's doing is now confessed as God's doing.
Do not delay me, since the Lord has made my journey successful;
Ten days seems little to ask, and it is a natural plea from a mother. The servant's urgency is the same as in his refusal to eat. When God has acted, one goes.
Will you go with this man?” She said, “I will.

This is the high point of the chapter, in a single word. She is told little and has no guarantee. Mary's “let it be with me according to your word” (Luke 1:38) comes to the Christian reader's mind at once.
May you, our sister, become thousands of myriads;
The blessing goes with her on the road. It is a good thing for a family that cannot keep a daughter to send her with such words.
Then Rebekah and her maids rose up, mounted the camels, and followed the man;
The camels she watered now carry her. She “follows” a servant toward someone she has not seen.
ch: The Fathers saw in this journey the Church going to Christ. The first letter of Peter describes the same love: “Although you have not seen him, you love him” (1 Peter 1:8). St Ambrose wrote on Isaac and on the soul as a bride going to her bridegroom (On Isaac, or the Soul, in substance). On the eve of Hosanna, the question to Rebekah is put to each of us: will you go with him, along this road, this week?

set: Some in Corinth were saying that “there is no resurrection of the dead” (15:12). Paul has answered that if that were so, Christ was not raised, and faith is futile (15:13–19). Now he turns: “But in fact Christ has been raised”. He then sets out what follows from it, from Adam to the very end of all things.

He writes around the years 54 or 55, and this is among the oldest Christian writing we have on the Resurrection. A few verses earlier he has handed on an ancient list of those who saw the risen Lord (15:3–8).
str: v. 20: Christ the first fruits.
vv. 21–22: Adam and Christ.
vv. 23–24: the order: Christ; those who are his; the end.
vv. 25–27: he must reign (Psalm 110; Psalm 8); death is the last enemy.
v. 28: the Son and the Father: God all in all.
kw: The first sheaf of the harvest was offered to God (Leviticus 23:10–11), and it stood for the whole harvest to come. Christ's Resurrection is not a single wonder that stands alone. It is the start of the harvest in which we too will be gathered.

Literally, “those who have fallen asleep”, as the Malayalam POC has it. Jesus uses the same image of Lazarus (John 11:11). For Christians this became a way of speaking about death in the hope of waking.
An ordered rank, often used of a body of soldiers. The victory comes in sequence: Christ first, then, “at his coming”, those who are his.
To be made powerless, put out of action. Death is an enemy here. Paul does not call it a friend or a natural end that needs no remedy. It is defeated.
vv: But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the first fruits of those who have died.
The whole argument rests on this one fact. The Christian hope does not begin from a general idea about the soul, but from something that has happened to one man.
for as all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ.
The Catechism quotes this on Christ's Resurrection as the source of ours (CCC 655). Paul means two heads of a humanity: what the one brought to all, the other brings to all who belong to him (15:23).
The last enemy to be destroyed is death.
Death will not be left standing at the end. Lazarus will die again, as every person raised before Easter did, but in the end death itself goes.
so that God may be all in all.
The last line of the whole story. The Catechism uses it to speak of the fullness of the Kingdom, when God will be all in all in eternal life (CCC 1060).
ch: The Catechism sets Christ's Resurrection as “the principle and source of our future resurrection” (CCC 655), and the Creed that we pray at each Holy Qurbono ends on the same point: we look for the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come. On a Saturday when the Church looks at one raised man, Paul supplies the larger horizon. Lazarus's rising is a sign; Christ's is the reality; ours is the promise.

set: Bethany is close to Jerusalem (11:18). Lazarus, Martha and Mary are friends whom Jesus loves (11:5). He has delayed coming, and Lazarus is now four days in the tomb. Martha has already met him on the road and heard the great word, “I am the resurrection and the life” (11:25). Today's reading begins as she goes to fetch her sister.

In this scene “the Jews” are not authorities opposing Jesus. They are neighbours and friends who have come from Jerusalem to comfort the sisters, as good people do (11:19). Many of them will come to believe (11:45), and some will report to the Pharisees (11:46). Elsewhere in John the word often means the leaders who oppose him, and it never means a whole people bearing blame (CCC 597).
str: vv. 28–32: Mary goes to Jesus and says what Martha said.
vv. 33–37: Jesus is deeply moved, and he weeps.
vv. 38–40: at the tomb: “Take away the stone”.
vv. 41–42: the prayer of thanks.
vv. 43–44: the command, and the man unbound.
¶ In John this is the last and greatest of the signs before the Passion. It leads directly to the council's decision that he must die (11:47–53).
kw: A strong word (vv. 33, 38). Used of people, it often expresses indignation; here it shows deep emotion, and commentators differ on whether anger at death itself is part of it. John does not picture a calm and untouched Lord.
Used only here in the New Testament. Mary and the mourners are wailing (klaiō); Jesus sheds tears. They are real tears for a friend.
John's word for Jesus' mighty works (compare 12:18). They point beyond themselves. This one shows who he is: the one who gives life.
Just two words in Greek, spoken “with a loud voice”. In 5:28 Jesus has said that all who are in their graves will hear his voice and come out.
vv: The Teacher is here and is calling for you.
A sentence that any disciple can hear in a time of grief.
Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.
She says just what Martha said (11:21), and this is not a lack of faith. It is the honest prayer of grief. Jesus does not correct her, and he does not reply with a teaching.
Jesus began to weep.
The shortest verse in most English Bibles, and among the deepest. He knows what he is about to do, yet he weeps. God's Son truly takes our sorrow on himself.
Jesus said, “Take away the stone.”
Jesus lets people do what people can do. Raising the dead is his part. Moving the stone is theirs, and so is the unbinding afterwards.
Father, I thank you for having heard me.

The prayer of thanks comes before the miracle. The Catechism notes this: thanksgiving comes before the event (CCC 2604). The prayer is said aloud so that the crowd may believe that the Father sent him (11:42).
Unbind him, and let him go.

The cloths remain on Lazarus, for he will need them again. When John tells of Jesus' tomb, the cloths are left behind (20:6–7). St Augustine hears in this verse also what the Lord gives through his Church in Confession (in substance).
ch: The Catechism sees the raising of Lazarus as a sign that announces the Lord's own Resurrection (CCC 994), and it draws a careful line between them. Those raised before Easter returned to ordinary earthly life, and would die again, but Christ's Resurrection is entry into a life beyond death (CCC 646).

St Leo the Great saw in this scene the two natures of the one Christ: it does not belong to the same nature to weep with pity over a dead friend and to call him back to life with a word (Letter to Flavian, in substance). Our own Syriac tradition keeps this Saturday as the door to the Lord's Passion.

qa: If Jesus knew he would raise Lazarus, why did he weep?

Because grief is real even where hope is certain. He weeps with Mary, and he weeps as a friend. His tears show that God does not stand at a distance from human sorrow.
