The Christian, too, may weep at a funeral without any lack of faith. Paul says we do not grieve “as others do who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13). He does not say we do not grieve.
Why does John say Lazarus had been dead four days?

It stresses that he was truly dead. Commentators often mention a later Jewish tradition that the soul stayed near the body for three days, so that by the fourth day all hope was gone. We cannot be sure how widely this was held in Jesus' time. In any case Martha's words about the stench say the same thing in plain terms (11:39).
Paul says the Son will be “subjected” to the Father. Is the Son less than the Father?

No. The Church confesses in the Creed that the Son is of one being with the Father. Fathers such as St Gregory of Nazianzus answered this very question in the fourth century, and they read the verse of Christ in his humanity and as head of his body (in substance). Paul's point is the end of the story: the Son, having conquered every enemy, hands over the Kingdom, and all creation rests in God.
rite: For our Church, this Saturday stands between the close of the Great Fast and the entry of the Lord into Jerusalem. Tomorrow we bring palm leaves and flowers, and the Week of the Passion (Hasha) begins in the evening. The order is John's own. The crowd who come out with palms come partly because they have heard of this sign (John 12:18). Before we carry a palm tomorrow, it is good to stand today at this tomb, and to hear the call to come out.
study: Rebekah says “I will” without knowing much of what lies ahead. What are you being asked to say “I will” to this Holy Week?
Mary brings Jesus her honest grief. What do you need to say to him as plainly as she did?
Jesus asks others to move the stone and to unbind Lazarus. Whom can you help to be unbound this week, perhaps by helping them return to Confession?
How would your way of attending a funeral change if you really held that “the last enemy” is already defeated?

lead: Hosanna Sunday has more readings than any one study can hold, and they all circle one question: what kind of king is this? The evening Gospel (Luke 19:28–40) shows the disciples praising “the king who comes in the name of the Lord”, and the stones ready to shout if they fall silent. Genesis 49:8–15 gives Jacob's blessing of Judah, with the scepter and the donkey's colt bound to the vine. In 2 Samuel 6:1–7 the ark starts toward Jerusalem with joy and with fear. Proverbs 16:13–25 sets the wisdom of the lowly against the pride that “goes before destruction”. Revelation 7:9–12 shows the end of the procession: a multitude from every nation, “with palm branches in their hands”.

We study three more closely. Zechariah foretells a humble king who brings peace to the nations. Paul reminds believers from the nations that they have been grafted onto Israel's olive tree, and the root supports them. John tells how the crowd went out with palm branches, while the disciples did not yet understand. The key words are humble, root and Hosanna.

set: Many scholars think chapters 9–14 of Zechariah come from a later hand than chapters 1–8, in the time after the exile, and the mention of Greece in verse 13 may point to the years of Greek power in the region. There is no king on David's throne, and the people live under foreign rule. The chapter opens with God's advance through the lands to the north and the coast (9:1–7), and today's reading begins with God camping at his house as a guard.
Into that setting comes a surprising figure: a king who arrives not in a war chariot but on a donkey.
str: v. 8: God guards his house.
vv. 9–10: the humble king and his peace.
vv. 11–12: the prisoners of hope are called home.
vv. 13–15: God as the warrior of his people, in the old language of battle.
vv. 16–17: the flock saved; plenty in the land.
kw: More literally “just, and saved” or “one who has been given victory”. His victory comes from God, and he receives it. It is not something he has seized.

The Hebrew word also means poor or afflicted. It is the word for those without power whom God hears. The Greek Old Testament renders it praus, “meek”, the word Matthew uses when he quotes this verse (Matthew 21:5).

A young male donkey. David's son Solomon rode his father's mule to be proclaimed king (1 Kings 1:33). A donkey is an honourable mount, but it is not a war-horse, as the next verse makes plain. Jacob's blessing speaks of Judah's “donkey’s colt” too (Genesis 49:11).
vv: Lo, your king comes to you; triumphant and victorious is he, humble and riding on a donkey,

All four Gospels tell of the Lord's entry into Jerusalem, and Matthew and John quote this verse. Jesus chooses this sign himself. It is a claim to kingship and a correction of what people expected of a king.
and he shall command peace to the nations;
Chariot, war-horse and bow are removed, and even from God's own people. His rule, “from sea to sea”, is not won by arms. The same reach is promised to the king in Psalm 72:8.
because of the blood of my covenant with you,
The phrase recalls Moses at Sinai (Exodus 24:8). Christians hear in it what Jesus will say at the Supper this very week: “This is my blood of the covenant” (Mark 14:24).
O prisoners of hope;
A striking phrase. They are captives, but what holds them is the hope that God will bring them home. It is a good description of the Christian in this world.
ch: The Catechism says of Palm Sunday that Jesus enters as the humble King whose kingdom is won by the Passover of his Death and Resurrection, and that this entry solemnly opens Holy Week (CCC 559–560). Verses 13–15 speak in the language of war, as much of the Old Testament does, and the Christian reads them in the light of verses 9–10. The victory of this king is the Cross, and his weapon is the blood of the covenant. St Justin Martyr already joins Jacob's blessing of Judah to the colt of the entry into Jerusalem (First Apology 32, in substance).

set: Romans 9–11 is Paul's long reflection, with deep sorrow (9:2), on why many of his own people have not come to believe in Jesus. He will not allow anyone to conclude that God has rejected them: “By no means!” (11:1). At 11:13 he turns directly to believers of Gentile background, who may have started to think that they had taken Israel's place. This passage is his warning to them.
The olive tree is an image of Israel known from the prophets (Jeremiah 11:16; Hosea 14:6).
str: vv. 17–18: do not boast: the root supports you.
vv. 19–21: stand in awe, and not in pride.
v. 22: God's kindness and severity.
vv. 23–24: God has the power to graft them in again, and how much more naturally.
kw: A tree that yields little. It is how Paul describes those from the nations before they came to share in the promises. There is no room here for pride.

Paul does not say here exactly who the root is. In the context of 11:16 and 11:28 many take it to be the patriarchs and the promises made to them. Either way, the church of the nations lives from Israel's root.
A gardener normally grafts a good branch onto rough stock. Paul's picture runs the other way, and he says so. What has happened to the Gentiles is not natural but pure gift.
vv: you, a wild olive shoot, were grafted in their place to share the rich root of the olive tree,
The word is “some” of the branches. The tree is still there, and it is the same tree. Newcomers share in a life that is not theirs.
it is not you that support the root, but the root that supports you.
Every Christian should keep this sentence in mind when speaking about the Jewish people. All that we have received, from the Psalms to the Lord himself, comes from that root.
So do not become proud, but stand in awe.
The warning is addressed to the Christian, not to Israel. The one who stands does so “through faith”, and therefore by God's gift, with no ground for boasting.
for God has the power to graft them in again.
Paul ends the whole section by saying that “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (11:29). Israel's place in God's plan remains.
ch: The Second Vatican Council quotes this passage directly. The Church “draws sustenance from the root of that well-cultivated olive tree onto which have been grafted the wild shoot, the Gentiles” (Nostra Aetate 4). The Catechism speaks of the Church's unique link with the Jewish people and recalls Romans 11:29 (CCC 839). Reading this on Hosanna Sunday keeps us honest, for the week ahead has too often been told in Christian history with contempt for Jews. The Church rejects that. The King of Israel enters his city, and those who were far off are welcomed by his grace.

set: It is the Passover season, and Jerusalem is full of pilgrims. Jesus has been at Bethany, where Mary anointed him (12:1–8), and word has spread about Lazarus, whom many came to see (12:9). The chief priests are by now planning his death (11:53). So John's account of the entry is short, and it has its own emphasis. In John, the crowd comes out to meet Jesus before he has found the donkey. He then sits on it, as if to give the crowd's acclamation its true meaning.

Only John says that the branches were from palm trees. Palms had been carried at the rededication of the Temple (2 Maccabees 10:7) and at Simon's victorious entry into the citadel (1 Maccabees 13:51), and many scholars think they had a strong national meaning.
str: vv. 12–13: the crowd, the palms and the shout.
vv. 14–15: the young donkey and the Scripture.
v. 16: what the disciples understood only later.
vv. 17–18: the witness of those who saw Lazarus raised.
v. 19: the Pharisees' dismay.
kw: From the Hebrew of Psalm 118:25, “Save us, we beseech you”. By this time it was also a shout of praise. Psalm 118 was sung at the great feasts, and verse 26 gives the words that follow: “Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord”.
John alone names the tree. Revelation 7:9 uses phoinikes for those who stand before the Lamb “with palm branches in their hands”, so the palms of this day are matched by the palms of heaven.

Nathanael said it at the start (1:49). John adds it to the words of the psalm. The inscription on the Cross will carry a similar title, in three languages (19:19–20). This is where the kingship of today is headed.
vv: So they took branches of palm trees and went out to meet him,
They go out as a city goes out to greet a ruler. The Church goes out with them today, palm in hand.
Jesus found a young donkey and sat on it;
No war-horse, no procession prepared. His action quietly corrects what the palms might suggest. The kingdom will not be of this world (18:36).
Look, your king is coming, sitting on a donkey’s colt!

John's short quotation joins Zechariah 9:9 with the opening “Do not be afraid”, a phrase that recalls Zephaniah 3:16, among other passages. A king who is no cause for fear: that is the good news of this procession.
His disciples did not understand these things at first;
John is honest about this. It takes the Resurrection and the Spirit to read the Scriptures rightly (see 2:22; 14:26). Those who do not grasp all of this week's mysteries are in good company.
Look, the world has gone after him!
The Pharisees say it in dismay, but John hears more in it. In the very next verse some Greeks come asking to see Jesus (12:20–21). The words are truer than the speakers know.
ch: The Catechism says that the Church's liturgy solemnly opens Holy Week with this entry, and it links the crowd's shout with the Sanctus of the Eucharistic liturgy (CCC 559–560). The same word passes from the road outside Jerusalem into the holiest part of our prayer. Whoever says Hosanna today is asking the Lord to save, and is greeting him as the one who comes.

qa: What does “Hosanna” mean?

It comes from the Hebrew of Psalm 118:25 and means “Save us, we beseech you”. By the time of Jesus it could also be a cry of praise and welcome, as in the phrase “Hosanna in the highest”. Both senses belong in our prayer. We sing it to the Lord who comes, and we ask him to save us.
Did this same crowd shout “Crucify him” a few days later?

The Gospels do not say so. It has become a common way of preaching, and it can be a useful warning about our own changeable hearts. It must never become a charge against the Jewish people. The Church teaches that the Passion cannot be charged against all the Jews then living, nor against the Jews today (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597), and that sinners were “the authors and the ministers” of the Lord's sufferings (CCC 598). That means all of us.
Does Romans 11 say that the Church has taken the place of Israel?

No. Paul says the opposite to those who might think it. The root supports the branches, God's gifts and calling “are irrevocable” (11:29), and God has the power to graft in again. The Church confesses her own link to the Jewish people (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 839). How God will bring his plan to its end is, as Paul says, a mystery (11:25, 33).
rite: In our Malankara churches the palms are blessed and carried in procession, and the faithful bring flowers as well. We join the crowd of Jerusalem and the multitude of Revelation 7. This evening, Holy Week (Hasha) begins, with its special prayers and abstinence. So the day itself makes the turn from the shouting of the morning to the sorrow of the evening. In every Holy Qurbono the Church sings “Hosanna” in the anaphora, so the word we use on this road is not left behind when the palms have dried.
study: What kind of king were you hoping for when you first came to faith? How has the Lord corrected that?
Zechariah calls God's people “prisoners of hope”. What holds you to him when other things would pull you away?
How would Romans 11:18 change the way Christians speak of the Jewish people, especially in Holy Week?
Which part of this week's services will be hardest for you to attend? What would help you be there?

lead: Hasha Week opens with a question about hearing. In Isaiah, God offers rest to the weary, and the leaders of the city, unsteady with wine, call his plain teaching baby talk. In Matthew, Jesus stands in the temple a few days before his death, and those in charge ask by what authority he acts. The Epistle (Hebrews 1:10–14) gives the answer that neither crowd could yet see: heaven and earth will wear out like clothing, “But you are the same.” The key words are rest, authority and hearing.

r.h: This is rest; give rest to the weary
set: Isaiah spoke in Jerusalem in the eighth century before Christ, when Assyria was swallowing the small kingdoms around Judah. Chapter 28 opens with a cry over “the proud garland of the drunkards of Ephraim” (28:1), that is, the northern kingdom and its capital Samaria, which fell in 722 BC. Today's reading then turns. “These also” reel with wine (v. 7), and a few verses after our passage the prophet names them: “you scoffers who rule this people in Jerusalem” (28:14). What happened to the north can happen in the south.
str: vv. 5–6: a promise: the Lord himself will be the crown of those who remain.
vv. 7–8: priest and prophet staggering at table.
vv. 9–10: the leaders mock Isaiah: is he teaching toddlers?
vv. 11–13: God takes up their mockery and turns it into judgment.
kw: In v. 1 the garland is the drunkards' pride, and it fades. In v. 5 the Lord himself is the garland. The people's crown is either something they have made or someone they have received.
precept upon precept, line upon line

The Hebrew of v. 10 is a string of short sounds, and scholars are not sure of its exact meaning. The NRSV takes the words as “precept” and “line”. Many think they imitate a child's lesson or the babble of a drunk. Either way, the leaders are mocking the prophet by making his teaching sound like nonsense.
The word used of the rest God promised Israel in the land (Deuteronomy 12:9). Here the rest is tied to mercy: it is found by giving rest to the weary.
vv: In that day the Lord of hosts will be a garland of glory, and a diadem of beauty, to the remnant of his people;
The promise comes before the rebuke. God's first word is that a people will remain, and that he himself will be their beauty.
the priest and the prophet reel with strong drink,
The drunkenness may be literal, and it is also a picture. Those whose office was to see clearly and to judge fairly “err in vision” and “stumble in giving judgment”.
to whom he has said, “This is rest; give rest to the weary; and this is repose”; yet they would not hear.
This is the centre of the passage. The message was never complicated. God's word for a frightened city was to care for the tired, and not to trust in clever alliances.
Truly, with stammering lip and with alien tongue he will speak to this people,
Those who refused a plain word in their own tongue will hear God through the speech of foreign invaders. Paul takes up this verse in another setting (1 Corinthians 14:21).
ch: On a Monday of Hasha Week the reading sounds a note of warning to all who hold office in God's house, and first of all to us who hear it. Jesus' own invitation, “Come to me, all you that are weary” and “I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28), is the same offer made in person. The Catechism says that Christ himself is the Word in whom the Father says everything (CCC 65): the danger is the one Isaiah names, to be near the word and not to hear it.

set: In Matthew's order, Jesus has entered Jerusalem to the cry of Hosanna (21:1–11), driven the buyers and sellers from the temple (21:12–17), and cursed a barren fig tree (21:18–22). Now he returns to the temple to teach. “These things” in the question may cover all of this. The chief priests and the elders had charge of the temple and of public order, so the question is one they had a right to ask. The trouble lies in how they weigh the answer.

Matthew is speaking of these particular leaders at this moment, not of a whole people. The Catechism recalls that there was division among the authorities themselves, and that Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea were secret disciples (CCC 595). The crowd in this very passage holds John to be a prophet.
str: v. 23: the question.
vv. 24–25a: Jesus' counter-question about John.
vv. 25b–26: the debate among the questioners.
v. 27: “We do not know”, and Jesus' refusal to answer.
¶ Three parables follow at once (21:28–22:14), and they carry on the same argument. The first of them returns to John (21:32).
kw: The right and the power to act. The crowds noticed it at the end of the Sermon on the Mount: “he taught them as one having authority” (7:29). The Gospel ends on the same word: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (28:18).
“Heaven” here is a reverent way of saying God. The question is simply whether John's call to repent came from God.
Two words in Greek. It is the one answer in the passage that is untrue to what they were actually discussing, since their debate was about consequences, not knowledge.
vv: By what authority are you doing these things, and who gave you this authority?
The question is the right one. All of Matthew's Gospel exists to answer it.
Did the baptism of John come from heaven, or was it of human origin?
This is no dodge. John had pointed to Jesus (3:11–17). Whoever accepts John from heaven has the answer to the first question in his hands.
we are afraid of the crowd; for all regard John as a prophet.
The debate has two columns, what it will cost if we say this and what it will cost if we say that. The column that is missing is whether it is true.
Neither will I tell you by what authority I am doing these things.
Jesus does not refuse a person who wants to learn. He declines to play a game whose result has been fixed in advance. He will give his answer before the high priest (26:64), and on the Cross.
ch: St John Chrysostom notes that the Lord did not refuse people who wished to learn, but people who asked in order to trap him (in substance). The Church reads the passage as a lesson on conscience: a person must seek what is true and good and follow it, even when the cost is high (CCC 1776–1778). The risen Lord's words in 28:18 are the last word on the question. His authority comes from the Father, and it was shown not in force but in the Cross and the empty tomb.

qa: Was Jesus avoiding the question?

No. His counter-question is an answer for anyone willing to take it up. John said that one mightier than he was coming, and baptized Jesus. To say that John was from heaven is to take the first step toward Jesus. Those who will not take that step would not be helped by a further statement.
rite: Our Church entered Hasha Week on the evening of Hosanna Sunday. Hasho is the Syriac word for suffering. The Panchangam notes that the newly prepared Hasha Week lectionary provides readings for every hour of prayer this week, and it also remembers today Fr Seraphion Attupurathu OIC, who came into Catholic communion in the reunion of 1930 and died in 1975.
study: When have I said “I do not know” because the truth would ask too much of me?
Isaiah's word was “give rest to the weary”. Who is the tired person God is asking me to care for this week?

lead: Two men face death today, and both are told what lies beyond it. Moses, at the end of his road, hands his people to Joshua and writes them a song, knowing how they will fail. In John, Jesus says, “Now my soul is troubled”, and then asks only that the Father's name be glorified. The Epistle (Hebrews 4:1–5) connects them: the promised rest is still open, and it is a rest Joshua's land could only point to. The key words are with you, the hour and lifted up.

r.h: Be strong and bold; I will be with you
set: Deuteronomy is presented as Moses' farewell on the plains of Moab, on the edge of the land he will not enter. He is one hundred twenty years old, and the Lord has told him he shall not cross the Jordan (31:2). This chapter prepares the people for life after him, and it weaves together three things he leaves behind: a successor, a book and a song. Many scholars think the chapter joins strands from different stages of the book's growth, which may explain why it moves back and forth among the three. The song itself follows in chapter 32.
str: vv. 14–15: Moses and Joshua at the tent; the pillar of cloud.
vv. 16–22: God foretells that the people will turn away, and orders the song as a witness.
v. 23: Joshua is commissioned.
vv. 24–29: the book of the law is placed beside the ark.
v. 30: Moses recites the song to the assembly.
kw: Moses has said it to the people and to Joshua (31:6–7). The Lord says it now (v. 23), and he will say it again at the start of Joshua's book (Joshua 1:6–9). The courage rests on the promise that follows it.

The song (v. 19) and the book (v. 26) will both stand as witnesses. They do not exist to condemn for the sake of condemning. They will let a suffering people remember why things went wrong, and that the same God can be found again.

The Hebrew Bible's strong picture of God seeming absent (vv. 17–18). The Psalms pray against it again and again. The verse is hard, and it is also an unexpected mercy that the people are told about it in advance.
vv: Your time to die is near; call Joshua and present yourselves in the tent of meeting,
God's first concern at Moses' death is the people's future. The greatest leader in Israel's memory must also let go.
In that day they will say, ‘Have not these troubles come upon us because our God is not in our midst?’

Part of the trial will be the feeling that God has gone. The song is given so that they will know that the God who seems absent is the one who foretold this, and that he has not stopped speaking to them.
Be strong and bold, for you shall bring the Israelites into the land that I promised them; I will be with you.

The only words spoken directly to Joshua in this reading. His name in Hebrew, Yehoshua, is the same name as Jesus. The promise is the one the risen Lord gives his Church: “I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20).
Take this book of the law and put it beside the ark of the covenant of the Lord your God;
Moses will die, and the word stays. Here is a people learning to live by what is written down.
For I know well how rebellious and stubborn you are.

This is the voice of a man who loves his people and has stood between them and God (Exodus 32:11–14). It is the same honesty the prophets used, spoken from within. Christians read such verses as a mirror, as Paul says, “they were written down to instruct us” (1 Corinthians 10:11).
ch: St Justin Martyr saw in Joshua, whose name Moses changed (Numbers 13:16), a figure of Jesus, who leads God's people into the true inheritance (Dialogue with Trypho 113, in substance). Hebrews says this directly, in the chapter from which today's Epistle comes: “if Joshua had given them rest, God would not speak later about another day” (4:8). The letter also takes up the promise of this chapter for Christians: “I will never leave you or forsake you” (13:5; compare Deuteronomy 31:6). The Book of Revelation shows the saved singing “the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb” (15:3).

set: These words come near the end of Jesus' public teaching in John; after them he departs and hides (12:36). Some Greeks have come asking to see him (12:20–22), and he has answered, “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified”, speaking of the grain of wheat that dies to bear fruit (12:23–24). John does not tell the story of the agony in the garden as the other Gospels do. Here, in the temple days, is where he shows us the troubled heart of Jesus.
str: vv. 27–28a: the prayer of the troubled soul.
vv. 28b–30: the voice from heaven, and how it is heard.
vv. 31–33: judgment, and being lifted up.
v. 34: the crowd's puzzle about the Messiah.
vv. 35–36: the appeal: walk while you have the light.
kw: Throughout John, the hour of Jesus is not yet (2:4; 7:30; 8:20). Now it has come. It means the whole movement of the Cross, the Resurrection and the return to the Father.

The word means both to raise physically and to exalt. John uses it for the Cross on purpose (3:14; 8:28). Isaiah says the Servant shall be “exalted and lifted up” (52:13). In John the Cross is already the throne.
In the Old Testament, God's glory is his weighty, visible presence. Here God's glory will be seen in the place where no one would look for it, in love going to the end.
vv: Now my soul is troubled. And what should I say
The words are close to the Psalms of lament (compare Psalm 42:5–6). Jesus is truly human, and he truly dreads what is coming. Faith in his divinity must never make his fear unreal.
No, it is for this reason that I have come to this hour.
The Catechism quotes this verse to show that Jesus embraced the Father's plan with his whole human will (CCC 607).
Father, glorify your name.
This is the first petition of the Lord's Prayer in other words. The Father's answer covers both past and future, “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.”
Now is the judgment of this world; now the ruler of this world will be driven out.
The Cross looks like the world's judgment on Jesus. John says that it is the reverse. The Catechism teaches that victory over the “prince of this world” was won once for all at this Hour (CCC 2853).
And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.

A note on the text: some ancient manuscripts and the Latin Vulgate read “all things” where others read “all people”. NRSV and the Malayalam POC both follow “all people”. Either way, the reach of the Cross has no limit (CCC 542, 662).
Walk while you have the light, so that the darkness may not overtake you.
Near the end of his public teaching, his word is an invitation, not a condemnation. Light is a gift that can be received today.
ch: The Catechism's teaching on the Ascension quotes this very verse, and says that the lifting up on the Cross signifies and announces the lifting up into heaven, and indeed begins it (CCC 662). Hebrews speaks of the same prayer: “with loud cries and tears” he offered prayers to the one who could save him, “and he was heard because of his reverent submission” (5:7). The Church sees in this the pattern of Christian prayer in fear: to say honestly what we feel, and then to say, “Father, glorify your name.”

qa: In the other Gospels Jesus prays that the cup may pass. In John he seems to refuse that prayer. Is this a contradiction?

No. The Gospels show one obedience from different sides. Mark, Matthew and Luke let us hear the request and the “yet, not what I want”. John starts at the same fear and passes straight to the “Father, glorify your name”. Both accounts show a real human struggle and a real human yes.
study: Moses knew he would not see what came next, and he still prepared others for it. What am I being asked to hand on with trust?
“Now my soul is troubled.” What do I usually do with my fear when I pray, and what would it mean to pray as Jesus does here?

lead: Today's readings hold a sword and a purse. Ezekiel sees a sword drawn over a people who trusted in false visions. In Matthew, one of the twelve walks to the chief priests and asks what he will be paid. Between them stands the Epistle (Hebrews 9:23–28), which says that Christ “has appeared once for all at the end of the age to remove sin by the sacrifice of himself”. Tomorrow is Pesaha: this is the last evening before the Supper. The key words are judgment, price and handing over.

set: Ezekiel preached among the exiles in Babylon before and after the fall of Jerusalem (587/586 BC). Chapter 21 is the chapter of the sword. A little earlier, the king of Babylon stands at a fork in the road, casting lots whether to march on Rabbah of the Ammonites or on Jerusalem, and the lot falls on Jerusalem (21:18–23). This reading is the sequel. Ammon, east of the Jordan, may think that it has escaped, and it mocks Judah in her disaster (compare 25:3). The word comes: the sword has not forgotten you.

The Hebrew here is hard, and translators differ. Chapter 21 in English Bibles is numbered differently in the Hebrew, where these verses are 21:33–37. In the NRSV, “Return it to its sheath!” begins v. 30, while the Malayalam POC closes v. 29 with it and reads v. 29 as the sword falling on the false seers. Scholars also differ on whose sword is meant to be sheathed, Ammon's or that of Babylon, and so on who is addressed in the verses that follow.
str: v. 28: the song of the sword against the Ammonites.
v. 29: false visions, and the time of final punishment.
v. 30: back in the sheath: judgment in the land of your origin.
vv. 31–32: fire, blood and being forgotten.
kw: Repeated throughout the chapter. In Ezekiel, it stands for an actual army and at the same time for God's judgment working through history.
The sin of Ammon named here is scorn. To laugh at a neighbour in his ruin is treated as a grave matter.
Literally “the time of the guilt of the end”. The same phrase is used of Israel's prince (21:25). The judgment falls on all alike: no nation is outside God's justice.
vv: A sword, a sword! Drawn for slaughter, polished to consume, to flash like lightning.
The poem is frightening on purpose. Before there is a lesson, there is the plain terror of what war does.
Offering false visions for you, divining lies for you,
Ammon had seers who told it what it wished to hear. The danger is an old one. A comforting lie is the most costly thing that a people can buy.
Return it to its sheath! In the place where you were created, in the land of your origin, I will judge you.

God's judgment reaches a person at home. There is no road on which one can leave oneself behind. A Christian reader in Hasha Week may also hear another voice here, though this is not a quotation: on Thursday night Jesus will say to Peter, “Put your sword back into its sheath” (John 18:11), and he will drink the cup himself.
you shall be remembered no more, for I the Lord have spoken.
The hardest line. Jeremiah 49:6 gives the larger view of God's plan: “But afterward I will restore the fortunes of the Ammonites.”
ch: The language of wrath in the prophets is the Bible's way of saying that God is not indifferent to evil, and that he hears the cry of those who are mocked and destroyed. It is not a human temper. The New Testament does not soften the seriousness of sin, but it shows how far God goes to deal with it: he “did not withhold his own Son, but gave him up for all of us” (Romans 8:32). In her reading of the Cross, the Church holds that Jesus, in an act of love, atones for our faults and makes satisfaction for our sins to the Father (CCC 615–616). The sword of this chapter is thus read in Hasha Week with the eyes turned to the Cross.

set: These three short verses are set between two meals. Just before them, a woman at Bethany pours a very costly ointment over Jesus' head, and he calls it preparation for his burial (26:6–13). Just after, the disciples prepare the Passover (26:17–19). The contrast is plain: she gives away what is costly, and he asks what he can get. At the start of the chapter the chief priests and elders have decided to arrest Jesus by stealth, but not during the festival (26:3–5). Judas offers them the opportunity they lacked.

Matthew's word “then” joins the scene to the anointing, but neither he nor the other Gospels fully explain why Judas did this. John 12:6 says that he kept the common purse and stole from it. Later theories of disappointed political hopes are only guesses.
str: v. 14: one of the twelve goes to the chief priests.
v. 15: his question and the price.
v. 16: he begins to look for an opportunity.
kw: The word that recurs through the Passion (26:2, 15, 16). It can mean to betray and also simply to hand over. Paul uses it of the Father who “gave up” his Son (Romans 8:32), and of Christ who “gave himself for me” (Galatians 2:20). Judas hands him over for money; God, out of love, gives his Son to us.

Only Matthew gives the sum. It recalls the compensation for a slave gored by an ox (Exodus 21:32) and the insulting wage of the shepherd in Zechariah 11:12. Matthew will return to the coins in 27:3–10.
A good moment, a convenient time. Judas now watches for it as the others keep watch for the Passover.
vv: Then one of the twelve, who was called Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests

“One of the twelve”: all four Gospels keep this painful phrase or something like it. The Church did not hide it. Betrayal came from the inner circle, from one who had been called, sent out, and had eaten with the Lord (compare Psalm 41:9).
What will you give me if I betray him to you?

The first words of Judas in Matthew's account. He is the one who names the transaction. A note on the wording: the NRSV says that they “paid him”, while the Malayalam POC says they promised (വാഗ്ദാനം ചെയ്തു). The Greek verb can mean to weigh out, and Matthew may be echoing Zechariah's “weighed out”. Mark and Luke speak of a promise of money.
And from that moment he began to look for an opportunity to betray him.
Sin is often less a single act than a slow keeping of watch. Judas will sit at the Supper with this already in his heart.
ch: St John Chrysostom, preaching on this passage, dwells on the love of money that led one of the twelve so far, and warns his hearers against it (in substance). Hebrews gives the same warning against the love of money, and in the same breath promises, “I will never leave you or forsake you” (13:5). An ancient Christian custom, recorded in the Apostolic Constitutions (7.23, in substance), kept Wednesday as a fast because of this betrayal. The Syriac Churches have long kept Wednesday and Friday as days of fasting.

qa: If the betrayal was foretold, was Judas forced to do it? Is he in hell?

God's knowing beforehand does not force anyone. The Catechism teaches that God's plan takes in each person's response, and that he permitted the acts that flowed from their blindness in order to bring about salvation (CCC 600). Judas acted of his own will. Jesus speaks of him with great gravity (26:24). Yet the Church, which declares that certain persons are saints, has never declared that any named person is damned, and she teaches that God predestines no one to go to hell (CCC 1037). We leave Judas to God's judgment, and we ask what price we ourselves have put on Christ.
rite: Tomorrow is Pesaha, and in 2027 the date of the Annunciation (25 March) falls on the same day. The Panchangam gives readings for the Annunciation as well, and asks us to follow the direction of our eparchy.
study: The woman at Bethany gave what was costly, and Judas asked what he could get. Which of these two is closer to how I have been praying lately?
Ezekiel warns about comforting lies. Whose false visions have I been paying for, and whose honest word have I avoided?

lead: Tonight every reading leads to one table. The Lectionary gives eight, and they circle the upper room. The Evening Gospel (John 7:37–53) hears Jesus cry out, “Let anyone who is thirsty come to me”. Leviticus 16:3–10 shows the high priest preparing for the Day of Atonement. Proverbs 1:10–19 warns against those who lie in wait for blood, and one of the Twelve is doing that this very night. Isaiah 24:16–23 sees the Lord reigning on Mount Zion, and Revelation 19:5–16 opens the marriage supper of the Lamb.

We study here the three that carry the night. Exodus gives the lamb and the blood on the door. Paul hands on what he received about the bread and the cup, and warns a divided community. Luke sets us at the table itself, where the Lord gives his Body and Blood and then tells his quarrelling apostles that he is among them as one who serves. The key words are remembrance, covenant and service.

r.h: It is the passover of the Lord
set: Nine plagues have struck Egypt, and Pharaoh will not let Israel go. Before the last plague, and before anyone has left, God tells the people how to eat a meal. The liberation has not yet happened, and already its memorial is being instituted. The story stops for instructions because this night is meant for every generation who will come after.

Many scholars think that older customs of the shepherd's spring offering and of the farmer's unleavened bread lie behind this rite, and that Israel received them anew as the memorial of the Exodus. Whatever the prehistory, the Bible's concern is what God did. The Jewish people keep this night to this day, and the Catechism speaks of it with reverence: for Jews it is the Passover of history, tending toward the future, and for Christians it is fulfilled in the death and Resurrection of Christ, while we await its definitive completion (CCC 1096).
str: vv. 1–2: a new beginning for the calendar.
vv. 3–5: choosing the lamb, household by household.
v. 6: the slaughter at twilight on the fourteenth.
v. 7: the blood on the doorposts and lintel.
vv. 8–10: how it is to be cooked and eaten; nothing left over.
v. 11: dressed for the road: “It is the passover of the Lord.”
kw: The name is explained by the verb pāsaḥ in 12:13, “I will pass over you”. Isaiah 31:5 uses the same verb alongside words of protection, and so some scholars hear in it also “to stand guard over”. God passes over, and God shields.
Whole, sound, complete. It is the requirement for sacrifice (Leviticus 22:19–21). Peter applies the idea to Christ, “a lamb without defect or blemish” (1 Peter 1:19).
Literally “between the two evenings”. The hour matters to the text. The Gospel of John notes the hour and the day of Jesus' condemnation with the same care (19:14).
vv: This month shall mark for you the beginning of months;
Before God changes Israel's place, he changes its calendar. Redemption becomes the beginning of time. In the same way, the Lord's Pasch stands at the centre of the Church's year (CCC 1169).
a lamb for each family, a lamb for each household.
This feast is kept in the home. If a household is too small, it joins its neighbour (v. 4). Salvation has a family shape, and no one is meant to eat alone.
Your lamb shall be without blemish, a year-old male; you may take it from the sheep or from the goats.
The Hebrew word for the animal covers both a lamb and a kid. John the Baptist's words will gather all this up: “Here is the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29).
They shall take some of the blood and put it on the two doorposts and the lintel of the houses in which they eat it.

The blood marks the very place of the meal. Those who eat are those under the sign. “When I see the blood, I will pass over you” (12:13) is God's promise, not a magic rule: he binds himself to a sign that he gave.
This is how you shall eat it: your loins girded, your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hand; and you shall eat it hurriedly.
A meal eaten standing ready. The bread of the Exodus is food for people on the way, and that is what the Holy Qurbono remains for us.
ch: St Paul says it in a sentence: “For our paschal lamb, Christ, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). John notes that no bone of Jesus was broken (John 19:36), echoing the rule of the lamb (Exodus 12:46). The Catechism places the Last Supper within this memorial: by celebrating it in the setting of the Passover, Jesus gave the Jewish Passover its definitive meaning (CCC 1340), and in the Bible a memorial is not only a recollection but a making present of what God did (CCC 1363). St Melito of Sardis built a whole Easter homily on this chapter, reading the lamb as the figure of Christ (On the Pascha, in substance), and Aphrahat the Persian sage, writing in Syriac, teaches that the Lord gave his Body and Blood to his disciples with his own hands before he was crucified (Demonstration 12, in substance).

r.h: I received from the Lord what I also handed on to you
set: Paul writes from Ephesus (16:8), probably in the mid-50s. This is the oldest written account we have of the Lord's Supper, older than the writing of the Gospels. He brings it up because of a scandal. When the Corinthians gather, each goes ahead with his own supper, “and one goes hungry and another becomes drunk” (11:21). Many scholars think that those of means, who could arrive early, ate well while the poor came late from their work and found little. Paul's answer to a social problem is to go back to the night of the betrayal.
str: v. 23a: the tradition received and handed on.
vv. 23b–25: the bread and the cup.
v. 26: what eating and drinking proclaim.
vv. 27–29: unworthy eating and discerning the body.
vv. 30–32: the Lord's discipline.
vv. 33–34: a practical rule: wait for one another.
kw: Technical words for passing on a sacred tradition, used again of the Resurrection (15:3). The second is the same verb translated “was betrayed” in the same verse. On the night he was handed over, he handed himself over, and Paul hands on the handing over.
More than memory in our ordinary sense. It is the biblical memorial, where God's saving act is made present to those who celebrate it (CCC 1362–1363).
To tell apart, to recognize for what it is. Paul plays on this family of words in vv. 29–32: discern, judge, be judged, condemn.
vv: For I received from the Lord what I also handed on to you, that the Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed took a loaf of bread,

Paul was not in the upper room. He stands within a chain which begins with the Lord. He begins his account by saying when it took place: on the night of the betrayal. It is love's answer to the worst thing done to it.
This is my body that is for you. Do this in remembrance of me.

“For you” is the heart of it. Paul takes the words literally enough to say in v. 27 that the one who eats unworthily “will be answerable for the body and blood of the Lord”. Earlier he has asked, “The bread that we break, is it not a sharing in the body of Christ?” (10:16).
This cup is the new covenant in my blood.

This recalls the “new covenant” of Jeremiah 31:31, and the blood of the covenant at Sinai (Exodus 24:8). God's covenant with Israel, which he has never revoked (CCC 121), comes in Jesus to the fullness which the prophets promised.
For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.
The liturgy itself is a proclamation. It looks to the past, to his death, and to the future, “until he comes”, and it does so in the present, at this table.
Examine yourselves, and only then eat of the bread and drink of the cup.
The Catechism takes this as the basis of preparing for Communion: anyone conscious of grave sin must receive the sacrament of Reconciliation first (CCC 1385, 1457).
For all who eat and drink without discerning the body, eat and drink judgment against themselves.

“The body” means the Lord's Body in the sacrament, and in this letter it also means the Church: “we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread” (10:17). To shame the poor at the table is to fail to see both.
So then, my brothers and sisters, when you come together to eat, wait for one another.
After such a solemn teaching, a very simple rule. Reverence for the Body at the altar shows itself in how we treat the body at the door.
ch: The Council of Trent and the Catechism teach that with “Do this in remembrance of me” the Lord made his apostles priests of the New Covenant (CCC 611, 1337), and that the Eucharist re-presents the one sacrifice of the Cross, in an unbloody manner, and does not add another to it (CCC 1366–1367). St Cyril of Jerusalem tells the newly baptized not to regard the bread and wine as simple elements, since by the Lord's declaration they are his Body and Blood (Mystagogical Catecheses 4, in substance). St John Chrysostom presses Paul's other point: you have tasted the Blood of the Lord, and you do not recognize your brother (Homilies on 1 Corinthians 27, quoted in CCC 1397).

r.h: I am among you as one who serves
set: Luke presents the Supper as a Passover meal (22:7–13) and as a farewell. Ancient farewell speeches often gather a leader's last instructions at a table, and Luke places here sayings about betrayal, greatness and the future of the Twelve. Only Luke places the dispute about greatness at the Supper itself. It stands right after the gift of the Eucharist, and no reader can miss how sad that is. John 13 teaches the same lesson with the washing of the feet.
Later Jewish sources describe several cups of wine at the Passover table. That may be why Luke mentions a cup before the bread (v. 17) and another after supper (v. 20).
str: vv. 14–18: the desire of Jesus; the Passover and the Kingdom.
vv. 19–20: the bread and the cup.
vv. 21–23: the betrayer at the table.
vv. 24–27: the dispute, and the one who serves.
vv. 28–30: the Kingdom conferred, the table promised.
kw: Literally “with desire I have desired”, a Hebrew way of adding force. This meal is what Jesus wanted. He does not come to it as a victim of events.
From this verb the Church takes the name Eucharist (CCC 1328). On the night of his betrayal, his first act over the bread is thanksgiving.
To wait on someone at table, then more widely to serve (vv. 26–27). The word gives us “deacon”. The Son of Man came “to serve” (Mark 10:45).
“I confer on you” (v. 29) comes from the same root as diathēkē, covenant (v. 20). The covenant in his blood and the Kingdom he gives are linked by the word itself.
vv: I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer;
“With you” matters as much as “this Passover”. He knows what awaits him, and what he longs for is to be at table with these men.
This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.

A note on the text: a few ancient witnesses, chiefly Codex Bezae, lack the words from “which is given” through v. 20. Nearly all the manuscripts have them, and the NRSV and POC print them, as the Church reads them. He took, gave thanks, broke and gave: Luke's disciples at Emmaus will know the Lord “in the breaking of the bread” (24:35).
This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood.

“Poured out” is the language of sacrifice, the blood at the altar (Leviticus 4:7). Before anything is done to him, Jesus gives his death its meaning. He gives himself before anyone can take him (John 10:18; CCC 609–610).
But see, the one who betrays me is with me, and his hand is on the table.
The Eucharist is given in the same room as the betrayal, and Jesus does not send anyone away. Mercy and warning are in the same sentence (v. 22).
But not so with you; rather the greatest among you must become like the youngest, and the leader like one who serves.
“Benefactor” (v. 25) was a title that Hellenistic kings actually took. Jesus does not abolish leadership among the Twelve. He gives it a different form.
But I am among you as one who serves.
The one giving the banquet is on his feet. Here is the charter of all authority in the Church, and our tradition makes it visible in the washing of the feet.
so that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom, and you will sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.

The men who were arguing a moment ago are promised a table and thrones, and are told that they “have stood by me in my trials” (v. 28), though they will shortly run away. This is what grace looks like. The Twelve, whose number recalls Israel's twelve tribes, will share his work (CCC 551, 765).
ch: The Catechism sets the Lord's words beside the Passover: by the Last Supper he gave it its new meaning, and anticipated his passing over to the Father (CCC 1339–1340). He looked forward to its fulfilment in the Kingdom (Luke 22:16, 18), and so the Eucharist is a pledge of the glory to come (CCC 1403). St John Chrysostom, preaching on the betrayal, says that it is not a man who makes the gifts become the Body and Blood of Christ, but Christ himself, who was crucified for us: the priest stands there, and the power and grace are of God (in substance). St Ephrem (Mar Aprem), in his hymns on the Unleavened Bread, sings of the true Lamb to whom the paschal lamb pointed, at that table (in substance).

qa: Was the Last Supper a Passover meal? The Gospels seem to differ.

Mark, Matthew and Luke present it as a Passover meal. John places the death of Jesus on the day of Preparation, when the Passover had not yet been eaten (18:28; 19:14), so that he dies at the hour of the lambs. Scholars discuss how to reconcile them, and no answer has won general agreement. All four agree on what matters: it took place in the setting of Passover, and Jesus is its true Lamb (CCC 1339–1340).
If Christ's sacrifice was once for all, how is the Holy Qurbono a sacrifice?

It is not a second sacrifice. Christ's offering of himself is one and is never repeated (Hebrews 9:26). The Qurbono is its memorial and makes it present: the same victim, the same priest, offering now through the ministry of priests, only the manner of offering being different (CCC 1366–1367).
Does 1 Corinthians 11:30 mean that sickness is punishment for bad Communions?

Paul is speaking about what he sees in this one community at a particular time, and he reads it as discipline that saves, “so that we may not be condemned” (v. 32). He does not teach that every illness has such a cause. Jesus himself refuses that reasoning (John 9:2–3).
rite: We celebrate the Holy Qurbono tonight at the hour of its institution, and the words the priest says over the bread and wine are the words of the upper room. In our tradition the washing of the feet makes visible what Luke teaches. In many Kerala Christian homes, Pesaha bread is also broken and shared in the family on this night, and customs differ from place to place. In 2027 the date of the Annunciation falls on this same day, and we follow the direction of our eparchy on how it is kept. St Augustine records an old belief that the Lord was both conceived and crucified on 25 March (On the Trinity 4.5, in substance). The flesh that the Word took in Mary's womb is the Body given at this table.
study: The first Passover was eaten by people ready to leave. What would it mean for me to receive the Holy Qurbono ready to leave something behind?
Paul's teaching on the Eucharist answers a scandal about the poor. Who is going hungry at the edge of my own parish, and do I see them?
The apostles quarrelled about greatness minutes after receiving the Eucharist. Where in my family, parish or work do I need to hear, “But not so with you”?
Jesus told weak men that they had stood by him in his trials. How does his way of seeing them change the way I look at my own failures?

lead: Today our Church reads through the hours of the day from the Hasha Week service book, whose readings are not listed in the Sacred Lectionary, and so they are not studied here. Around those hours stands one great reading: the Passion, told four times. Matthew shows the Son who fulfils the Scriptures while innocent blood is argued over. Mark shows him stripped of every friend, and at that moment a Roman soldier says who he is. Luke shows mercy going on to the last breath. John shows a King who is enthroned on the Cross and says, “It is finished.”
We take the four together, as one reading in four voices. The key words are cup, king and finished.

set: All four Gospels slow down here. Weeks of ministry have passed in a few lines, and now the story moves hour by hour. Many scholars think that this was the first part of the Gospel story to be told as a continuous account, since the first Christians had to explain from the Scriptures why the Messiah had been crucified. Crucifixion was a Roman punishment, used for slaves and rebels and carried out in public as a warning. Only the Roman governor could order it, and Pontius Pilate held that office in Judea from about AD 26 to 36.

Matthew writes for readers who know the Scriptures, and he keeps saying that they are being fulfilled (26:54, 56; 27:9). Jesus is in command of what happens: he could call on more than twelve legions of angels, and does not (26:53). Matthew alone tells of Judas's end, Pilate's wife, and Pilate washing his hands, and he circles the question of “innocent blood” (27:4, 19, 24).

Mark is the starkest. Everyone leaves: “All of them deserted him and fled” (14:50). Jesus hardly speaks, and from the Cross Mark gives us only one saying, the cry of Psalm 22. Yet it is at this lowest point that the centurion speaks the title with which the Gospel opened (1:1; 15:39).

Luke's Passion is a Gospel of mercy to the end. Jesus heals the ear of the high priest's slave (22:51), looks at Peter (22:61), speaks to the women on the road (23:28), prays for those crucifying him (23:34), and receives a dying criminal. Pilate says three times that he finds no guilt in him (23:4, 14, 22), and the centurion sums it up: “Certainly this man was innocent” (23:47).

John begins after the Supper, in a garden, and shows a Jesus who goes forward to meet those who have come for him. There is no scene of Simon of Cyrene: he carries the Cross “by himself” (19:17). The long trial before Pilate turns on one word, “king”, and the Cross bears the title in three languages. When John says “the Jews” in these chapters, he mostly means the authorities in Jerusalem who pressed the case: Jesus, his Mother and the beloved disciple were all Jews themselves.
str: The plot and the betrayal: Matthew 26:1–16; Mark 14:1–11; Luke 22:1–6.
The Supper: Matthew 26:17–35; Mark 14:12–31; Luke 22:7–38.
The garden and the arrest: Matthew 26:36–56; Mark 14:32–52; Luke 22:39–53; John 18:1–11.
Before the high priest; Peter's denial: Matthew 26:57–27:10; Mark 14:53–72; Luke 22:54–71; John 18:12–27.
Before Pilate: Matthew 27:11–31; Mark 15:1–20; Luke 23:1–25; John 18:28–19:16.
The way and the Crucifixion: Matthew 27:32–44; Mark 15:21–32; Luke 23:26–43; John 19:16–27.
The death: Matthew 27:45–56; Mark 15:33–41; Luke 23:44–49; John 19:28–37.
The burial: Matthew 27:57–66; Mark 15:42–47; Luke 23:50–56; John 19:38–42.
kw: In the prophets the cup can be the portion God gives to drink in judgment (Isaiah 51:17). All four Gospels use the word at the arrest or in the garden. The cup that he dreads and the cup he gave at the table belong together.
Aramaic, the word of a child and a grown son or daughter to a father. Only Mark keeps it from Jesus' own lips (14:36). Paul says that the Spirit puts it on our lips too (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6).

The word John repeats in these chapters more than any other Gospel, from Pilate's first question (18:33) to the title on the Cross (19:19). The Catechism says that the true meaning of Jesus' kingship is revealed only when he is raised high on the Cross (CCC 440).

A word of Persian origin for a walled garden, used in the Greek Old Testament for Eden (Genesis 2:8). It occurs only three times in the New Testament (Luke 23:43; 2 Corinthians 12:4; Revelation 2:7). The first to be told he is going there is a dying criminal.

One Greek word, from telos, end or goal. It means completed, brought to its goal. John 13:1 prepared for it: “he loved them to the end (eis telos)”. It is not a sigh of exhaustion but the end of a work done.

John's phrase for the death of Jesus (19:30). The verb is the “handing over” that runs through the Passion. Now he himself does it. Many readers have also heard in it the gift of the Spirit promised for the hour of his glory (7:39).
vv: Abba, Father, for you all things are possible; remove this cup from me; yet, not what I want, but what you want.
Mark 14:36

The whole Passion is here in one sentence. He asks, as any human being would, and he consents. The Catechism sees in this prayer the human will of the Son in its full reality, making the Father's will its own (CCC 612).
Put your sword back into its place; for all who take the sword will perish by the sword.
Matthew 26:52
The first thing he does when he is seized is to protect his attackers from his friends. The way of his Kingdom cannot be defended by the means that killed him.
In his anguish he prayed more earnestly, and his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down on the ground.
Luke 22:44

A note on the text: vv. 43–44 are missing from some very old manuscripts and present in others, and the NRSV prints them in double brackets. The Fathers knew them from early on, and the Church reads them as Scripture.
Jesus said, “I am; and ‘you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the Power,’ and ‘coming with the clouds of heaven.’”
Mark 14:62
After a Gospel of silence about his identity, the answer comes at the moment when it can only cost him his life. He combines Psalm 110 and Daniel 7.
The Lord turned and looked at Peter.
Luke 22:61
Only Luke has it. No word is said. Peter goes out and weeps, and this look, and not his own courage, will make him the man who strengthens the others (22:32).
They answered, “Jesus of Nazareth.” Jesus replied, “I am he.”
John 18:5

In Greek it is egō eimi, “I am”, the words he has used of himself through this Gospel (8:58). John says that those who came to arrest him stepped back and fell to the ground (18:6). They take him only because he allows it (10:18).
My kingdom is not from this world.
John 18:36

It does not mean that his Kingdom has nothing to do with this world. It means that its source and its way of ruling do not come from here: his followers do not fight. Pilate goes on to ask, “What is truth?” (18:38), with the Truth standing in front of him.
Then Jesus said, “Father, forgive them; for they do not know what they are doing.”
Luke 23:34

A note on the text: this saying too is missing from some early manuscripts and is present in many others, and the NRSV brackets it. It is thoroughly in Luke's spirit, and Stephen echoes it (Acts 7:60). The Church has treasured it from early times.
Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.
Luke 23:42
He sees a king where everyone else sees a condemned man. He asks to be remembered, and he is given much more: “today you will be with me in Paradise” (23:43).
Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?
Mark 15:34

The opening of Psalm 22, in Aramaic. This is real desolation prayed in the words of Israel. The psalm moves toward the God who “did not hide his face from me, but heard when I cried to him” (22:24). See the question below.
At that moment the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom.
Matthew 27:51

“From top to bottom” suggests God's own act. Hebrews speaks of a new and living way opened for us through the curtain (10:19–20). Matthew alone goes on to say that the tombs were opened (27:52), so this death already has the Resurrection inside it.
Truly this man was God’s Son!
Mark 15:39
Mark says that the centurion “saw that in this way he breathed his last”. It is the manner of the death, not any miracle, that opens the eyes of this Gentile.
When Jesus saw his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing beside her, he said to his mother, “Woman, here is your son.”
John 19:26

Mary stands at the Cross. The title “Woman” recalls Cana (2:4), where his hour had not yet come. With “Here is your mother” (19:27) the Lord gives her to the disciple, and the Church has heard in this that she is given to all disciples (CCC 964, 2618; Lumen Gentium 58).
When Jesus had received the wine, he said, “It is finished.” Then he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.
John 19:30
He bows his head and then gives up his spirit. In John even this is an act, and he does it himself. The work the Father gave him is done (17:4).
Instead, one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once blood and water came out.
John 19:34
John swears to it (19:35) and points to the Passover lamb, none of whose bones were to be broken (19:36; Exodus 12:46). See how the Church reads it below.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christ's death is both the Paschal sacrifice which accomplishes the definitive redemption of mankind, and the sacrifice of the New Covenant (CCC 613). He went to it out of love for the Father and for us: he knew and loved each of us during his Passion, and gave himself up for each one of us (CCC 478, 616). The Church also says who bears the guilt: sinners were the authors of Christ's Passion, and she does not hesitate to give Christians the gravest responsibility for it (CCC 598). As Paul writes, “who loved me and gave himself for me” (Galatians 2:20).

St John Chrysostom teaches his newly baptized that the water and the blood from Jesus' side are the symbols of Baptism and the Mysteries, and that from these two the Church is born, as Eve from the side of Adam (Baptismal Catecheses 3, in substance). The Catechism says the same: the Church was born from the side of Christ asleep on the Cross (CCC 766; Sacrosanctum Concilium 5). St Augustine observes that John does not say “struck” or “wounded” but “opened”, so that the door of life is thrown wide (Tractates on John 120, in substance; the Latin Bible he read has “opened”). Mar Aprem sings that the spear which pierced Christ's side removed the sword that had barred the way to Paradise (in substance).

The Passion must always be read as the Church asks: without hatred. The Second Vatican Council teaches that what happened in the Passion cannot be charged against all the Jews then living, nor against the Jews of today, and that they are not to be presented as rejected or accursed (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597).

qa: What about “His blood be on us and on our children” (Matthew 27:25)?

Terrible things have been done with this verse, and the Church has clearly rejected them. It is the shout of one crowd at one moment, in a scene that Matthew shapes as Pilate's attempt to shift his own guilt. Many scholars think that Matthew's own painful situation, when his community was at odds with other Jewish teachers, colours how the scene is told. It does not lay any curse on a people (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597–598). Pope Benedict XVI recalled that for Christians the blood of Jesus is not a curse but a redemption: it speaks “a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24), and all of us stand in need of it (Jesus of Nazareth, Part II, in substance).
Did the Father really abandon Jesus on the Cross?

Jesus truly prays this, and we must not soften it. In the love that always united him to the Father, he took on himself our state of being far from God, so that he could cry out in our name. He was never rejected by the Father as if he himself had sinned (CCC 603). The words are the opening of a psalm, a prayer of faith that addresses the very God it feels far from: “My God, my God.” In the psalm the lament turns to praise. Luke gives us another psalm on his lips at the end, “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (23:46; Psalm 31:5).
Why are the four accounts different? Which one is right?

The Evangelists do not give us four police reports. Each writes from the memory of the Church and draws out a truth of the same event, and differences of detail are what one expects from several witnesses. The Church has refused to reduce them to one: she received four Gospels, and teaches that they tell “the honest truth about Jesus” while selecting and arranging according to the needs of their hearers (Dei Verbum 19). The traditional seven last words come from gathering what the Gospels preserve. Mark and Matthew give one, Luke three, John three.
rite: On this day there is no Holy Qurbono in our tradition. The altar is bare, because the one Sacrifice is contemplated on the Cross, and every Qurbono we celebrate makes this same sacrifice present. We read the hours from the Hasha Week book, venerate the Cross, keep fast and silence, and stand with Mary. The collection of the day goes to the Holy Land, as the Holy Father directs: we pray for all who live in that land, and for all who suffer in many lands.
study: Read one Passion account straight through today. Which moment stops you, and why?
Mark's Jesus is left by all, and Luke's forgives to the end. Which of these do I most need to see today?
“They do not know what they are doing.” Who is it hardest for me to say this about, and can I pray it?
The Church was born from the pierced side. How does this change the way I come to the font and to the altar?

lead: On Holy Saturday the Church stands before a closed tomb, and each of the three readings speaks out of that stillness. The lectionary prints the Old Testament lesson as Amos 6:10–14, where someone in a house of death whispers, “Hush!” Paul tells the baptized that they were buried with Christ so that they might walk in newness of life. Matthew shows a stone being sealed and a guard being posted, by men who remember the words about rising better than the disciples do. The line runs from a silence of judgement to a silence of hope, and its key words are hush, buried and sealed.

r.h: Hush, in the house of the dead
set: Amos was a herdsman from Tekoa in Judah who was sent to preach in the northern kingdom in the days of King Jeroboam II (1:1), in the eighth century before Christ. It was a time of wealth and of military success, and the prophet looked behind both. Chapter 6 opens against “those who are at ease in Zion” (6:1), the people who lie on ivory beds and drink wine from bowls “but are not grieved over the ruin of Joseph” (6:6).

Just before our reading the Lord swears that he will hand the city over, and adds, “If ten people remain in one house, they shall die” (6:9). Our verses begin inside such a house. Verse 10 is hard Hebrew and translators differ on its details, but the picture is clear: a relative comes for the dead, and finds one survivor hiding in the back of the house.
str: v. 10: the relative, the survivor, and the whispered “Hush!”
v. 11: great house and little house alike are broken.
v. 12: two absurd questions, and the charge: justice has been turned into poison.
v. 13: the boast over two captured towns.
v. 14: the Lord raises up a nation against Israel.
¶ The reason for the disaster stands in the middle. The ruin is not bad luck. It is what follows when a people twists justice and then trusts its own strength.
kw: A word that is almost a sound, like our “sh”. Amos uses it again in 8:3 (“Be silent!”). Habakkuk 2:20, Zephaniah 1:7 and Zechariah 2:13 use it for the silence of all creatures before the Lord.

The pair Amos cares about most: “let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream” (5:24). They mean fair dealing in court and right relations in daily life, above all toward the poor.

Two towns east of the Jordan, apparently won back in Jeroboam's wars. Amos plays on their names. Lo-debar sounds like “nothing”, and Karnaim means “two horns”, the horn being a sign of strength. They are boasting of a Nothing and of a strength that will not last.
vv: Hush! We must not mention the name of the Lord.

The survivor has been so struck by the disaster that he is afraid to pray. Most commentators take the meaning to be that speaking the Lord's name might draw his judgement down again. It is a terrible moment: the people who once called on that name now dare not say it.
See, the Lord commands, and the great house shall be shattered to bits, and the little house to pieces.
No one's house is safe, rich or poor, when a whole society has gone wrong.
Do horses run on rocks? Does one plow the sea with oxen?

A note on the text. The usual Hebrew reads as “Does one plow with oxen?”, which would not be an absurd question. By dividing one Hebrew word differently, most modern translators get “the sea with oxen”, as the NRSV does, and the Malayalam POC has the same sense. To turn justice into poison, says Amos, is as much against nature as ploughing the sea.
Have we not by our own strength taken Karnaim for ourselves?
Israel's true sin here is the words “by our own strength”. The God who gave the victories has dropped out of the story.
Indeed, I am raising up against you a nation, O house of Israel, says the Lord, the God of hosts,

Amos does not name the nation; history gives the name of Assyria, which took Samaria in 722/721 BC (2 Kings 17:6). The map in this verse, from Lebo-hamath to the Arabah, is the very territory that Jeroboam had won back (2 Kings 14:25). What they boasted of is what they will lose.
ch: The Catechism recalls the fierce words of Amos against those who buy the poor for silver (Amos 8:6) and says that Jesus does not soften them (CCC 2449). The prophet's first meaning must stand: it is a warning about injustice and false security, and it speaks to every age. Amos also does not end here. His last chapter promises, “On that day I will raise up the booth of David that is fallen” (9:11), and in the Acts of the Apostles James hears that promise at work when the Gentiles are welcomed into the Church (Acts 15:16). On this day of all days, the Christian ear also hears “Hush” differently. An ancient homily for Holy Saturday, quoted by the Catechism, begins: “Today a great silence reigns on earth” (CCC 635). That silence is not fear. The King is asleep, and the name of the Lord will soon be spoken again in joy.

r.h: Buried with him, alive to God
set: Most scholars think Paul wrote to the Romans from Corinth around AD 57, to a Church he had not founded and hoped to visit. In chapter 5 he has said that “where sin increased, grace abounded all the more” (5:20). That raises an obvious objection, and he states it himself: then why not go on sinning?

His answer does not begin with a rule but with an event. He reminds them of what happened to them in Baptism. For Paul, the believer's life has a before and an after, and the line between them runs through the death and burial of Christ.
str: vv. 1–2: the objection and the reply: “By no means!”
vv. 3–4: baptized into his death, buried with him, so as to walk in newness of life.
vv. 5–7: united with him in death and resurrection; the old self crucified.
vv. 8–10: Christ will never die again; death has no more dominion over him.
v. 11: the conclusion: count yourselves dead to sin and alive to God.
kw: One Greek word built on syn, “with”. Paul uses such “with” words again and again in this chapter: buried with, crucified with, live with. The Christian life is lived in company with Christ.
In verse 5 the word has the sense of “grown together”, as parts of a living thing grow together. Union with Christ is not only an imitation from outside.
Christ's death is never repeated, because it is complete (v. 10). Hebrews uses the same word of his entry into the sanctuary (Hebrews 9:12).
vv: Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?
The Greek word for baptize means to plunge or immerse. The Catechism says that the plunging into the water symbolizes burial into Christ's death (CCC 1214).
Therefore we have been buried with him by baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life.
This is the verse for today. Burial is not the end of the sentence, which ends in a way of walking. “Walk” is Paul's ordinary word for daily conduct.
We know that our old self was crucified with him so that the body of sin might be destroyed,
“Body of sin” does not mean that the human body is evil; our bodies will rise. It means the whole person as held under the power of sin. That self has been put to death with Christ.
For whoever has died is freed from sin.
The Greek says literally “has been justified from sin”. Sin is pictured as a master whose claim ends at death.
So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus.
Paul asks for a daily reckoning. What God has done in Baptism must be taken up by grace, in choices made every day.
ch: The Catechism uses this passage for Baptism: the believer enters into communion with Christ's death, is buried with him, and rises with him (CCC 1227). It also says that Baptism, whose original and full sign is immersion, signifies the descent into the tomb of the Christian who dies to sin with Christ in order to live a new life (CCC 628), and it uses verse 11 in its teaching on life in Christ (CCC 1694). St Cyril of Jerusalem told the newly baptized that the water of salvation was at once their grave and their mother (Mystagogical Catecheses 2, in substance). This is why Holy Saturday is the day to read this page: the tomb of Christ and the font of the Church belong together.

set: Only Matthew tells of the guard at the tomb. The Lord has been buried by Joseph of Arimathea, and Mary Magdalene and the other Mary sit opposite the tomb (27:57–61). Matthew then names the next day in an unusual way, “after the day of Preparation”. The Preparation is Friday, so this is the Sabbath.

Many scholars think that Matthew tells this story partly to answer a claim that was going round in his own day, that the disciples stole the body (28:13–15). He takes up the thread again after the Resurrection, so the two passages should be read together. The people in this scene are particular leaders in a particular moment. Neither Matthew nor the Church lays the events of the Passion on the Jewish people (CCC 597–598; Nostra Aetate 4).
str: v. 62: the chief priests and the Pharisees go to Pilate.
v. 63: they recall the words “After three days I will rise again.”
v. 64: the request, and the fear of a “last deception”.
v. 65: Pilate's short answer.
v. 66: the tomb is secured, the stone is sealed, and the guard is posted.
¶ This is the end of the Passion in Matthew. Everything human power can do has now been done.
kw: From a verb meaning to lead astray. It is the leaders' verdict on Jesus. Matthew lets the reader weigh it against what the angel says at the tomb (28:5–6).

A Latin word (custodia) in Greek letters. Pilate's “You have a guard” can also be taken in Greek as “Take a guard”, so scholars discuss whether these are Temple police or Roman soldiers. The mention of the governor in 28:14 inclines many to think they were Roman.
Probably a cord across the stone, fixed with clay or wax and an official mark, so that any tampering would show. The seal does not make the stone heavier. It makes it a matter of public record.
vv: Sir, we remember what that impostor said while he was still alive, ‘After three days I will rise again.’
The ones who remember are the Lord's opponents. Nowhere on this day does Matthew say that the disciples recalled his promise (16:21; 17:23; 20:19). It is a small and humbling irony.
and the last deception would be worse than the first.
Without meaning to, they state what is at stake. If he rose, all that he taught stands. Paul will say the same from the other side (1 Corinthians 15:14).
Pilate said to them, “You have a guard of soldiers; go, make it as secure as you can.”
“As secure as you can”: the phrase hangs in the air. The reader knows that there is a limit to what anyone can make secure.
So they went with the guard and made the tomb secure by sealing the stone.

The last line of the Passion. By the next chapter's dawn the stone is rolled away, and “the guards shook and became like dead men” (28:4). The living guards lie as if dead, at the tomb of the One who was dead and now lives.
ch: St John Chrysostom, preaching on Matthew, points out that these precautions only strengthen the proof: with a seal and a guard, no one can claim that the body was quietly removed (in substance). The Church's own attention on this day goes to the Lord who lies in the tomb. The Catechism says that his stay there is the real link between his state of suffering and his glorious state after the Resurrection (CCC 625), and it names this day as “God's great sabbath rest” after the fulfilment of man's salvation (CCC 624). The body in the tomb did not see corruption, because the divine person kept hold of both soul and body in death (CCC 627, 630).

qa: What does “he descended to the dead” mean?

The word in Scripture is Sheol or Hades, the realm of all the dead, who were deprived of the vision of God while they awaited the Redeemer (CCC 632–633). Jesus truly died and went there as Saviour, proclaiming the good news to those who had waited (1 Peter 3:19; 4:6). The Catechism is careful: he did not go down to deliver the damned or to destroy the hell of damnation, but to set the just who had gone before him at liberty (CCC 633). Eastern icons show him breaking the gates and raising Adam and Eve by the hand. So Holy Saturday is not an empty day between two great days. It is the hidden part of the victory.
Why is such a harsh prophecy read on Holy Saturday?

The lectionary does not give its reason, and we should not pretend to know it. Amos is first of all a warning against injustice, and it should be heard as one. But set beside the closed tomb, its picture of a house of death, of whispered fear, and of a name no one dares to say, helps us feel what a world without the Resurrection would be. The Christian hears it knowing that this silence will be broken.
If Baptism means we have died to sin, why do we still sin?

Baptism truly takes away original sin and all personal sin, but it leaves in us certain consequences of sin, among them an inclination to sin that Tradition calls concupiscence. This is left for us “to wrestle with” by the grace of Christ (CCC 1263–1264). That is why Paul, right after saying that we have died to sin, goes on to say, “do not let sin exercise dominion” (6:12). We become by grace what we already are by Baptism, and the Sacrament of Reconciliation is there for the road.
rite: Our Antiochene and Syriac tradition loves to look into Sheol on this day. Mar Aprem, in his Nisibene Hymns, gives Death himself a voice: he complains that this one dead man has undone his kingdom, and that those he held have heard a voice calling them out (in substance). The tomb is seen from below, as a defeat for Death. The Church keeps the day in quiet with Mary, the mother of the Lord, and as evening comes it prepares for Qyomtho. This is a good day for families to speak about their own Baptism, to learn its date, and to pray for those they have buried.
