study: Amos accuses people who say “by our own strength”. Where in my life do I speak of God's gifts as my own achievement?
Do I know the date of my Baptism? What would it mean this year to “walk in newness of life” in one concrete thing?
The opponents in Matthew remembered the Lord's words about rising, and the disciples seemed to have forgotten them. Which of his promises have I let slip out of memory?
How does the belief that Christ went down to the dead change the way I pray for my own departed?

lead: Qyomtho is the Syriac word for resurrection, and today every reading of the Church's rich table leans toward it. The Evening Gospel (Matthew 28:1–10) gives the angel's word, “He is not here; for he has been raised, as he said.” Four Old Testament lessons follow. Exodus 40:17–23 sets up the tabernacle on the first day of the first month. Sirach 30:21–25 speaks of the joyful heart. Daniel 6:18–24 brings a man up alive from a sealed pit at daybreak. Isaiah 57:14–21 proclaims, “Peace, peace, to the far and the near.” Then in Acts 2:29–36 Peter says, “This Jesus God raised up, and of that all of us are witnesses.”

We study three of these closely. Daniel is the lesson nearest to the Gospel, with its stone, its seal and its dawn. Paul gives the oldest written list we have of the Lord's appearances. John takes us to the empty tomb itself, with two men running and linen lying where it had been left. The line runs from a sealed pit to an open tomb, and its key words are daybreak, witness and saw and believed.

r.h: Brought up from the pit at daybreak
set: The book of Daniel sets this story in Babylon under “Darius the Mede” (5:31), and chapter 6 belongs to the part of the book written in Aramaic (2:4b–7:28). Many scholars think the book reached its final form in the persecution under Antiochus IV, around 167–164 BC, using older tales of faithful Jews at a foreign court. Whatever its date, its purpose is plain: to strengthen people who must choose between their God and the power of the state.

Daniel's offence was prayer. He went on praying three times a day, with his windows open toward Jerusalem, despite the decree against it (6:10). The king, who respected him, was caught by his own unchangeable law. The verse just before our reading says, “A stone was brought and laid on the mouth of the den, and the king sealed it with his own signet” (6:17).
str: v. 18: the king's sleepless night.
vv. 19–20: at daybreak he hurries to the pit and calls out.
vv. 21–22: Daniel answers: an angel shut the lions' mouths.
v. 23: Daniel is brought up unharmed, because he trusted.
v. 24: those who accused him meet the fate they planned for him.
kw: A pit in the ground, covered here with a stone (6:17). For the Christian reader, a closed hollow with a sealed stone on it is hard to read today without thinking of another place.

The king twice calls Daniel the one who serves God “continually” (6:16, 20), which the NRSV renders “faithfully serve”. The word is used for worship as well as work. Daniel's whole life is one act of service.
This is the title on the king's lips at the mouth of the pit (6:20), and the king repeats it in his decree (6:26). The question of the chapter is whether Daniel's God is alive and can act.
vv: Then the king went to his palace and spent the night fasting; no food was brought to him,

A note on the text. The Aramaic word rendered “food” occurs only here, and its meaning is uncertain. Translators have guessed at food, entertainment or music. The Malayalam POC says that he gave up all his diversions. Either way, the point is the same: the king cannot rest.
Then, at break of day, the king got up and hurried to the den of lions.
The hurrying at daybreak toward a sealed place is a detail that speaks to us on this morning, when the women come to the tomb and the disciples run.
O Daniel, servant of the living God, has your God whom you faithfully serve been able to deliver you from the lions?
A pagan king asks the true Easter question: is this God able?
My God sent his angel and shut the lions’ mouths so that they would not hurt me,
Hebrews remembers those who by faith “shut the mouths of lions” (Hebrews 11:33). The credit here goes to God, not to Daniel's courage.
So Daniel was taken up out of the den, and no kind of harm was found on him, because he had trusted in his God.

The words “taken up” help us to hear this lesson today. The difference must also be kept in view: Daniel was kept from death, whereas Christ truly died and passed through death to a life that does not end.
ch: The Church reads the Old Testament in the light of Christ, and the Catechism calls this typology, while warning that it must not make us forget the Old Testament's own value as Revelation (CCC 128–129). Daniel between the lions is one of the most common pictures in the earliest Christian art, including the catacombs, as a sign of deliverance from death. Aphrahat, the Persian Sage, one of the earliest Syriac Fathers, sets Daniel beside Jesus: the one went down into the lions' pit and came up, and the other went down into the deep pit of Sheol and came up, and death had no dominion over him (Demonstrations 21, in substance). So from very early the Syriac Church was reading this pit with the Lord's tomb in mind.

r.h: What Paul received and handed on
set: Paul writes from Ephesus (16:8), in the mid-50s, to a lively and divided Church he had founded. Some there were saying “there is no resurrection of the dead” (15:12). Rather than begin with an argument, he reminds them of what they first received. The Catechism notes that this was written about AD 56, and that Paul is speaking of the living tradition he had himself received after his conversion (CCC 639).

Many scholars think that verses 3–5 are a formula older than the letter, one Paul was given and is now passing on. He had gone up to Jerusalem “to visit Cephas” within a few years of his conversion (Galatians 1:18). This carries us very close to the events themselves.
str: vv. 1–2: the good news you received, in which you stand.
vv. 3–5: the tradition: died, buried, raised, appeared.
vv. 6–7: more witnesses: the five hundred, James, all the apostles.
vv. 8–10: last of all, Paul himself, and the grace that made him what he is.
v. 11: one proclamation, one faith.
¶ This is the chapter's foundation. The long argument about the resurrection of our own bodies is built on it.
kw: The words used for passing on a sacred tradition, the same pair Paul uses of the Eucharist (11:23). The Gospel is received and handed on. It is not invented by each generation.

Paul's other verbs here describe past events: died, was buried. This one is in a Greek tense that also speaks of a state that goes on: he was raised, and he remains risen. The passive voice points to the Father's act, while the Catechism also teaches that the Son rose by his own divine power (CCC 648–649).

Literally “he was seen” or “he let himself be seen”. The word comes four times (vv. 5, 6, 7, 8). It speaks of the initiative of the risen Lord. These people did not go looking for this meeting and bring it about.

A rare word found only here in the New Testament. It means a birth out of its proper time, even a miscarriage, and it may have been an insult that Paul takes on himself. He does not rank himself with the others by right.
vv: For I handed on to you as of first importance what I in turn had received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the scriptures, and that he was buried, and that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the scriptures,

Here is the Creed in seed. “In accordance with the scriptures” means that these events fulfil God's long purpose. Paul names no text; Isaiah 53 and Hosea 6:2 are often proposed. The burial, mentioned so plainly, shows a real death and a real body.
and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve.
Cephas is the Aramaic form of Peter's name. Luke too preserves the early cry, “he has appeared to Simon!” (Luke 24:34). “The twelve” is a title for the group, even though Judas was gone.
Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers and sisters at one time, most of whom are still alive,
“Still alive”: Paul is, in effect, saying that the witnesses can be asked. The Resurrection is presented as something that happened, with people who can speak of it.
But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me has not been in vain.

The persecutor became an apostle. Paul says that he worked harder than any of them, then at once corrects himself: “though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me.” Here human labour and God's grace are not rivals.
ch: The Catechism calls the Resurrection “the crowning truth of our faith” and treats this passage as its earliest testimony (CCC 638–639). It teaches that the Resurrection is a real, historical event with manifestations that can be verified, and also a mystery that passes beyond history (CCC 639, 647). The Creed of Nicaea and Constantinople, in its Greek text, takes its words from this passage: “on the third day he rose again in accordance with the Scriptures.” Paul goes on to say bluntly that if Christ has not been raised, “your faith has been in vain” (15:14). The Church has never softened that. The “James” of verse 7 is the one Paul calls “the Lord's brother” (Galatians 1:19), and the Church understands “brother” here in the wider biblical sense of a close relation (CCC 500).

set: John has told of the burial in a garden near the place of crucifixion, with linen wrappings and a great weight of spices (19:39–42). Now it is the first day of the week, and “still dark”. In this Gospel the darkness is more than the time of day; it is the state of the world before the light is recognized.

Mary Magdalene comes alone in John's telling, though her “we do not know” in verse 2 may hint at other women, as in the other Gospels. She draws the natural conclusion: someone has moved the body. No one in this passage expects a resurrection. That is itself part of its witness.
str: vv. 1–2: Mary Magdalene sees the stone removed and runs to tell the two disciples.
vv. 3–5: the two run; the other disciple arrives first, looks in, and waits.
vv. 6–7: Peter goes in and sees the wrappings and the head cloth.
v. 8: the other disciple goes in, “and he saw and believed”.
vv. 9–10: the note on Scripture, and the return home.
kw: The same word used for the burial cloths in 19:40. They are still there. A thief would have had no reason to leave them behind.
From the Latin sudarium, a face cloth. Lazarus came out of his tomb with such a cloth still on his face (11:44), since he was returning to a life that would end. Jesus has left his behind.

John uses three different verbs in this passage: the other disciple looks in and sees (v. 5); Peter sees and takes note (v. 6); and the other disciple sees and believes (v. 8). One should not press the differences too far, since John likes variety in such words, but the passage does move from looking to believing.
vv: Early on the first day of the week, while it was still dark, Mary Magdalene came to the tomb and saw that the stone had been removed from the tomb.
The first day: the day of creation's beginning, and from now on the Lord's Day. As preachers have often said, the stone was moved so that witnesses could go in, not so that he could come out.
The two were running together, but the other disciple outran Peter and reached the tomb first.

Christian tradition identifies this disciple with John, though the Gospel keeps him unnamed. A common reading among preachers is that love runs fastest. Yet he waits, and Peter is the first to enter. Love and office in the Church do not compete.
and the cloth that had been on Jesus’ head, not lying with the linen wrappings but rolled up in a place by itself.

St John Chrysostom reasons that those who steal a body do not first take time to strip it and fold the cloths (in substance). The detail has the feel of an eyewitness who remembered exactly what he saw.
Then the other disciple, who reached the tomb first, also went in, and he saw and believed;

He has not yet seen the risen Lord. He sees an absence with a certain shape to it, and he believes. This is the first Easter faith in John's Gospel, and it stands close to the blessing still to come: “Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe” (20:29).
for as yet they did not understand the scripture, that he must rise from the dead.
Faith comes first here and understanding later. That is why the Lord will open the Scriptures to his disciples, and why the Church reads so many of them today.
ch: The Catechism says that the empty tomb is not by itself a direct proof, since the absence of Christ's body could be explained otherwise, but that it is still an essential sign and the first step toward recognizing the Resurrection. It adds that the beloved disciple's “he saw and believed” suggests he realized that the absence of the body could not be of human doing, and that Jesus had not simply returned to earthly life as Lazarus had (CCC 640). It also notes that Mary Magdalene and the holy women were the first to meet the risen Lord and thus became the first messengers of the Resurrection to the apostles themselves (CCC 641). St Thomas Aquinas, in his commentary on John, calls her “apostle of the apostles”.

qa: Paul lists those who saw the risen Lord. Why does he not mention the women?

Paul does not explain this. He is handing on a short summary, and it does not say that its list is complete. Many scholars think that it records those whose testimony counted officially in the public preaching of the Church. The Gospels do not leave the women out: all four place them first at the tomb, and the Catechism says plainly that they were the first messengers of the Resurrection (CCC 641). The two accounts complement one another.
What did the beloved disciple believe, if he did not yet understand the Scripture?

St Augustine took the words narrowly: he believed what Mary had said, that the body was gone (in substance). Most readers, ancient and modern, and the Catechism too (CCC 640), understand a real beginning of faith in the Resurrection. The note in verse 9 is then saying that this faith did not come from a clear grasp of the prophecies, which came only later. It came from what he saw at the tomb.
The reading from Daniel ends with whole families thrown to the lions. How should we hear that?

The verse describes the decision of a king of that time, in a world in which whole families shared a man's punishment. The text does not say that God commanded it. Vatican II teaches that the Old Testament contains “some things which are incomplete and temporary” (Dei Verbum 15), and that we must pay attention to literary forms (Dei Verbum 12). The story's lesson is that evil plots fall back on those who make them. Christ, the one who was raised, prayed on the Cross for those who crucified him (Luke 23:34), and no Christian can take this verse as a pattern.
rite: Our tradition keeps the great joy of Qyomtho, and the Church now enters the season that takes its name. This first week is Hevoro week, “white” week. White is the colour of Easter joy and of the Baptism we recalled yesterday, since the white garment says that the baptized person has put on Christ (CCC 1243). Each Holy Qurbono in the Antiochene tradition carries this morning within it: after the words of institution the people answer, in substance, “We remember your death, O Lord; we confess your resurrection; and we await your second coming.” The Catechism calls Easter the “feast of feasts” (CCC 1169). A sermon that bears the name of St John Chrysostom, priest of Antioch before he was bishop of Constantinople, cries out on this day that Christ is risen and life reigns (in substance). In this spirit Christians greet one another this morning: Christ is risen.
study: Daniel was carried through the night by his trust in God. What dark or sealed place in my life do I need to bring to the God who is able to deliver?
Paul says, “by the grace of God I am what I am”. What in my own story can only be explained in this way?
The beloved disciple saw very little, and believed. What small signs of the risen Lord have I seen this year?
Who first handed on the faith to me? To whom am I handing it on, “as of first importance”?

lead: Hevoro week is kept as one great day of Easter joy. On its first weekday Paul tells the baptized that they now belong to the one who has been raised, and that they may bear fruit for God. Matthew shows the other response to the same morning: a report that is paid to change. One reading says what the Resurrection does to a life, and the other shows how far some were willing to go to keep it out.

r.h: Belonging to the one who has been raised
set: Paul has just said that the baptized have died to sin (chapter 6). Now he goes one step further, and speaks to “those who know the law” (7:1). The law he means is the Law of Moses, which, he insists a few verses later, “is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good” (7:12). His question is not whether the Law is good but whether it has the power to give life. On its own it can name sin but cannot give the strength to overcome it.
str: vv. 1–3: the example: a wife is released from the law of marriage when her husband dies.
v. 4: the application: you have died to the law through the body of Christ, so as to belong to another.
vv. 5–6: then and now: fruit for death, and the new life of the Spirit.

¶ The comparison is not exact, since in the example the husband dies and in the application the believer does. Paul is using a single point: death ends a legal bond and makes a new belonging possible.
kw: Literally “you were put to death”. The form is passive. It happened to them in union with the crucified body of Christ, as chapter 6 has explained.
The word appears in both v. 4 and v. 5. Everyone's life bears fruit of some kind, and the question is for whom. The image may also follow on from the marriage comparison.
The same word as “newness of life” in 6:4. Here it is the newness of the Spirit, set against the oldness of the letter.
vv: In the same way, my friends, you have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, to him who has been raised from the dead
“Through the body of Christ” most naturally means his body given up on the Cross. The goal is not independence but belonging. The Christian changes from one bond to a better one.
But now we are discharged from the law, dead to that which held us captive, so that we are slaves not under the old written code but in the new life of the Spirit.

“Written code” is gramma, the letter, as in “the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:6). Paul does not mean that Christians may now do as they please. The next chapter says that the just requirement of the law is fulfilled in those who walk by the Spirit (8:4).
ch: The Catechism says that the Old Law is holy and is the first stage on the way to the Kingdom, but that it shows what must be done without of itself giving the strength to do it (CCC 1962–1963). It calls the New Law “the grace of the Holy Spirit given to the faithful through faith in Christ” (CCC 1966). St Augustine, in his work On the Spirit and the Letter, argues from this teaching that the commandment without grace cannot bring us to life, and that with grace it is fulfilled in love (in substance). None of this sets Christians above the people of Israel, to whom, as Paul says, the Law and the promises belong (Romans 9:4).

r.h: The report that was paid for
set: These verses complete the story of the guard that began on Holy Saturday (27:62–66). The women have just left the tomb, have met the risen Lord and are on their way to the disciples (28:8–10). Matthew deliberately cuts from them to the soldiers: “While they were going, some of the guard went into the city.” Both groups are carrying news from the same tomb.
str: v. 11: some of the guard report everything to the chief priests.
vv. 12–14: the plan, the money, and a promise of protection.
v. 15: they take the money, and the story spreads.
kw: Literally “silver”, the same word as the pieces of silver paid to Judas (26:15; 27:6). Matthew's account of the Passion opens and closes with money that buys betrayal and falsehood.
In Greek there is no “the”. Matthew is noting a story current in some circles in his own time, as a historian would, and is not making a statement about a whole people.
vv: some of the guard went into the city and told the chief priests everything that had happened.
The first to report what happened at the tomb to those in power are the soldiers. So the truth was told before it was hidden.
You must say, ‘His disciples came by night and stole him away while we were asleep.’

St Augustine, preaching on the Psalms, gently mocks the story: if they were asleep, how can they say what happened (in substance)? Sleeping witnesses are no witnesses. The very claim admits that the tomb was empty.
So they took the money and did as they were directed. And this story is still told among the Jews to this day.
St Justin Martyr, in the second century, also knows of this claim (Dialogue with Trypho 108). Yet the phrase should not be turned against the Jewish people, then or now (see the question below).
ch: The Church's confidence in the Resurrection does not rest on an argument about guards. It rests on the witness of those who met the risen Lord (CCC 642). Still, the empty tomb remains a real sign (CCC 640), and even the story told here against the Resurrection takes for granted that the tomb was empty. The Church reads the passage above all as a warning about what people can do to a truth that is inconvenient, a warning to Christians first of all.

qa: Does verse 15 blame the Jewish people for not believing?

No. Matthew describes a particular group of leaders and a particular story. The first believers in the Resurrection, the women, the Twelve, and Paul himself, were all Jews. The Second Vatican Council teaches that what happened in the Passion cannot be charged against all Jews then alive or against the Jews of today (Nostra Aetate 4), and the Catechism says the same (CCC 597–598). Many scholars think that Matthew writes at a time of painful disagreement in the late first century, and we should read his words with that in mind.
study: Paul says that the question is who I belong to. In what part of my life am I still living under the “old written code”, merely keeping rules without love?
Have I ever been offered a reward, large or small, to change what I knew to be true? What helps me to tell the truth when it costs me something?

lead: Paul gives the Church her Easter vocabulary: “our paschal lamb, Christ, has been sacrificed”, so “let us celebrate the festival”, and he says that this feast must be kept in daily life. The Gospel, from Mark, speaks of a lamp that is meant for the lampstand and of hidden things that are to come to light. Both fit this white week: what was done in the dark of the tomb is now to shine, and a clean life is the way it shines.

r.h: Our paschal lamb has been sacrificed
set: Paul is dealing with a scandal at Corinth. A man is living with his father's wife, and Paul finds the community “arrogant” about it (5:1–2). Paul has told them to put him out, with the hope that “his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord” (5:5). Now he turns to the community, and he reaches for the Passover.

Every Jewish household knew this image and many still keep the custom: before the feast the house is cleared of leaven (Exodus 12:15). Paul is writing from Ephesus and plans to stay until Pentecost (16:8), so some scholars think that Passover was near, or at least on his mind.
str: v. 6: a little yeast works through the whole batch.
v. 7: clear out the old yeast; you are unleavened; Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.
v. 8: so let us keep the feast with sincerity and truth.
kw: Yeast here is a picture of something small that spreads through everything, so it stands for corruption that is tolerated. In itself it is not evil: Jesus uses it for the Kingdom in Matthew 13:33.
The word can mean the feast or the lamb, and here it is the lamb. It comes from the Hebrew pesaḥ through Aramaic, and our own word Pesaha keeps it.
The verb is in a form that suggests continuing action: let us go on keeping the feast. Paul is speaking of a whole way of life.
vv: Clean out the old yeast so that you may be a new batch, as you really are unleavened.
Paul uses the same pattern as Romans 6: become what you already are. The grace comes first, and then the command.
For our paschal lamb, Christ, has been sacrificed.

One of the earliest written statements that Christ's death is a Passover. It is given in passing, as something that the Corinthians already know. The Lord's death is treated as a sacrifice that sets people at liberty, just as the blood of the lamb marked the night of Israel's going out.
Therefore, let us celebrate the festival, not with the old yeast, the yeast of malice and evil, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.
Eilikrineia, “sincerity”, is the quality of something pure and unmixed. The feast is kept not only at the altar but also in honest dealing.
ch: The Second Vatican Council quotes this verse: as often as the sacrifice of the Cross, by which “Christ our Pasch has been sacrificed”, is celebrated on the altar, the work of our redemption is carried out (Lumen Gentium 3; CCC 1364). St John Chrysostom, preaching on this passage, says that for Christians the whole of time is a festival because of the good things given to them, and that for this reason it must be kept in purity (in substance). So Pesaha is not over: each Holy Qurbono is the feast that Paul invites us to keep.

set: Jesus is teaching from a boat beside the sea (4:1). He has told the parable of the sower and explained it to those around him (4:1–20). These sayings follow, and several of them also appear in other settings in Matthew and Luke (Matthew 5:15; 7:2; Luke 11:33), so it seems that Mark has gathered them here to go with the theme of hearing.
str: vv. 21–23: the lamp, the hidden things, and the call to listen.
vv. 24–25: pay attention; the measure; to those who have, more will be given.
kw: A small clay oil lamp. In Greek the verse says, oddly, “Does the lamp come…?”, and many commentators think that Mark's wording hints at Jesus himself, the one who has come.
A household grain measure of a little under nine litres, from the Latin modius. The Malayalam POC's para gives the familiar Kerala equivalent.
The same household picture carries over into v. 24. How much you bring to the word is how much you take away from it.
vv: Is a lamp brought in to be put under the bushel basket, or under the bed, and not on the lampstand?
The question is put in a way that expects the answer: no one would do such a thing. The answer is obvious, and that is the point.
For there is nothing hidden, except to be disclosed; nor is anything secret, except to come to light.

In Mark, Jesus often asks for silence about who he is, and he gives the reason in 9:9: until “after the Son of Man had risen from the dead”. So in Easter week this saying finds its time. The secret is out, and it is to be told.
Pay attention to what you hear; the measure you give will be the measure you get, and still more will be given you.
Matthew 7:2 uses this saying of judging others. Here Mark applies it to listening. Attention given to the word comes back with interest. God is not a strict accountant: “still more will be given”.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus' invitation to enter his Kingdom comes in the form of parables, and that one must do more than hear them, one must enter the mystery they speak of (CCC 546). The Second Vatican Council begins its teaching on the Church by saying that Christ is the light of the nations (Lumen Gentium 1), and the Catechism adds the Fathers' favourite image: the Church is like the moon, all its light reflected from the sun (CCC 748). The Church is the lampstand, not the lamp.

qa: Paul speaks of unleavened bread. Why do we use leavened bread at the Holy Qurbono?

Paul's image here is about moral life. He is not giving a rule about bread for the altar. The Churches of the East and West have kept different customs: the Latin Church uses unleavened bread, while the Antiochene Syriac tradition has kept leavened bread. The Council of Florence said that the Body of Christ is truly confected in wheat bread, whether leavened or unleavened, and that priests should follow the custom of their own Church (Laetentur Caeli, 1439). Both customs are ancient, and both are honoured.
study: What small “old yeast” have I learned to tolerate at home or at work because it seems harmless? What would it mean to clear it out in this white week?
How is the faith I have received being kept “under the bushel basket”? Who around me might need to see its light?

lead: Today's readings are about keeping going and about what cannot be done alone. Timothy is told to fight the good fight with faith and a good conscience, because some have made a wreck of theirs. A man runs up to Jesus, is looked at with love, and walks away grieving. The disciples ask, “Then who can be saved?” In Easter week the answer has particular force: the God for whom all things are possible has just emptied a tomb.

r.h: Fight the good fight; keep the ship whole
set: Timothy has been left at Ephesus to deal with false teachers (1:3). The letter comes to us under Paul's name, and the Church has received it as Scripture. Many modern scholars think that it was written by a follower in Paul's name after his death, while others defend Paul's own authorship; either way, the Church receives its teaching as the word of God. These verses gather up the “instruction” mentioned in 1:5 and bring the first chapter to an end.
str: v. 18: the charge to Timothy, in line with earlier prophecies about him.
v. 19: faith and a good conscience; some have been shipwrecked.
v. 20: Hymenaeus and Alexander, handed over to Satan so that they may learn.
kw: A military image: literally “serve the good campaign”. Compare 2 Timothy 4:7, where the same English phrase renders a Greek word taken from athletics.
The inner witness to what is right. In this letter it is paired with sincere faith (1:5). Faith and conscience stand or fall together.
Paul knew the real thing: “Three times I was shipwrecked” (2 Corinthians 11:25). It is a vivid word for losing one's faith, which is damage that can be done, not merely a change of opinion.
vv: in accordance with the prophecies made earlier about you,

These are probably the words spoken when he was set apart for ministry: “which was given to you through prophecy with the laying on of hands” (4:14). What sustains a minister is the gift he has been given.
having faith and a good conscience. By rejecting conscience, certain persons have suffered shipwreck in the faith;
The order matters. It is the rejection of conscience that wrecks faith. People who go on living against what they know to be right often end by changing what they believe.
whom I have turned over to Satan, so that they may learn not to blaspheme.

This is a severe act, like the one in 1 Corinthians 5:5: being put out of the community into the realm outside it. The purpose is still healing. “Learn” is the verb for teaching or disciplining a child. 2 Timothy 2:17–18 names a Hymenaeus who claimed “that the resurrection has already taken place”, which is a striking link for Easter week. We cannot be sure whether the Alexander here is the coppersmith of 2 Timothy 4:14.
ch: The Catechism quotes these verses when it teaches that faith is a gift that can be lost, and that we must beg the Lord to increase it and must nourish it with the word of God (CCC 162). It cites 1 Timothy 1:5 to say that a good and pure conscience is enlightened by true faith (CCC 1794). The Church's practice of excommunication is meant to be medicinal, with the hope of return (compare CCC 1463). Ministry in the Church is received by the laying on of hands, as Timothy received it (CCC 1590).

set: Jesus is on the road toward Jerusalem, and in chapters 8–10 he three times tells his disciples what awaits him there. The man's story stands between the blessing of the children (10:13–16) and the third of these announcements (10:32–34). Matthew calls him young (19:20), and Luke calls him a ruler (18:18), while Mark only says that he had many possessions. Only Mark says that he ran and knelt, and only Mark says that Jesus loved him.
str: vv. 17–20: the question, the commandments, and “I have kept all these”.
vv. 21–22: the look of love, the call, and the grieving departure.
vv. 23–25: how hard it is; the camel and the needle.
vv. 26–27: “Then who can be saved?” God's possibility.
kw: Emblepō is to look intently. The call comes out of this love. It is not the demand of a hard master. The same look returns in v. 27 for the frightened disciples.

The largest animal in the land and the smallest opening anyone could think of: a picture of what cannot be done. The popular story about a low gate in Jerusalem called the “Needle's Eye” has no ancient support, and the point is impossibility, not difficulty.
The word of the last line. It is the same word Jesus uses in Gethsemane: “for you all things are possible” (14:36).
vv: Why do you call me good? No one is good but God alone.
See the question below. Jesus directs the man's attention to God, who alone is the source of good.
Jesus, looking at him, loved him and said, “You lack one thing; go, sell what you own, and give the money to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.”

The last two words are what it all leads to. Selling is the way to clear the road, and the goal is following. This is a personal call, one that the Church has seen as the root of religious poverty, while all are called to detachment of heart (CCC 2544–2545).
When he heard this, he was shocked and went away grieving, for he had many possessions.
He is the only person in Mark who is called this way and walks away. Mark does not tell us how his story ended, and we should not decide it for him.
For mortals it is impossible, but not for God; for God all things are possible.

Salvation is God's gift first of all, and whatever we do toward it is done by his grace. This is said not to the rich alone but to all. The way is open only by grace, and grace can even open a closed hand.
ch: The Catechism uses the encounter as its introduction to the Ten Commandments (CCC 2052–2053), and St John Paul II opens his encyclical Veritatis Splendor with it, in Matthew's form. The Catechism also cites the same saying, “for him all things are possible” (Matthew 19:26), in teaching that the Church prays that no one be lost (CCC 1058). Clement of Alexandria wrote a whole sermon on this Gospel, Who Is the Rich Man That Is Saved?, arguing that what the Lord asks above all is to strip the soul of its disordered attachment to wealth, and that possessions used well serve others (in substance). St Athanasius tells how St Antony heard this call read in church, and how he took it as spoken to himself.

qa: Is Jesus denying that he himself is good, or that he is God?

No. Nowhere does Mark doubt the goodness of Jesus. The man has used “Good” rather lightly, as a compliment, and Jesus is asking him to think about what the word means. Since God alone is good, the man is being led toward a question: who then is this? St John Chrysostom explains that the Lord is raising him up by degrees (in substance). The call that follows, “follow me”, is something that only God has the right to ask.
study: Where has my conscience been telling me something that I have stopped listening to? What is the danger to my faith in that?
Jesus looked at this man and loved him before he asked anything of him. What is the “one thing” I would find hardest to leave if he asked it of me today?
